email_papers.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
email_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present

Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments
Yao et al. (2023)
;
Zhou et al. (2024)
. As these tasks grow more complex, multi-agent systems (MAS) offer a way to divide work among agents with complementary roles. Instead of asking one agent to plan, gather information, act, and verify every step, MAS can organize these activities through specialization, parallel exploration, and iterative feedback. Systems such as AutoGen, MetaGPT, ChatDev, and Magentic-One demonstrate how agents can coordinate their contributions toward a shared task
Wu et al. (2023)
;
Hong et al. (2024)
;
Qian et al. (2024)
;
Fourney et al. (2024)
.
However, the collaboration that makes MAS useful also reshapes LLM serving demand; its diverse, framework-specific patterns hinder reusable workload construction. Conventional serving treats model requests as independent arrivals, while a single-agent workflow typically follows one evolving interaction. In MAS, requests may depend on other agents’ progress and outputs: parallel branches may release several calls together, synchronization may delay downstream calls, and refinement or debate may trigger repeated exchanges. Agents may inherit histories, share intermediate results, or build new contexts for later calls, changing opportunities for reuse
Bian et al. (2026a)
;
Bian et al. (2026b)
. Thus, even tasks with similar request counts and token lengths can differ in request readiness, batching opportunities, and memory demand (Fig.
1
). These differences arise from task structure, not merely scheduling decisions; request traces record the realized work, not the collaboration rules generating it.
Collaboration shapes serving demand in two distinct ways.

Work generation
determines which model calls, inputs, and token lengths emerge as agents coordinate and exchange results.

Figure
2
illustrates this abstraction; §
4
describes its realization and replay.
3.1

Experimental Setup
We use vLLM and vLLM-Ascend on the GPU/NPU platforms in Table
4
, with BF16, tensor parallelism one, and one exposed accelerator per serving instance. Qwen3.5 combines recurrent linear and full attention; Qwen3-8B
Yang et al. (2025)
provides full-attention workloads.
Seven structures cover the four templates, two compositions (Spawn–Fork–Join–Refinement and Fork–Join–Debate–Refinement), and a research–review–writing Sequence. Thirty shared task bindings retain generated artifacts and natural output lengths across code, reasoning, finance, evidence processing, and science.
Three-block native runs use 32/64/128 users, each issuing one ordinary call or executing a MAS workflow. Three paired Qwen3-8B/910C blocks fix work and arrivals for release/resource interventions. The GPU composition study limits requests to 64. Fixed-work serving evaluations use length-locked replay unless stated otherwise.
Table 4:
Application and operator coverage.
910C applications use one logical chip per dual-chip card; operator probes are separate from application runs.

Discussion
Reuse-aware compute and tiered KV memory.
The GPU reversal motivates SRAM/L2 retention for reusable weights and cache bypass with HBM streaming for rotating weights; Gather motivates programmable SIMT with access-aware path selection. A page-managed HBM pool could asynchronously extend KV into DRAM when migration and remote access cost less than saved prefill. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) could hold cold, read-mostly weights with low update traffic; 3D near-memory attention could benefit long contexts when saved data movement exceeds transfer overhead. These hypotheses must advance timely task completion; dependency hints and input-prefix reuse could guide retention and prefetch.
Multi-replica and disaggregated serving.
Consider a production MAS whose agents invoke model APIs backed by replicas across machines or clusters. Prefix affinity can save prefill but concentrate demand on a contended replica, making routing and load balancing affect complete-task latency and SLOs even with fixed dependencies. MAServeBench separates logical collaboration from physical placement; an API-facing replay adapter could preserve recorded work and arrivals while exposing per-replica routing and queueing, including delays before submission.
At the phase level, systems such as Mooncake
Qin et al. (2025)
separate prefill and decode
Zhong et al. (2024)
;
Patel et al. (2024)
. Parallel MAS stages create prefill bursts, while refinement and debate repeatedly release dependent calls. Phase specialization must offset KV/state-transfer costs and cross-pool queueing, especially for long contexts and hybrid-model recurrent state. Replay extensions that associate phase placement and state transfers with each operation could evaluate these designs through complete-task SLOs.
7

Conclusion
MAServeBench provides a source-grounded, extensible benchmark for multi-agent serving. Composable stages vary collaboration and context construction under shared task bindings, generating distinct workloads through native execution. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for controlled comparisons of legal release and serving resources at fixed work. Task-linked measurements reveal how collaboration shapes parallelism, locality affects compute efficiency, and KV pressure impacts task completion. Decoupling workflow semantics from backend execution lets Semantic Traces serve as workloads for serving backends and architecture simulators, supporting MAS serving and hardware evaluation.

Acknowledgments
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to Jianming Tong for his insightful discussions, thoughtful suggestions, and valuable feedback throughout the development of this work. His perspectives and constructive comments helped
us refine our understanding of the research challenges and improve the presentation of this study. We greatly appreciate his generous support
and encouragement.

The paired realizations track their source workflows in task quality: absolute differences are 1.2–3.8 percentage points on the success/accuracy measures and at most 0.019 on RACE. Execution demand varies within this quality range. For example, GPT Researcher’s realization invokes more tools, while OWL’s realization uses fewer input tokens with nearly the same call counts. Across the pairs, task functionality is accompanied by distinct model, tool, and context-processing demands. These measurements ground the realizations used to study collaboration as a serving workload.

article.headline: MAServeBench：多智能体服务基准
article.lede: 新基准把多智能体协作规则变成可复现的服务负载，用语义轨迹比较不同释放与资源条件下的表现。
article.problem: 多智能体系统把一次用户请求拆成相互依赖的模型调用与工具操作，这些操作在不同时刻就绪、携带演化上下文，带来变化的并发、计算和内存需求。传统服务基准把请求视为独立到达，而执行轨迹只记录已发生的工作，不记录生成这些工作的协作规则。
article.method: MAServeBench 用可组合阶段在共享任务绑定下改变协作与上下文构建，并通过原生执行生成负载。它引入分层语义轨迹，保留实际操作与依赖关系，从而在固定工作下控制释放时机和资源条件进行比较。实验在 vLLM 与 vLLM-Ascend 上运行，覆盖七种结构、30 个任务绑定和 32/64/128 用户规模。
article.results: 配对实现与源工作流在任务质量上接近：成功/准确率指标的绝对差异为 1.2–3.8 个百分点，RACE 至多 0.019，但执行需求仍有差异，例如 GPT Researcher 调用更多工具，OWL 在几乎相同调用数下输入 token 更少。在 27 个目标中，首调用驻留均短于第二调用，后者在 GSM8K 与 PubMedQA 超过前者，在 Science 仅部分抵消。
article.why_it_matters: 它把工作流语义与后端执行解耦，使语义轨迹可作为服务后端和架构模拟器的负载，便于用完整任务指标评估 MAS 服务与硬件设计。
article.limitations: 当前实验限于 vLLM/vLLM-Ascend、单加速器与 TP=1，且模型主要覆盖 Qwen3.5/Qwen3-8B，结论对其他后端和硬件的可迁移性仍待验证。论文把多副本与分离式服务列为后续方向，说明真实跨副本路由、排队和端到端 SLO 尚未纳入评测。
article.figure_caption_zh: 协作重塑服务需求：独立请求到达与多智能体任务引发的依赖请求、产物交换和同步不同，MAServeBench 提供可控、可复现的评测。

figure.caption: {Collaboration reshapes serving demand.} (a) Independent request arrivals. (b) A multi-agent task induces dependent requests with artifact exchange and synchronization. Both can use continuous batching. (c) MAServeBench enables controlled, reproducible evaluation of collaboration-induced serving demand and hardware resource behavior.

email_papers.title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
email_papers.abstract: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses
to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
Kehong Gong
Xiaoxu Zheng
Guanli Hou
Seunghun Lee
Mengqi Guo

Abstract
Robot agents built on vision–language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher’s harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost?
We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher’s trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness.
On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher’s success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%.
Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining.
On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors’ harnesses.
It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher’s accelerator time.

(a) With teacher weights frozen, RSI improves the harness; we then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories, and distill small students.
(b) Harness evolution improves the teacher and other frozen planners. Students trained separately at four harness versions each approach their corresponding teacher.

Introduction
Vision–language models (VLMs) can operate robot arms by reading images and calling perception and motion tools
[
25
,
18
,
11
,
12
]
.
The model chooses the object, action sequence, and stopping point; the surrounding
harness
grounds these choices, executes them, and reports what happened. Tool interfaces, feedback, task memory, and failure recovery therefore contribute to the agent’s performance alongside the model itself
[
57
,
40
,
46
,
10
]
.
Two lines of work offer complementary ways to build these agents. Harness evolution improves the system around a frozen planner
[
40
,
46
,
10
]
; agent distillation trains compact models from a stronger agent’s trajectories
[
27
,
24
,
56
]
.
We connect these approaches by asking:
can we first improve a large teacher’s harness, then transfer the resulting decision-making capability to a small model?
This would allow the improved system to run with substantially less inference compute.
We present
TinyAstral
, a family of 0.8B–4B manipulation agents built in two stages (
Fig.
2
).
First, we freeze the weights of an open-weight teacher, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
[
34
]
, and improve its harness through a master-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. Humans specify the rules and budget in advance. Frontier LLM agents then inspect failures and propose harness edits, which the system automatically accepts or rejects according to pre-registered paired statistical tests.
Second, we freeze the final harness and collect teacher trajectories containing reasoning, tool calls, and recovery from injected failures. Together with auxiliary offline real-robot supervision, these trajectories train a compact student to interpret feedback, choose actions, recover from failure, and decide when to finish. At deployment, the student replaces the teacher in the same frozen harness.
We evaluate both stages and the connection between them. Harness evolution raises the frozen teacher’s RoboTwin success from 33.4% to 63.6%, and distillation produces a 4B student at 62.8%.
To test whether this connection holds beyond the final endpoint, we distill students at four harness versions. The four students score 36.2%, 49.8%, 60.0%, and 62.8%, each close to its corresponding teacher.
The same evolved harness also improves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the untrained 4B initialization, showing that its gains are reusable across planners. On identical episodes the student outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses (93.6% vs. 78.9% on Guava; 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% on LIBERO-PRO), and on unseen benchmarks the small 4B student scores close to a 552B planner in the same harness.
Our contributions are:
•
Harness evolution followed by distillation.
A two-stage approach first improves a frozen teacher’s manipulation harness, then trains a compact planner from that teacher’s reasoning and recovery trajectories for deployment in the same harness.
•
Evidence that evolution gains transfer.
The harness improves other frozen planners, and distilled students at four harness versions track the performance of their corresponding teachers, showing that system improvements carry into compact models.
•
Compact agents with lower inference compute cost.
A single TinyAstral-4B model covers six benchmarks: on identical episodes it outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses, scores close to its teacher on the three training benchmarks and close to a 552B planner on unseen ones, and uses about one fifth of the teacher’s accelerator time per episode in our deployment measurement.
2
Related Work
Large models operating robots through a harness.
Language and vision-language models can operate robots by writing code or issuing tool calls over perception and motion primitives

Recent work shows that the harness around the model, namely its tool interface, feedback, memory, and recovery logic, is a first-order factor.
Harness VLA

We share the view that the harness is what improves while model weights stay fixed.
TinyAstral differs in three ways: the harness of a locally hosted open-weight teacher evolves continually under paired statistical selection, its gains are measured across planners at successive snapshots, and the evolved teacher is distilled into 0.8B, 2B, and 4B students that stay close to it.

Language agents can improve through stored experience and reflection

ADAS also reports transfer of discovered agents across models and domains. TinyAstral evolves the tools, execution feedback, task memory, and recovery logic of a manipulation harness under paired statistical selection, and carries the evolved system into a tiny student.

We supervise rationales together with tool calls inside a closed-loop visual interaction history, and distill from a teacher whose harness has already been evolved, into a student of a different size.

Humans specify the rules (including the pre-registered acceptance criteria) and budget before the loop begins. The master is a set of frontier LLM agents that read trajectories, propose edits, implement them, and audit one another’s code. The system applies the pre-registered paired statistical tests to determine acceptance.
Each round runs the current teacher, analyzes its failures, proposes edits, and tests a candidate against the current harness.
1. Read trajectories.
The current accepted harness
H
k
H_{k}
is run on development seeds. The master inspects the logged images, tool calls, tool results, and teacher reasoning, and assigns each failure to one of ten failure classes, such as off-target placement, false completion (
done
accepted but the final state fails), missing primitives, task-memory errors, and instance misidentification.
2. Propose edits.
For a target cluster of failing tasks, the master writes candidate components: new tools or primitives, more honest tool returns, perception fixes, failure handling, or local corrections to the task memory.
Edits must be general.
Code may not branch on the task name. In the final integration phase, the system prompt and existing tool descriptions must remain byte-identical to the parent. Memory may change only for the targeted tasks.
In addition, every new component must fire through an explicit trigger that writes a component-specific marker to the log.
A separate code audit verifies that, whenever the trigger does not fire, the candidate behaves step-for-step like the parent.
3. Test and accept edits.
Candidates are compared with the current harness on the same task/seed pairs. Training, selection, and evaluation seeds occupy disjoint ranges. The pre-registered gate requires positive evidence of improvement on targeted or triggered pairs and checks for regressions elsewhere; unsuccessful candidates are rejected or stopped early. The final integration phase accepted three of seven candidates.
Evaluation seeds are excluded from acceptance tests. The acceptance rules and capability ledger are in
Appendix
E

The other five benchmarks, including all zero-shot ones, use no task memory.

The distillation recipe combines reasoning targets, recovery branches, strict-success filtering, and training samples exported from the exact harness interactions.
Keep the teacher’s reasoning.
Each training target supervises the teacher’s stated rationale together with its next tool call,

Recovery branches.
Successful episodes rarely show how to recover from failure, so we add
recovery branches
.
Starting from a successful teacher episode, we replay its first
k
k
calls in a fresh simulator with the same seed, using the recorded results and without querying the model. At the branch point we inject a perturbation: on RoboTwin, the grasped object slips, or the target object is moved by 6–10 cm before the next grasp; on Guava and LIBERO, a grasp misses, a push falls short, or a placed object is displaced.
The teacher then continues online.
A branch is kept only if the perturbation took effect, the replay reproduced every recorded result code, and the teacher still reached strict success. Its samples begin at the first decision after the perturbation.
On RoboTwin, branches are subsampled to 20% of the RoboTwin samples (3,471 branch and 13,857 main-episode samples).

Each step is rendered with the final harness’s observation and history format, so the student sees real scenes through the same interface it uses in simulation.

Student versus teacher.
TinyAstral-4B stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks: 62.8% vs. 63.6% on RoboTwin, 93.6% vs. 94.7% on Guava, and 78.3% vs. 80.0% on LIBERO-PRO (
Tab.
2
). In the same harness, it also improves over the untrained 4B model by 18.4 pp on Guava and 42.0 pp on LIBERO-PRO; counting all undetermined outcomes as successes raises the untrained model’s LIBERO-PRO score to at most 57.3%.
Comparison with other agents.
On the same evaluation episodes, TinyAstral-4B outperforms the tested open agents, including Guava-4B, PyRUA-Lean-4B, and SenseNova-RoboRSI-27B (
Tab.
2
). It also exceeds systems using our teacher model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, in other harnesses: 93.6% vs. 78.9% for the Guava harness, and 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% for MotorMind and PyRUA-Lean on LIBERO-PRO. PyRUA-Lean-4B is trained and self-evaluated with a per-step environment success signal; without this signal, which our protocol withholds, it often declares success prematurely. These results highlight the contribution of the evolved harness and distilled policy to the final system’s performance. Competitor-specific execution and scoring protocols are detailed in
Appendix
B
.

2
). Compared with the untrained 4B model, distillation improves performance across all four evaluation settings, with gains of 10.0 pp on SimplerEnv Google VM and 13.6 pp on VLABench. Despite receiving no training on these benchmarks, the student also exceeds published results from

5
Conclusion
TinyAstral first improves a frozen teacher through harness evolution, then distills its reasoning and recovery behavior into a compact student deployed in the final harness. Across four harness versions, students trained from later versions perform better and stay close to their corresponding teachers, showing that harness improvements carry into compact agents. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners.
The final 4B student outperforms every open competitor we ran on identical episodes, stays close to its teacher on three training benchmarks, scores close to a 552B planner on unseen benchmarks, and uses about one fifth of the teacher’s accelerator time in our deployment measurement. These results support harness evolution followed by distillation as a route to capable robot agents with lower inference compute cost.
Future work will extend the approach to more RSI environments.

Same teacher in alternative systems.
Guava harness with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses the official prompt and parser with medium reasoning effort and default sampling, whereas our teacher uses its default xhigh reasoning and temperature 0. Both allow 25/30 calls per task. MotorMind with this planner uses its official stop-on-success protocol and uncapped calls (median 77, compared with 8 for our student on LIBERO-PRO). PyRUA-Lean with this planner uses benchmark-trained VLA executors and allows 30/40 calls on RoboTwin/LIBERO-PRO; it runs on all 500 RoboTwin episodes (91/500) and our 300 LIBERO-PRO episodes, and its reported success requires
finish(success)
and final-state success.

article.headline: TinyAstral：先进化再蒸馏的紧凑机器人智能
article.lede: 华为等提出两阶段方法：先在冻结教师上进化执行框架，再把教师推理与恢复轨迹蒸馏到 0.8B–4B 学生，4B 学生在 Ro
article.problem: 基于视觉语言模型的机器人智能体，其表现不仅取决于规划模型本身，也取决于围绕它的执行框架——工具接口、反馈、记忆与失败恢复逻辑。已有工作分别证明框架进化能提升冻结规划模型、智能体蒸馏能把强智能体轨迹迁移到小模型，但能否先改进大教师的框架、再把收益迁移到小模型以降低推理成本，尚未得到验证。
article.method: TinyAstral 分两阶段。第一阶段冻结教师（Qwen3.8-Flash-Next）权重，由前沿 LLM 智能体读取教师轨迹、提出框架修改（新工具、更诚实的工具返回、感知修正、失败处理、任务记忆），每次修改都要在预注册的配对 A/B 统计检验中通过才被接受，模型权重自始至终不变。第二阶段冻结最终框架 H*，采集教师含推理与失败恢复分支的轨迹，与离线真实机器人监督混合，蒸馏到 0.8B–4B 的 Qwen3.5 学生模型；部署时学生在同一个冻结框架中替换教师。
article.results: RoboTwin 500 个评测回合上，教师随框架演化从 H1 的 33.4% 升到 H* 的 63.6%，最终 4B 学生达 62.8%；在 H1、H7、H16、H* 四个框架版本上分别训练的 4B 学生为 36.2%、49.8%、60.0%、62.8%，各自接近对应的教师。在 Guava 和 LIBERO-PRO 上，4B 学生分别为 93.6% 与 78.3%，教师为 94.7% 与 80.0%。三个零样本基准上，学生与教师差距在 5.0 个百分点内，与同一框架下的 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 差距在 2.4 个百分点内。20 个共享 SimplerEnv 回合上，4B 学生每回合 25.3 加速器·秒，教师为 123.8（4.9 倍），DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 为 249.6（9.9 倍）。消融显示去掉教师推理文本会使 LIBERO-PRO 下降 19.3 个百分点、SimplerEnv Google VM 下降 11.2 个百分点、VLABench 下降 10.0 个百分点；加入真实机器人数据把离线下一调用准确率从 0.235 提到 0.923。
article.why_it_matters: 结果说明，对冻结教师做框架进化所得到的系统级改进可以被蒸馏进小模型，让紧凑智能体以约五分之一的加速器时间接近大模型乃至 552B 规划器的表现。
article.limitations: 真实机器人闭环只在 SO-ARM101 上演示了三个任务，推理成本仅基于 20 个共享 SimplerEnv 回合测量；RoboTwin 上框架还读取了每个任务一句话的终止状态注释（其余五个基准没有），且部分回合结果不确定被计为失败。0.8B 学生在 LIBERO-PRO 上降到 54.7%，明显落后于 4B 学生的 78.3%，说明小模型容量在扰动基准上仍有代价。
article.figure_caption_zh: TinyAstral 总览：第一阶段冻结教师，由前沿 LLM 智能体提出框架修改并通过配对统计门控接受；第二阶段冻结最终框架 H*、采集教师含推理与恢复分支的轨迹，蒸馏出 0.8B–4B 学生，部署时在相同框架中替换教师。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} Stage~1: humans specify the rules and budget in advance. A master of frontier LLM agents reads trajectories of the frozen teacher acting through the harness (tools, feedback, memory, recovery) and proposes harness edits, which are accepted only if a paired A/B test on selection seeds passes a pre-registered statistical gate; model weights never change. Stage~2: after evolution ends, we freeze $H^*$ and collect teacher trajectories, including reasoning and recovery branches. These are mixed with offline real-robot supervision to train tiny students (0.8B--4B), which replace the teacher in the same harness. Evaluation covers three training domains and three unseen benchmarks, plus three closed-loop real-robot tasks on an SO-ARM101 arm.

email_papers.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
email_papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.

Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning

Abstract
Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations.
Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance.
These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
Our data and code are available at
https://regap-bench.github.io
.
1
Introduction
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become increasingly capable at recognizing objects, shapes, and spatial relations in single-step perceptual tasks
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Team et al., 2026
)
, yet they often struggle to maintain and use that information across multiple reasoning steps. For example, a model may detect every object in a scene but still miscount them. Much of the field’s response to such failures has focused on perception, pursuing higher-resolution encoders and finer-grained visual features
(
Tong et al., 2024b
)
. However, the missing capability may instead lie between perception and reasoning: models lack a stable mechanism for referring to objects, regions, or locations while reasoning. Figure
1
shows an example of a counting problem. The model refers to shapes by vague locations such as “on the left side” and counts one ellipse twice; when every shape carries a number, it lists the ellipses by label and answers correctly.
Following
Lu et al. (2026)
, we call this the
reference gap
: the failure to maintain stable bindings between language-based reasoning and the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Recent work addresses it either by training a model to produce coordinates within its reasoning
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
, or by drawing lines on the image and instructing the model to scan along them
(
Izadi et al., 2025
)
. Two questions remain open. First, neither isolates the effect of the reference itself.
Lu et al. (2026)
compare a newly trained model with other models, so part of the gain may come from training data or architecture.
Izadi et al. (2025)
varies both the image and the prompt together, so it is unclear if MLLMs can perform systematic scanning of the image without additional instructions from the prompt. Second, each applies the same reference to every task, although tasks might need different visual operations. It thus remains unclear which reference a task needs, and whether any added structure would help equally.
Figure 1:
The same question to GPT-5.4 mini about the same scene, without and with numbering reference. In the plain setting (left), the model refers to shapes by vague locations and double counts. With numbering (right), it lists the ellipses by label and answers correctly.
To design such a diagnostic framework, we identify visual routines used for complex visual reasoning, such as marking visited items, activating bounded regions, and tracing boundaries
(
Ullman, 1984
)
. We hypothesize that MLLMs lack internal reference frames for reliable execution of these visual routines, and that external references such as numbering, shading, or grid lines can support them, with each reference helping most on tasks that demand its visual routines.
To test this hypothesis, we introduce
ReGap-Bench
, a controlled benchmark of paired reference interventions across five tasks: shape counting, angle ranking, size ranking, clock ranking, and transformation prediction. Each underlying scene is rendered with and without explicit visual references, while its task-relevant objects, geometry, question, and gold answer remain fixed.
Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy on all five tasks. Numbering yields gains of up to 17.5% on shape counting and 25% clock ranking; shading improves angle and size ranking; and grids improve size ranking and transformation prediction. Next, we show that the gains depend on matching the reference to the task, not on adding marks. Additionally, model scale across six Qwen3-VL models from 2B to 235B does not remove the reference gap.
Building on these findings,
we introduce a
training-free visual skill
that enables an agent to dynamically identify the required visual routine and select the corresponding reference scaffold. Evaluated on CartoMapQA
(
Ung et al., 2025
)
, this skill enables autonomous reference selection and improves complex map understanding without finetuning.
We summarize our contributions as follows:
•
We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired evaluation framework that measures the reference gap. It spans five visual reasoning tasks and three reference systems, with scene semantics, questions, and answers held fixed across reference conditions.
•
We show that task-matched references improve all evaluated models on all five tasks. Mismatched, incomplete, and model-scale analyses provide evidence that the gains come from supporting the visual routine a task requires, and that they persist from 2B to 235B parameters.
•
We introduce a training-free visual skill that enables an agent to identify the visual routine required by a task and dynamically construct a corresponding visual reference at inference time.
2
Diagnosing the Reference Gap with Visual Interventions
2.1
The reference gap
We use the reference gap to describe the failure to maintain a stable link between language and the relevant visual entity, region, or location that the language corresponds to. Models might perceive the relevant visual information, yet struggle to identify, revisit, or distinguish from other visual elements as reasoning proceeds. Consider shape counting. A model may correctly recognize individual triangles when asked about them separately yet still miscount them (see preliminary analysis in Appendix
A
). The model needs to repeatedly select an object, determine whether it belongs to the target class, keep track of counted objects, and then move to the next. Without a stable internal reference, it can lose track of which objects have been counted, resulting in omissions or duplicates. The reference gap is therefore distinct from a perception failure, and it should matter most in visual reasoning that spans multiple steps.
Most benchmarks do not reveal whether the model failed to perceive the relevant content or failed to maintain reference to it during reasoning. To address this, we diagnose the reference gap by testing whether performance changes when the underlying visual problem is held fixed but the model is given explicitly external reference to refer to its visual elements.
2.2
External references for visual routines
To choose useful visual references, we draw on Ullman’s theory of visual routines
(
Ullman, 1984
)
, which describes complex visual reasoning as a sequence of elementary operations such as shifting the processing focus, bounded activation, boundary tracing, indexing, and marking. We propose three types of visual references that externalize intermediate visual states to support these routines.
Numbering.
Numbering supports marking and indexing. It turns description-dependent visual elements into addressable entities. For instance, instead of using ambiguous phrases like “the upper-left triangle”, the model can refer to “shape 7”. This makes it easier to find an item again and to track which items have already been processed.
Shading.
Shading supports bounded activation by making a region explicit. For example, shading the interior of an angle makes the angular region itself visible. Filling a shape similarly emphasizes its bounded area rather than only its outline.
Grid lines.
Grids provide spatial marks that can support systematic focus shifts and boundary tracing. They divide the image into regular grid intervals and can provide a reference for position, width, height, displacement, and alignment.
These scaffolds provide different kinds of reference information. Therefore, we do not expect every scaffold to help every task. Our main hypothesis is that: a reference scaffold helps most when the type of reference it provides matches the visual routines that the reasoning process needs.
2.3

For each problem, we create a plain image and one or more versions with added references, all generated from the same underlying scene.

3
ReGap-Bench
: A Reference-Intervention Benchmark
Figure 2:
Example ReGap-Bench scenes. Each row shows a crop of one scene under the plain and each reference condition. The scene content, question, and answer are identical across a row. Numbering is not applied to angle ranking, size ranking, or transformation prediction.
We introduce
ReGap-Bench
, applying the paired design of Section
2.3
to five tasks: shape counting, angle ranking, size ranking, clock ranking, and transformation prediction. Each task has 200 scenes, each rendered to different reference conditions, as shown in Figure
2
. A reference only adds numbers, fills interiors with light gray, or adds faint grid lines. It does not move, remove, or cover any original (
content preservation
), and it treats all elements alike, so it does not reveal the answer (
no answer leakage
). Appendix
B
shows generation details and dataset statistics.
3.1
Tasks
We design five tasks that share a common requirement: the model must shift its focus across different parts of an image and repeatedly bind reasoning steps to particular visual elements. For each task, we identify the visual routine it relies on most and the reference scaffolds we expect to support that routine, which we call
matched
.
Shape counting.
The scene contains outlined shapes such as triangles, quadrilaterals, and pentagons, arranged in rows and columns at random orientations. We annotate the shapes with standard geometry marks, such as tick marks on equal sides and small squares at right angles, to make each shape’s class unambiguous. The question asks for the count of a specific shape. The model must select each shape, classify it, and record it as counted without skipping or repeating any. The task therefore relies on indexing and marking. Numbering could be a matched reference because it assigns each object a stable address that can be used throughout the counting process.
Angle ranking.
The scene contains several angles, each formed by two rays from a vertex, and marked by a red arc. The model is tasked to rank the angles by size, from smallest to largest, or the reverse. The main difficulty is keeping the correct angular region active: looking at the wrong side of the rays turns an angle into its conjugate angle. Shading the angular wedge could be helpful in making the region being compared explicit and thus supports bounded activation.
Size ranking.
The scene contains several shapes of one class. The model is asked to rank the shapes according to their visual size. This requires estimating the size of each shape and maintain these estimates while shifting the focus to other shapes. We expect two references to help: shading makes each shape’s area explicit as a bounded region, and grid lines provide a common scale for comparing width and height across locations.
Clock ranking.
The scene contains several analog clocks, each with twelve tick marks, an hour hand, a minute hand, and an “AM” or “PM” label. The task is to rank the clocks from earliest to latest, or the reverse. The main reference challenge is mapping hand positions onto a stable circular reference frame. We expect dial numbering to help, because it marks positions on that frame directly.
Transformation prediction.
Given a source figure and a chain of transformation steps, the model needs to determine which of the four given options is the final figure. Transformation operations include translation, reflection, rotation, and dilation. To solve the task, the model must trace the shape through each step and shift focus across panels to compare final positions.
We expect grid lines to help, because they provide a common frame for position and scale.
3.2
Evaluation Setup
We evaluate five MLLMs from both proprietary and open-source families: Claude-Opus-4.7
(
Anthropic, 2026
)
, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite
(
Gemini Team, 2026
)
, GPT-5.4-mini
(
OpenAI, 2026
)
, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking
(
Team, 2025
)
, and InternVL3.5-38B
(
Wang et al., 2025
)

4.1
Task-matched references improve visual reasoning
We begin with the operation-matched setting: for each reference, we test two tasks whose required visual routine could be supported by that scaffold.

Numbering supports indexing and marking.
Figure
3
shows that numbering consistently improves performance, with a performance gain of 6.0% to 17.5% on shape counting, and 8.5% to 25.0% on clock ranking.
On shape counting, models with low accuracy in the plain condition gain the most: GPT and Qwen gain about 17%, while Gemini and Claude gain 6%. To examine how numbering changes the counting process, we manually label each model response by the reference strategy it uses: (i)
systematic references
, which use numbered identifiers (e.g., “shape (7)”) and a explicit row- or column-based scheme (e.g., “Top row”); and (ii)
ambiguous references
, which use vague spatial descriptions (e.g., “the upper-left one”) or provide no clear reference scheme.
On plain images, Gemini frequently constructs its own reference system: 52.0% of its responses assign numbers to the shapes, and 31.5% explicitly scan them by rows or columns.
In contrast, GPT does so much less often: only 15.5% of its responses use either
systematic references
strategy, and the other 84.5% use
ambiguous references
. With numbering, 100% of Gemini’s and 86.0% of GPT’s responses refer to the printed numbers. This suggests that
numbering supplies stable symbolic addresses that are particularly useful for models that lack their own reference system
.
For clock ranking, we extract the time each model stated for each clock from its response and count a clock as correctly-read if it is within 5 minutes of the ground truth. Among clocks with a stated time, numbering raises this rate from 10.6% to 28.6% for Claude, 58.2% to 82.5% for Gemini, 67.5% to 75.6% for Qwen3-VL, and 2.9% to 17.4% for InternVL.
Thus,
dial numbers improve these models’ ability to read individual clocks, an intermediate step required for correct ranking
.
GPT behaves slightly differently: when it states a time, it is almost accurate (90.3% plain vs. 90.8% with numbering), but on plain images it gives no time for 34% of the clocks, and this propotion is reduced to 12% with numbering. For GPT, therefore,
numbering primarily improves the completeness of the intermediate clock-reading process rather than the accuracy of readings
.

4.2
Analysis on Matched Versus Mismatched References
The positive scaffold results establish that each reference method can help in matched settings. However, it is unclear whether these gains simply come from adding more visual marks. We test this by applying numbering, shading, and grid lines to the same shape counting and clock ranking scenes. If improvements were caused merely by additional visual information, then numbering, shading, and grid lines should help similarly. If the reference gap exists, then the operation-matched scaffold should produce the largest gain. Figure
6
supports the second explanation. In shape counting, numbering improves accuracy by 11.3% on average, compared to only 1.7% for shading, while grid lines reduce accuracy by 4.1%. The same separation appears in clock ranking.
These results show that added visual structure is not always beneficial: a scaffold can be neutral or harmful when it does not provide the kind of reference the task needs.
The effectiveness of a scaffold therefore depends on its alignment with the visual routine needed for solving the task.
4.3
Analysis on Incomplete References
Figure 7:
Performance improves as dial numbering becomes more complete.
Next, we test whether references help because they provide complete reference structure, or whether partial reference is sufficient. We test this on clock ranking by varying how many dial numerals are shown while keeping the clocks themselves fixed. The four conditions contain zero, two, four, or all twelve numerals. If numbering helps because it provides stable addresses, then a more complete reference system should be more useful than a sparse one.
Figure
7
confirms this, mean accuracy rises from 23.9% with no numerals to 25.3% with two, 31.8% with four, and 38.0% with all twelve. The trend is non-decreasing for every evaluated model. Sparse numbering therefore provides only a small benefit, whereas a complete reference system produces a substantially larger gain. This result is consistent with a reference-based mechanism: a scaffold is most useful when it supplies stable addresses that the model must repeatedly identify during reasoning.
Partial references can still help, but they leave a larger portion of the task dependent on the model’s own spatial descriptions or implicit object bindings.
4.4
Analysis of Model Scale
The final question is whether the reference gap is primarily a limitation of small models. We evaluate six Qwen3-VL Thinking models ranging from 2B to 235B parameters on shape counting. Figure
8
shows a clear overall increase in accuracy with model scale. However, the advantage of numbering remains at every scale: the gain ranges from 9.0% to 23.5% and does not decrease monotonically as models become larger. Thus,
a larger model size improves the task performance but does not eliminate the benefit of an explicit reference system
.

5
Task-matched references as training-free visual skills
In Section
4
, we show that models that lack an internal reference system can benefit from task-matched references
without any training
. One implication is that agents can add these references on their own using a visual skill when a task requires such reference. Unlike most skills that are text-only, we package the three references as a visual skill that can refer to visual examples and overlay the reference onto the image similarly.
We test the skill on CartoMapQA
(
Ung et al., 2025
)
that contains street-level OpenStreetMap renderings with icons for points of interest (POIs), road labels, markers, and a scale bar. We use stratified sampling to draw 100 tasks across the eight subtasks, and run the Codex GPT-5.5 agent on the same tasks with and without the skill, using the BenchFlow framework
(
BenchFlow Team, 2026
)
.
The skill contains three components: First, written rules specify which reference to use for each type of visual operation: numbering for counting, listing, or matching discrete map elements, as well as tracking junctions along a route; grid lines, calibrated using the map’s scale bar, for measuring distances or comparing positions; shading for isolating bounded regions; and no overlay when the answer can be obtained from a single clearly labeled element.
Second, a pair of before-and-after example images demonstrating how to draw each reference. Third, a script draws the chosen reference on a copy of the map and leaves the original unchanged.

Related Work
Visual perception and reasoning in MLLMs.
Benchmarks including BLINK
(
Fu et al., 2024
)
, MMVP
(
Tong et al., 2024b
)
, BlindTest
(
Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024
)
, CV-Bench
(
Tong et al., 2024a
)
, and V*Bench
(
Wu & Xie, 2024
)
study limitations in visual perception and reasoning. Related studies report difficulties in spatial reasoning
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, enumeration
(
Tamarapalli et al., 2025
;
Deng et al., 2026
)
, and chart understanding and reasoning
(
Masry et al., 2025
)
. However, they do not distinguish failures to encode visual elements from failures to maintain references during reasoning. Our paired design probes the effects of visual references by holding the underlying scene, question, and answer fixed while varying the reference system.
Grounding intermediate reasoning in visual references.
Lu et al. (2026)
identify the
reference gap
as a failure to ground verbal reasoning in precise visual entities and locations. Such failures can propagate across reasoning steps in dense counting, spatial deduction, and path tracing. Their approach trains models to generate points and bounding boxes within their reasoning trajectories through large-scale primitive supervision, reinforcement learning, and distillation. BLINK highlights tasks that are difficult to mediate through natural language
(
Fu et al., 2024
)
. On VSI-Bench,
Yang et al. (2025)
find that chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, and tree-of-thoughts reduce Gemini-1.5 Pro
Team et al. (2024)
’s average performance in their evaluation, while explicitly generating cognitive maps improves its relative-distance accuracy. We examine whether references supplied in the input image can support these bindings in a fixed, off-the-shelf model, and under what conditions the model uses them.
Visual prompting and grounded reasoning.
Prior work supports visual reasoning through annotations, auxiliary visual states, and modular computation. Red-circle prompting directs CLIP towards selected regions
(
Shtedritski et al., 2023
)
, while Set-of-Mark supplies identifiers for segmented regions
(
Yang et al., 2023
)
. Visual Sketchpad generates auxiliary drawings
(
Hu et al., 2024
)
, PIVOT refines action proposals through numbered annotations
(
Nasiriany et al., 2024
)
, and Draw-and-Understand trains models to interpret user-drawn prompts
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
. VisAidMath evaluates mathematical reasoning with textually described visual aids
(
Ma et al., 2026
)
. Other approaches compose vision modules through code
(
Surís et al., 2023
)
, incorporate visual features into rationale generation
(
Zhang et al., 2024
)
, or represent intermediate reasoning states as images
(
Meng et al., 2023
)
. Our study systematically varying references rendered in the input image to test which reference systems support particular visual routines and whether their benefits depend on task alignment, with task-matched references implemented as reusable skills that require no model training.
7
Conclusion
We identify the
reference gap
as a distinct bottleneck in multimodal reasoning: models may perceive the relevant visual content yet fail to maintain stable references to it during multi-step reasoning. Using ReGap-Bench, we show that task-matched visual references consistently improve performance, whereas mismatched references provide little benefit or can be harmful, and that this gap persists even at larger model scales. These results suggest that improving multimodal reasoning requires
mechanisms that support the visual routines needed by the task. Finally, our training-free visual skill demonstrates that an agent can dynamically construct such references at inference time, offering a simple way to improve visual reasoning without additional model training.

Preliminary Check: Can Models Perceive the Shapes?
Section
2.1
claims that a model can perceive the shapes in a scene yet still fail to count a target class. As a preliminary check of this claim, we run two simpler probes on the plain shape-counting scenes with Claude-Opus-4.7.
Finding the shapes.
We ask the model how many shapes the image contains, regardless of class. It answers correctly in 193 of the 200 scenes (96.5%; Table
3
). The errors grow with the number of shapes.

Recognizing single shapes.
For each scene, we crop one shape from the plain image and ask whether it belongs to the scene’s target class, with the same inclusion rules as in the counting prompt. For example, the scene question “How many parallelograms are there?” becomes “Is this shape a parallelogram?”. If the scene contains the target class, we crop a random target shape (answer Yes); otherwise, we crop a random shape (answer No). The model answers correctly for 95.9%.
Summary.
The model counts all shapes correctly in 96.5% of scenes and recognizes the single shape in 95.9%, but counts the target class correctly in only 72.0%. Most counting errors therefore do not come from missing or misreading individual shapes.

B.2
Task Generation
We pre-define shapes from 11 classes: square, rectangle, trapezium, parallelogram, regular pentagon, equilateral triangle, isosceles triangle, right triangle, right isosceles triangle, circle, and ellipse.
Shape counting.
We randomly sample shapes from the 11 classes to fill the cells. Some cells are left empty. We add marks as follows: squares and rectangles have right-angle marks at all corners; squares, pentagons, and equilateral triangles have one tick on every side; rectangles and parallelograms have one tick on one pair of opposite sides and two ticks on the other; isosceles triangles have one tick on each equal side; right triangles have a right-angle mark; right isosceles triangles have a right-angle mark and one tick on each leg; circles have two dotted radii, each with one tick. Trapezia and ellipses have no marks. Each shape has a random orientation and a random size, and classes with free proportions (e.g., rectangles, isosceles triangles, ellipses) also get random proportions. The target class is drawn from all 11 classes, not only those present, so the answer can be zero. The gold count follows class inclusion: a square also counts as a rectangle, parallelogram, and trapezium; a rectangle also counts as a parallelogram and trapezium; a parallelogram also counts as a trapezium; equilateral and right isosceles triangles also count as isosceles triangles; a right isosceles triangle also counts as a right triangle; and a circle also counts as an ellipse. The question uses one of five templates, such as “How many parallelograms are there?” and “What is the total number of circles in the image?”

We manually assign each shape-counting response of Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite and GPT-5.4-mini on plain and numbered images (800 responses) to one of four categories: (A) numbered reference, which uses object numbers as addresses, such as “(3)” or “shape 7”; (B) row-and-column reference, which uses a systematic row, column, or cell scheme, such as “row 2, column 3”; (C) vague spatial reference, which uses only phrases such as “top left” without a stable scheme; and (D) unclear or no reference, which gives the answer directly or cannot be classified. We call categories A and B
systematic references
. We call categories C and D
ambiguous
references.

article.headline: 多模态推理的参考缺口：视觉标记并非万能
article.lede: 配对基准ReGap-Bench显示，任务匹配的编号、阴影或网格可提升多模态推理，错配则可能有害。
article.problem: 多模态大模型能识别视觉内容，却常在多步推理中丢失对同一对象的稳定指代，例如计数时重复或漏数。作者认为这不只是感知失败，而是“参考缺口”：语言推理未能稳定绑定到对应的视觉实体、区域或位置。
article.method: 作者提出ReGap-Bench配对基准，覆盖形状计数、角度排序、尺寸排序、时钟排序和变换预测五个任务，每个任务200个场景，仅改变编号、阴影或网格等外部参考，题目与答案保持不变。实验评估五个多模态模型，并测试2B到235B的六款Qwen3-VL模型；随后把任务匹配的参考封装成免训练视觉技能，在CartoMapQA上验证。
article.results: 任务匹配的参考带来提升：编号使形状计数提升6.0%到17.5%、时钟排序提升8.5%到25.0%；阴影使尺寸排序提升4.0%到11.0%；网格使尺寸排序提升2.0%到8.0%、变换预测提升2.0%到5.5%。在形状计数中，编号平均提升11.3%，阴影仅1.7%，网格为-4.1%；时钟数字从0个增至12个时，平均准确率由23.9%升至38.0%。六款Qwen3-VL上编号增益为9.0%到23.5%，未随规模消失；CartoMapQA上智能体在100题中为57题绘制覆盖层，编号子集由63.7%升至70.1%。
article.why_it_matters: 把参考缺口视为独立于视觉感知的瓶颈，并给出免训练的干预方式，可能比单纯堆高分辨率编码器更直接地改善多步视觉推理。
article.limitations: 基准场景为合成渲染，任务与参考类型有限；CartoMapQA验证仅100题，阴影子集只有3题，外部有效性仍待检验。规模分析也只覆盖Qwen3-VL的形状计数。

page_papers.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
page_papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.

Abstract
Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data.
Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns.
To address these challenges, we introduce
CUA-Master
, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework.
At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations.
At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction;
The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks.
To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that
CUA-Master-27B
achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring
80.2
on OSWorld Verified,
36.9
on OSWorld 2.0,
43.9
on WeaveBench, and
25.0
on Agents’ Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.
Figure 1
:
Performance comparisons of our proposed CUA-Master-27B and other counterparts across four benchmarks.
1
Introduction
Computer-use agents (CUAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for automating real-world workflows across diverse software applications, and unlocking new levels of digital productivity.
Recent advances in both foundation models
[
37
,
30
,
47
,
40
,
32
,
3
]
and specialized agents
[
51
,
49
,
17
,
28
,
9
]
have substantially improved their capabilities not only grounding of computer scenarios, but also in interactive reasoning and long-horizon execution.
Besides, early CUAs operate predominantly via graphical user interfaces (GUIs), while subsequent works extend their capability scope by incorporating command-line interfaces (CLIs)
[
8
,
24
,
45
,
42
]
and extensible tools
[
16
,
19
]
.
Nevertheless, developing powerful CUAs capable of reliably executing diverse, long-horizon, and cross-application workflows remains challenging.
A fundamental bottleneck lies in how data construction and model optimization are coupled and recursively improved.
Many existing pipelines follow a
unidirectional
paradigm of data generation followed by model training
[
51
,
49
,
28
,
18
]
, where data construction is insufficiently informed by the evolving weaknesses. Consequently, additional data may provide lopsided benefits without addressing persistent capability gaps.
Recent recursive improvement approaches partially address this issue by incorporating iteratively self-generated data
[
50
,
33
,
75
]
. However, their exploration remains
closed-world
optimization, where such cycles still predominantly rely on the own knowledge and capabilities of the model itself.
It is bounded by existing capabilities, potentially reinforcing distributional biases, and yielding diminishing marginal returns.
These observations fundamentally motivate us to build a recursive system that continuously acquires new open-world knowledge, and systematically expands the performance boundary of the whole system.
Beyond system-level limitations, a more concrete concern is the availability of large-scale, high-quality data that adequately captures the diversity and complexity of real-world trajectories.
While human-annotated trajectories provide high-quality supervision, their substantial annotation costs and limited application coverage make large-scale collection impractical
[
51
,
20
,
25
,
50
,
13
]
.
Therefore, synthetic data generation emerges as a promising alternative
[
44
,
60
,
39
,
21
,
41
]
.
However, existing approaches face three intertwined challenges. First,
diversity
: tasks derived from restricted and similar sources often exhibit substantial homogeneity, leading to insufficient ability coverage and fast improvement saturation as data volume increases.
Second,
controllability
: direct instruction rewriting and template-based generation offer limited control over operational abilities, complexity, and task dependencies, particularly for long-horizon and cross-application workflows.
Third,
reliability
: scaling the collection of verified trajectories across diverse real-world environments becomes increasingly challenging as task complexity grows, leading to lower rollout success rates and frequent execution failures.
Collectively, these limitations constrain not only the quantity of synthetic data, but also its effective coverage of the capabilities required by general-purpose CUAs.
To address these limitations, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive framework that integrates an outer world-data-model flywheel with an inner data flywheel.
At the system level, the outer flywheel closes the loop among open-world exploration, data construction, and model optimization. By leveraging the evolving model’s capability gaps to guide subsequent exploration and data generation, while continuously incorporating external knowledge, it addresses both the unidirectionality of conventional training pipelines and the limited knowledge expansion of closed-world self-improvement.
At the data level, the inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation as two complementary driving forces.
Open-world seeding mines diverse seed tasks from real-world instructional videos through hierarchical retrieval and filtering, and reconstructs their trajectories via a visual-semantic dual-path mechanism.
The latter abstracts existing seeds into reusable primitives and composes them into verifiable tasks, with explicit control over task complexity and application scope.
To improve rollout reliability and efficiency, we introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism that preserves valid execution prefixes and recovers from localized failures without restarting entire rollouts.
Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of CUA-Master. With only
27B
parameters, it achieves scores of
80.2
on OSWorld Verified,
36.9
on OSWorld 2.0,
43.9
on WeaveBench, and
25.0
on Agents’ Last Exam, demonstrating competitive performance approaching markedly larger or closed-source models and strong execution efficiency.
Our double-loop flywheel also substantially improves the diversity and coverage of data distribution, reliability and controllability of synthesis, and progressive improvements across iterations.

2.1.3
Environment Infrastructure
Our rollout infrastructure is a backend-agnostic, profile-driven orchestration layer for reproducible CUA tasks across Linux, Windows, and MacOS.
We construct the VM pool through a semi-automated assembly pipeline. First, we manually prepare a set of base images spanning the application combinations defined in Table
9
. We then programmatically derive additional variants by perturbing these images,
e.g.
, by removing randomly selected applications and reorganizing desktop layouts, thereby expanding environment coverage at low marginal cost. Each generated image is registered in a catalog and accompanied by a descriptor recording its operating-system type and version, and application inventory, including version and package metadata.
To better manage and allocate CPUs and other resources, we employ a global resource-aware scheduler that bounds concurrency by occupied VM slots, while standardized lifecycle hooks manage resource acquisition, controller readiness, network tunneling, environment reset, and cleanup.
During rollout, each episode is instantiated from a versioned VM image catalog, typically using an immutable base image with a disposable writable overlay.
The writable overlay accommodates harness bootstrapping (Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw,
etc.
), task-specific initialization, and transient application states.
This infrastructure supports over 100 different CUA environments and allows over 2,000 concurrently running VMs, substantially increasing the richness, diversity, and efficiency of large-scale rollout.

2.2
Recursive Flywheel
2.2.1
Data Flywheel
As illustrated by the black dashed box in Figure
2(a)

Open-world seeding
(Section
2.3

[

Autocatalytic propagation
(Section
2.4

open-world seeding provides external knowledge and diversity and forms the necessary foundation, while autocatalytic propagation systematically amplifies its coverage, complexity, and scale.
2.2.2
World-Data-Model Flywheel
Beyond the inner data flywheel, we establish a broader world-data-model flywheel. Starting from the open world, diverse applications, operations, and workflows are distilled and expanded into executable tasks and trajectories, providing grounded supervision for model training. As the model evolves, its emerging capabilities and remaining limitations provide feedback to guide subsequent open-world exploration, directing data acquisition and scaling toward underrepresented workflows and increasingly challenging tasks. Through this iterative cycle of
world exploration, data construction, model improvement, and feedback-driven re-exploration, the agent progressively expands its capability frontier.

Moreover, although annotation-verified, trajectories reconstructed from instructional videos may contain annotation noise and do not necessarily correspond to real executions in the target environments.

2.5
Model Training
2.5.1
Recipe
As discussed in Section
2.2
, we integrate model training into the recursive world-data-model flywheel, where each iteration comprises a complete model optimization.
Specifically, preceding iterations employ SFT to progressively acquire diverse knowledge and capabilities. In each iteration, based on the in-house assessment of model, including domain- and application-level hierarchical failure cases and rollout success rates analyses, we identify the gaps and limitations of the current policy, guiding the next iteration of adaptive data scaling and the CUA ability frontier.
As capability gains from SFT gradually saturate, we transition to RL in the final iteration to further enhance the task-level capability upper limit. As discussed, the synthesized tasks are built upon controllable capability primitives, which renders native support for difficulty-level categorization. Combining this with task generation quality and rollout success rates, we curate a high-quality task collection for RL training.

Especially on the more long-horizon, complex Agents’ Last Exam benchmark, hybrid execution improves the score from 5.9 to 25.0 over GUI-only, with 26.7% fewer steps; on OSWorld 2.0, it achieves competitive scores while reducing execution steps by 43.8%.
As demonstrated in Figure
5
, the visualization of trajectories further illustrates the complementary strengths of GUI and CLI actions: CLI enables file processing, batch computation, structured data manipulation, and other efficient operations, while GUI supports visual inspection and interactive application operations. By adaptively switching between these modalities according to task requirements, CUA-Master effectively exploits their complementary capabilities, enabling more efficient, and effective computer-use workflows.

3.3.3
Analysis of World-data-model Flywheel
We analyze the effectiveness of our world-data-model flywheel from two perspectives.
As shown in Figure
9
, successive training iterations progressively improve performance across all four benchmarks, with OSWorld Verified and WeaveBench increasing by over 25 points. Notably, when SFT improvements on relatively simple tasks approach saturation, the final RL stage further boosts performance on OSWorld 2.0 and Agents’ Last Exam, which are more challenging and demand stronger exploration, by approximately 15 points, respectively.
Moreover, as illustrated in Figure
9

i.e.
, using the model from each training iteration as the annotator to generate data for the next iteration, can bring about some improvements, but its gains are relatively limited.
These results highlight the effectiveness of our flywheel in establishing a positive feedback loop that progressively enhances computer-use capabilities, particularly on challenging long-horizon tasks.
4
Conclusion
In this work, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive framework that advances CUA systems beyond unidirectional data pipelines and closed-world self-improvement.
At the system level, the world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world knowledge and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide further iterations.
At the data level, we establish a complementary flywheel that couples open-world seeding with autocatalytic propagation, which integrates visual-semantic trajectory reconstruction, primitive-based task composition, and feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retries to enable diverse, controllable, and reliable data synthesis.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, with strong execution efficiency and consistent improvements across recursive iterations.
These results highlight the potential of our method for developing increasingly general and capable CUA.

Research on CUAs has progressed from visual grounding to autonomous interaction and long-horizon task execution. Early works, including OS-Atlas
[
54

, Tong-UI
[
71

[

17

advance reliable data synthesis and specialized training paradigms. More recently, research has expanded beyond GUI-only interaction toward hybrid action spaces. UI-TARS-2
[
50
]

[
16

and HybridCUA
[
8
]
coordinate GUI actions with structured tools and command-line interfaces. Collectively, these advances mark a shift from fine-grained visual grounding toward scalable, practical, and reliable CUAs.
A.2
Scalable Data Synthesis
Scalable data synthesis has emerged as a key paradigm for overcoming the scarcity of high-quality computer-use trajectories. One line of research leverages naturally occurring interaction data and instructional resources. OpenCUA
[
51
]
, WildGUI
[
57
]
, and VideoCUA
[
20
]
exploit real-world interaction traces or videos, while AgentTrek
[
60
]
and TongUI
[
71
]
transform web tutorials into agent supervision. Another line synthesizes tasks and trajectories through environment interaction. OS-Genesis
[
44
]
adopts reverse task synthesis, whereas AutoPlay
[
39
]
discovers executable tasks through environment exploration. CUA-Gym
[
49
]
, EvoCUA
[
61
]
, and ScaleCUA
[
28
]
further scale supervision through verifiable task synthesis, large-scale environment interaction, and iterative policy optimization.
Despite these advances, jointly achieving real-world diversity, controllable task complexity, reliable verification, and efficient execution remains challenging.
Our work unifies open-world workflow acquisition with primitive-based compositional synthesis, enabling systematic expansion from authentic operational knowledge to diverse, verifiable, and increasingly complex computer-use tasks.
A.3
Recursive Improvements
Recursive improvement aims to expand agent capabilities through iterative data generation, experience refinement, and policy optimization. Early approaches such as Re-ReST
[
11
]
and Agent-R
[
70
]
exploit environmental feedback and iterative refinement to improve agent trajectories. Moving toward adaptive task generation, WebRL
[
33
]
introduces self-evolving curricula driven by failed executions, and Self-Challenging Agents
[
75
]
jointly develop task generation and policy learning through self-generated, verifiable challenges. WebEvolver
[
12
]
further couples agent improvement with an evolving world model.
Nevertheless, recursive training may suffer from distributional narrowing, accumulated synthetic errors, and diminishing task novelty
[
11
,
43
,
73
]
.
In contrast, our world-data-model flywheel anchors recursive improvement in continuously refreshed real-world knowledge. Open-world seeding introduces external diversity, compositional propagation expands task coverage and difficulty, and model feedback directs subsequent exploration and optimization, forming a grounded and adaptive cycle of capability expansion.

Appendix B
Details of Training Data
Our training data are constructed through open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation, yielding a dataset of 127K samples (115K for SFT training and 12K for RL training).
To ensure diverse application coverage, we organize data construction around a hierarchical taxonomy encompassing 8 domains, 36 subdomains, and over 650 applications. As illustrated in Figure
10(a)
, the taxonomy spans Business & Administration (18.4%), Creative Production (16.5%), Daily Life (13.4%), Developer Tools (11.4%), Engineering (10.6%), Data & Analytics (10.3%), Productivity (10.1%), and Science & Research (9.4%). This broad coverage supports the acquisition of heterogeneous operational skills across both everyday and specialized workflows.
As shown in Figure
10(b)
, the training data distribution evolves across successive iterations rather than following a fixed domain mixture. Compared with the initial SFT stage, subsequent iterations increase the relative representation of Software Development, Science & Research, and Productivity, while reducing the initial concentration in Business & Administration. The final RL stage adopts a more balanced distribution across domains. This adaptive reallocation aligns data construction with evolving model capability gaps while maintaining broad application coverage.

Appendix E
Limitations
Despite its effectiveness, CUA-Master still has two main limitations. First, the recursive improvement pipeline incurs substantial computational and infrastructure costs, particularly from large-scale environment interactions, trajectory collection, and iterative model optimization. Although our snapshot-rollback mechanism improves rollout efficiency, it requires large-scale extra support for the deployment of VMs, leading to challenges for infrastructure. Second, the upper limit of the quality of synthesized data relies on capable annotator models, with stronger annotators consistently yielding greater performance gains. This dependence introduces additional inference costs and may constrain the accessibility of the framework when strong annotators are unavailable.

article.headline: CUA-Master：双循环递归改进电脑智能体
article.lede: 27B模型在OSWorld Verified得80.2，OSWorld 2.0得36.9。
article.problem: 电脑操作智能体（CUA）受限于交互数据多样性、可控性和可靠性不足，传统“先造数据再训练”的流程缺少迭代反馈。已有递归自我改进多依赖模型自生成经验，属于封闭世界优化，能力扩展受限且收益递减。
article.method: 作者提出 CUA-Master，一个嵌套双循环递归框架：外层“世界—数据—模型”飞轮持续引入开放世界语料，并用模型当前弱点指导下一轮数据构建与优化。内层数据飞轮把教学视频挖掘为种子任务，经视觉—语义双路径重建轨迹，再抽象为可复用原语，组合成复杂度可控、可验证的合成任务；轨迹收集采用反馈引导的快照回滚重试。
article.results: CUA-Master-27B 在 OSWorld Verified 得 80.2，在 OSWorld 2.0 得 36.9，在 WeaveBench 得 43.9，在 Agents’ Last Exam 得 25.0；相比同规模 UI-Mate-27B 分别提升 2.6、12.9、25.6、11.8。OSWorld Verified 用时 8 分钟；OSWorld 2.0 以 36.9 略高于 Qwen-3.8-27B 的 36.5，运行时间减少 24%。在难例合成上，K=40、N=3 时 rollout 成功率为 49.8%，基线为 14.6%；K=50、N=8 时为 18.7% 对 0.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把开放世界数据获取、可控任务合成和模型迭代放进同一个闭环，为 CUA 提供了一条不依赖纯自生成经验的扩展路径。27B 规模在多个 GUI 与 GUI+CLI 基准上接近更大或闭源模型，说明数据飞轮和混合动作空间可能比单纯堆参数更关键。
article.limitations: 论文自述的局限是：递归改进依赖大规模虚拟机、轨迹采集和迭代训练，算力与基础设施成本高；合成数据质量上限受标注模型能力制约，强标注器收益更大，也带来额外推理成本。还需注意，OSWorld 2.0 与 Agents’ Last Exam 的绝对得分仍只有 36.9 和 25.0，距离可靠通用仍有差距。
