page_papers.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
page_papers.abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work
requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present

Introduction
Computer-use agents (CUAs) extend the capabilities of large language
models from generating responses to operating computers and automating
software tasks
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2025b
)
.
They can invoke software functions through application programming
interfaces (APIs) and command-line interfaces (CLIs).
Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) extend this access to functions that
applications do not expose programmatically, providing a critical last
mile for software automation
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
.
Through GUI interaction, agents interpret the screen and translate
natural-language goals into mouse and keyboard actions.
Advances in visual grounding and action generation have expanded the range of operations
these agents can perform
(
Qin et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
.
As agents combine these operations into longer workflows, earlier actions
shape the software state on which later decisions depend. Reliable completion
requires agents to preserve intermediate progress and the user’s
constraints, adapt to changing interfaces, and recover from errors while
keeping the overall goal in view
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
.
Training agents to coordinate such workflows therefore requires experience that
develops precise interface skills and connects successive decisions to
complete task outcomes. Obtaining this experience at scale begins with
constructing varied tasks, each of which needs a request grounded in available software and
content, a usable initial environment, and a reliable way to judge success
(
Ge et al., 2026
;
Zhou et al., 2026b
)
. Once these tasks are
available, collecting experience from them requires an agent framework that
sustains long interactions and records decisions and outcomes across desktop
and web environments. The resulting demonstrations can teach the policy how to
complete workflows, but independent execution may lead it into states
absent from those demonstrations. Continued improvement therefore requires
fresh interaction and outcome feedback from the policy’s own attempts
(
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Jung et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. Meeting these linked
needs calls for co-designing how tasks are constructed, how agents execute
them, and how the resulting experience is used for learning.

Harness as
full-lifecycle infrastructure
that
executes software tasks and turns the resulting attempts into inspectable
experience for learning. This requires keeping the agent’s decisions
connected to its workspace and outcomes, from environment preparation
through execution and evaluation to record preservation.
Within the shared runtime, visual context and task memory help agents
build on progress across long workflows
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025d
)
. An evaluator uses the execution record and
live workspace to check task completion and execution quality, supplementing task-specific verifiers where their
coverage is incomplete
(
Zhuge et al., 2025
)
.
To scale this process, the Batch Rollout Service coordinates parallel
workers and overlaps lifecycle stages, supporting efficient,
high-concurrency experience collection (Section
3
).
Experience Flywheel: scaling grounding and agentic experience.
With a runtime for collecting and checking software experience, the next
challenge is to supply enough varied, useful work for the agent to learn.
The

The resulting

NorthCUA
establishes state-of-the-art results among
open-source models in all three domains (Figure
1
).
With 397B parameters, Pro outperforms trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max and
Kimi-K3 on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and
WebArena-Verified
(
Qwen Team, 2026c
;
Kimi Team, 2026
)
.
The 35B Mini also surpasses Kimi-K3 on OSWorld-Verified and Qwen3.8-Max
on WebArena-Verified. Stage comparisons show desktop and Web gains across
all three model sizes after long-horizon SFT and joint RL
(Section
6
).
Long workflows also accumulate the latency of successive model decisions.
To reduce this cost,

Step
records one policy decision and the resulting tool
execution and feedback. Each step can contain multiple tool calls.
These runtime scopes organize interaction, while the task attempt supplies the
collection-level identity used to associate actions, artifacts, and
assessment. Each recorded action retains its request and session context,
supporting task-level inspection and collection recovery. Session resources
are managed within the broader environment lifecycle coordinated by the
collection or training system. Appendix
H.1

Desktop input, browser interaction, and workspace inspection expose
different operations, whose implementations may run beside the agent or
near a remotely hosted application. To make these capabilities available
to the shared decision loop, we use a common tool interface that allows
their implementations to evolve independently.
Tool definitions describe operations and their arguments, while dispatch

requesting step. The Agent Kit integrates local functions and tools exposed
through Model Context Protocol (MCP), whose standard tool descriptions and

To reduce the repeated inference overhead of long GUI workflows, we allow
the model to issue multiple action calls in a single response. The runtime
executes these calls serially in the specified order, allowing actions that
can be planned together to share one model invocation.
For computer use, tool feedback also needs to describe the state after an

and intermediate results into decisions made much later in a workflow.
3.2  Sustaining Long-Horizon Interaction
Long-horizon execution is a central challenge in practical computer use.
Real software work can require many fine-grained GUI operations across
applications, files, and intermediate artifacts, with later actions depending
on earlier discoveries and decisions
(

and an output requirement encountered much earlier. Meanwhile, repeated
visual observations and tool feedback enlarge the history supplied to each
decision
(

requires controlling context growth while keeping current state, earlier
progress, and task-relevant knowledge available for continued action.

We use the report’s separate rubric scores to select data for different
learning goals. Task fulfillment identifies completed work, while process
quality, efficiency, and side-effect assessments let us adjust selection

article.headline: NorthCUA用规模化经验加速电脑使用智能体
article.lede: NorthCUA以全生命周期运行时收集软件任务经验，训练桌面与网页GUI智能体；397B的Pro在多项基准上超过参数更大
article.problem: 电脑使用智能体正从单步点击扩展到跨应用的复杂软件工作，但要让模型把早期决策与最终结果连起来，需要大量「任务构造—执行—判定」闭环经验。构造这类任务本身就要有可落地的请求、可用的初始环境与可靠的成败判定，长程交互还会让截图与工具反馈不断膨胀上下文。因此任务如何生成、智能体如何长时间执行、经验如何回流训练，三者必须联合设计。
article.method: 作者把执行框架做成覆盖全生命周期的 Harness：环境准备、执行、评估到记录保存都在同一运行时内完成，Batch Rollout Service 负责并行调度工作节点并让各阶段重叠，以支撑高并发经验采集。在此之上，「经验飞轮」批量构造任务并按评估报告的分项打分筛选示范数据，再经长程监督微调与桌面—网页联合强化学习训练 Nano、Mini、Pro 三档模型。另有一个 NorthCUA-Ultrafast 变体，用轻量分类头直接选择有限动作以绕过解码。
article.results: 论文称 397B 的 Pro 在两个 grounding 基准、OSWorld-Verified 与 WebArena-Verified 上均超过「万亿参数」的 Qwen3.8-Max 与 Kimi-K3；35B 的 Mini 在 OSWorld-Verified 上超过 Kimi-K3、在 WebArena-Verified 上超过 Qwen3.8-Max。WebArena-Verified 的最终 RL 检查点为 Nano 67.2%、Mini 70.4%、Pro 73.9%，SFT 阶段 pass@3 分别是 Nano 69.3%、Mini 73.9%。作为对照，作者自测 GLM-5.3-Flash-Vision 在 OSWorld 2.0 全部 108 个任务、500 步预算下取得 14.8% 完全完成与 48.7% 部分得分。延迟方面，Full generation 在匹配任务集上的平均任务时间为 616.8 秒；Ultrafast 的头训练使用约 226,000 个决策状态，head-only 仅训练 4.21M 参数（约占完整多模态检查点的 0.045%），加 LoRA 后为 47.49M。ScreenSpot-Pro 与 OSWorld 2.0 上 NorthCUA 各档的具体分数，材料中未给出完整数值。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「造任务、跑环境、判结果、选数据」串成一条可并行的工程流水线，说明电脑使用智能体的提升不只靠模型规模，也靠经验采集基础设施与评估信号的设计。对做智能体 RL 的团队来说，这套 Harness 与经验筛选口径比单点 benchmark 分数更值得复用。
article.limitations: 材料中多数对比表被截断，第三方基线多为作者自测且部分标注未报告，Pro 的 WebArena-Verified 成绩只来自一次覆盖全部 812 个任务的完整评测，缺少方差信息。评估依赖评审模型的分项打分来补充任务专用验证器覆盖不足的部分，这类判断本身可能引入噪声；同时 Full generation 平均每个任务仍需约 617 秒，长程成本尚未解决。
article.figure_caption_zh: 请求驱动的桌面环境构建示意：EnvAgent 识别所需资源、检索订单表并据其标识符补建缺失的货运表，由 LLM 把请求对应到文件名与共享的 Order ID 字段，再规定启动与检查步骤、在检查失败时修改输入或指令，最后由 GUI 智能体完成所要求的比较（图示为示意）。

page_papers.title: Avatar Intelligence: Amplifying Human Agency Through Persistent Personal Agents
page_papers.abstract: Personal AI agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks across applications, yet users often need to invest substantial effort in specifying goals, resolving ambiguity, and verifying outcomes. We argue that progress should be measured by how effectively agents amplify human agency: enabling people to pursue their goals with less routine supervision while retaining control over consequential decisions. We advocate Avatar Intelligence, a paradigm of persistent personal agents that represent users' goals, values, and constraints through sustained decision delegation across contexts and time. We describe a maturity roadmap from human-directed execution to autonomous operation within delegated domains, and introduce the Agentic Oversight Index (AOI) as a framework for evaluating delivered value against agent-side operational cost and human oversight burden. We identify three core research challenges: identity-continuous personalization that carries user preferences across tasks, user-situated evolution through Rehearsal Engineering, and safety mechanisms that combine technical control with accountability and recourse. These directions define a research agenda for reliable decision delegation to personal agents across tasks and over time.

We advocate

Imagine an AI agent system that acts on your behalf: it makes decisions, executes actions, and communicates with humans or other agents with minimal human intervention. Such a system is more than a tool that waits for explicit commands; it resembles a user-centric operating system—a persistent digital representative that embodies your preferences, values, and goals and operates continuously across contexts and time.
Recent years have witnessed the rapid development of foundation models (e.g., GPT-5.5
[
1
]
, Gemini-3
[
2
]
, and DeepSeek-V4
[
3

), which establish a general-purpose backbone for autonomous agents such as MUSE

and dots

.
Meanwhile, agent frameworks (e.g., those equipped with prompt/context/harness engineering and memory systems) have enabled more robust long-horizon task capabilities
[
4
]
. Beyond the exchange of information in digital environments, agents can increasingly manipulate end-user devices such as computers and smartphones
[
5
]
.
These developments make persistent personal agents increasingly plausible, but leave a central question unresolved: how much work must users still do to make delegation effective?
When delegating a research task, for example, an agent may retrieve and summarize documents while the user continues to resolve ambiguous objectives, correct interpretations, and judge whether the result is sufficient.
Execution effort decreases, while the burden of specification, coordination, and verification remains substantial.
Our position is that personal agents should amplify human agency by allowing users to pursue more of their goals without supervising every intermediate decision.
Human agency includes the ability to set and revise goals, choose which decisions to delegate, and redirect action when circumstances change.
Progress in personal agents therefore depends on reducing the effort required to obtain reliable, user-aligned outcomes while preserving these forms of control.
We use
Avatar Intelligence
to describe persistent personal agents that represent a user’s goals, values, and constraints across tasks and over time.
Concretely, an avatar should maintain commitments while the user is unavailable, adapt to changing circumstances, and know when to seek clarification or additional authorization.
This requires learning from ongoing interactions and evaluating how reliably the agent represents the user over time.
We develop this position through four contributions:
•
We characterize Avatar Intelligence through persistent user representation and sustained decision delegation, and describe a user-centric system architecture that supports these functions.
•
We outline a maturity roadmap (L0–L3) for transferring operational and decision responsibilities within defined delegation scopes.
•
We introduce the Agentic Oversight Index (AOI), an evaluation framework that accounts for delivered value, agent-side operational cost, and human oversight burden.
•
We identify three core research directions: identity-continuous personalization, user-situated evolution through rehearsal, and safety mechanisms for controlled and accountable delegation.
2  Avatar Intelligence
The essence of Avatar Intelligence is to align AI agents with human needs and expectations.
At its core, Avatar Intelligence reshapes the AI–human relationship by transforming agents from passive instruments into autonomous digital representatives that embody user identity, preferences, and values.
Rather than merely automating isolated tasks, avatars extend human agency beyond biological constraints by enabling persistent, autonomous operation across contexts and time.
2.1  Avatar as a User-Centric System
Figure 2:
Avatar Intelligence as a user-centric operating system. A persistent user model and memory support the inner loop of perception, planning, decision, and execution. The outer ring identifies three system capabilities: work continuity, proactive service, and capability expansion. Work, assistant, social, and custom clones carry the shared user identity into distinct task contexts, connecting the avatar to tools, applications, and other agents.
We conceptualize Avatar Intelligence as a
user-centric operating system
that externalizes a user's cognition into a persistent and executable digital form (Figure
2
). The kernel of such a system is not a thin memory cache, but a faithful and continuously updated model of the user's cognitive identity.
More specifically, at the OS level, the Avatar continuously observes the user’s behavioral patterns and decision-making logic, implicitly modeling and iteratively refining its understanding of the user’s profile and behavioral patterns. Based on this evolving user model, it can automatically align with the user’s implicit intentions when carrying out tasks on the user’s behalf, thereby enabling more personalized and cognitively faithful task execution.
Existing personalization methods largely optimize behavioral outputs using both training-time methods
[
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
]
and decoding-time alignment
[
11
,
12

13

, while current memory systems mainly extend context and accumulate experience
[
14
,
15
,
16
]
.
However, current methods are still insufficient for an Avatar that must preserve identity across contexts and over time. Operationally, the Avatar is organized around four tightly coupled components:
perception
,
planning
,
decision
, and
execution
, grounded by a persistent memory substrate. Together, they form a closed loop that transforms environmental signals into user-aligned action, enabling cognition to operate beyond explicit interaction.
In practical deployment, the Avatar instantiates multiple task-specialized clones as contextual projections of a single underlying identity, including work, assistant, social, and custom clones. These clones inherit the same user model while interfacing with heterogeneous execution substrates such as tools, applications, sandboxed environments, and external agents. This clone layer gives the Avatar three system-level capabilities essential to Avatar Intelligence:
Work Continuity
allows task state to persist across time, applications, and contexts, making long-horizon execution possible without repeated user specification.
Proactive Service
enables the system to act on inferred intent rather than waiting for explicit invocation, shifting the paradigm from reactive response to continuous assistance.
Capability Expansion
allows clones to dynamically incorporate new tools, services, and agents, turning the Avatar into an open-ended system whose functional boundary evolves with the user’s needs.
As these clones persist and scale, they will increasingly interface with other users’ agents, leading to a
multi-avatar ecosystem
in which many routine digital interactions are mediated by delegated representatives rather than direct human operation. In such settings, the core unit of interaction shifts from
human–system
to
avatar–avatar
coordination: scheduling, negotiation, information exchange, and joint task execution can occur through policies that represent distinct users’ identities and constraints. This shift reframes the technical problem from single-agent task completion to the design of protocols, incentives, and safety boundaries that enable cooperation under conflict, accountability under delegation, and trust under partial autonomy.
2.2  Roadmap
We view the path from today's agents to full Avatar Intelligence as a staged decoupling of
human involvement
from
agentic capability
(Figure
3
). The stages differ not only in autonomy, but also in the required system guarantees (identity continuity, controllability, and accountability):
•
L0: Human-for-the-loop.
The agent behaves as an augmented application, automating fragmented subprocesses while the user remains embedded in both execution and decisions.
•
L1: Human-in-the-loop.
The agent executes longer workflows, but users still steer key decisions (goal refinement, routing, validation) and absorb most accountability.
•
L2: Human-on-the-loop.
An
avatar core
(persistent identity + memory + decision policy) takes over routine decisions and orchestration; humans intervene at a small number of calibrated checkpoints, with robust runtime guardrails and audit trails.
•
L3: Human-out-of-the-loop.
The avatar assumes end-to-end autonomy over both operations and decisions for delegated domains; humans primarily perform post-hoc auditing, dispute resolution, and policy updates.
These levels describe autonomy within a delegated domain, and the same avatar can operate at different levels across domains. Users retain the authority to revise goals and revoke delegation at every level.
This roadmap highlights a key research transition: moving from improving execution quality (L0/L1) to engineering
decision delegation
with bounded risk (L2), and ultimately
institutional-grade assurance
for high-stakes autonomy (L3).
Figure 3:
Maturity roadmap toward Avatar Intelligence. The blue solid and orange dashed curves schematically illustrate increasing agentic intelligence and decreasing human involvement across L0–L3. The central transition is from execution-centric assistance to checkpointed decision delegation and ultimately end-to-end autonomy within delegated domains. The same avatar can operate at different levels across domains; users retain authority to revise goals and revoke delegation at every level.

3  Applications
3.1  Current Industry Products
A new generation of personal agents is beginning to turn persistent assistance into sustained action. Grok Bot keeps named bots and their context across tasks, allowing them to work through applications and return to the user when approval is needed
[
17
]
. Muse pursues ongoing goals through connected applications and a persistent browser, while seeking permission for actions such as sending messages or making purchases
[
18
]
. Cue envisions agents with their own email, phone, computer, and wallet, subject to boundaries set by the user
[
19
]
. OpenAI’s dots likewise continue work between conversations, draw on connected applications and memory, and bring decisions requiring human judgment back to the user
[
20
]
.
These systems move beyond one-off responses by carrying work forward over time. Yet the user remains central to setting goals, defining authority, and deciding when consequential actions may proceed. In the roadmap of Avatar Intelligence, they mark a transition from
human-in-the-loop
execution toward
human-on-the-loop
oversight within delegated tasks.

Personal Avatars for Life Administration and Continuity.
A personal avatar must carry commitments forward even when they are no longer visible in the immediate request. When a work trip conflicts with a parent–teacher meeting the user promised to attend weeks earlier, the avatar might first look for a later departure rather than simply clearing the calendar. If neither obligation can move, it should bring the conflict back to the user. The value of continuity lies in protecting obligations that a task-by-task assistant would easily overlook.
Enterprise Avatars for Organizational Roles and Operations.
Suppose engineering flags a release-blocking defect, while the launch calendar and sales brief still promise a release today. Acting for the project manager, an avatar could decide to postpone the internal launch, update the shared schedule, and notify the teams relying on the old date. It cannot waive the engineering blocker or revise a customer commitment on the sales team’s behalf; those decisions must return to the people who hold that authority. Such coordination depends on a shared view of the project that changes with new evidence, and on the distinct authority of the roles involved
[
21
,
22
]
.
Financial Avatars for Economic Decision Making.
The same market move can call for different actions depending on whose money is at stake. A planned purchase that remains acceptable for one user may push another user’s portfolio beyond a chosen exposure limit. In the latter case, the avatar should pause the order and seek a decision, even if the original instruction was to buy. Financial delegation is credible only when the user’s risk preferences shape the action itself and changes to those preferences remain under the user’s control.
Multi Avatar Interaction and Coordination.
Once avatars act for different people, a locally sensible decision may be unacceptable to the other party. In arranging a meeting, one avatar may seek the earliest slot while another protects its user’s preparation time. They can exchange acceptable windows and settle on a time that respects both constraints, or return to their users if no such time exists. The question is how agents can reach agreements without exposing more of either user’s preferences than the negotiation requires.
4  Open Challenges
Avatar Intelligence sits at the interface between the user side and the rapidly advancing frontier of agent technology.
On the one hand, an avatar must learn a user’s cognitive and decision patterns—capturing not only preferences, but also reasoning habits, methodologies, and value commitments. As a result, it can reliably understand the user and act as a faithful proxy.
On the other hand, it must continuously grow and evolve in real-world environments: connecting the user to appropriate agent capabilities, simulating the likely consequences of alternative actions, and selecting options that are best aligned with the user’s objectives, thereby building calibrated trust.
Finally, as agents become embedded in everyday life, a central question is how to ensure that such autonomy remains safe and controllable, preventing harm to the user and their environment while preserving the benefits of proactive, long-horizon assistance.
4.1  Personalization: From Behavioral Alignment to Identity-Continuous Avatars
Personalization is central to Avatar Intelligence: an avatar must make decisions
as the user would
, not merely respond in the user's preferred style. This requires learning from diverse, authorized signals (instructions, interaction traces, and environmental context) to infer stable decision structure, including values, trade-offs, and reasoning habits.
Most existing approaches
[
23
,
24
]
, however, optimize
behavioral outputs
(what action to take in a particular moment) rather than the latent cognitive model that generates behavior across contexts and over time. In practice, such systems often rely on memory to store user-specific facts or preferences and retrieve them at inference time. While effective for conversational personalization, memory-heavy heuristics can be brittle for agentic tasks: coverage is incomplete, preferences are context-dependent, and user behavior may be internally inconsistent. A core open problem is therefore to model an
identity-continuous
user representation that generalizes across tasks while remaining stable yet updateable.
Complementary to learning-based personalization, many deployed systems also use explicit configuration of identity (values and constraints), memory policies, and skill/tool scopes. A typical example is OpenClaw.

The challenge is to unify these layers into a coherent user model that remains consistent across clones, environments, and time.
We argue that
Avatar Personalization
should be formalized as learning an
identity-continuous
user model that enables transfer and generalization across tasks, while remaining stable yet evolvable.

From Behavioral Alignment to Computable Identity
A central requirement for Avatar Intelligence is that the user's cognition becomes
computable
and

to the system. Concretely, we characterize Avatar Personalization with two properties:
•
Thought Computability.
The user's internal decision process admits a compact representation, enabling the avatar to simulate how the user would reason under diverse contexts.
•
Intent Predictability.
Given a context, the avatar can reliably anticipate the user's intended action without requiring explicit instruction at every step.
Together, these properties shift personalization from surface-level preference matching to learning an
identity-continuous

4.2  Evolving with Specialization
The engineering of autonomous agents has historically focused on improving intent understanding and task completion through external scaffolding. From this perspective,
prompt engineering
injects user intent and constraints into the instruction channel;
context engineering
injects situational state (documents, observations, and memory) to ground planning; and
harness engineering
injects executable rules and control policies (e.g., tool gating, verification, retries, and escalation) to stabilize the action loop. These paradigms primarily shape behavior
at inference time
by conditioning what the agent sees and what it is allowed to do.

Prompt engineering specifies intent and constraints; context engineering supplies task-relevant state; harness engineering governs execution; and Rehearsal Engineering uses staged scenarios and user-situated feedback to improve behavior across episodes. A growing challenge, however, is to make agents
evolve
proactively from interaction with the environment. Recent explorations either (i) construct simulators or games where agents can rehearse trajectories, compare alternatives, and improve through iterative critique

effective feedback
—signals that evaluate decisions, not just executions—and turning such feedback into better future policies.
For Avatar Intelligence, feedback cannot remain purely generic. Beyond learning in standardized benchmarks or public web contexts, an avatar must specialize within the user's own ecology: their tools, routines, constraints, and risk tolerances.
We refer to this user-situated specialization loop as
Rehearsal Engineering
: a system-level methodology for aligning a standardized, language-trained agent to the user's real environment by (1) collecting user- and environment-specific traces and preferences, (2) staging representative scenarios (via simulation, counterfactual rollouts, or controlled sandboxing), (3) evaluating candidate actions with explicit oversight policies, and (4) updating the avatar's memory, skill selection, and decision policy under bounded autonomy.
Situated cognition research in psychology suggests that knowledge is closely tied to the contexts in which it is used
[
29
]
. By rehearsing within the user’s own work and life contexts, an agent may learn which contextual cues shape the user’s choices, and how those cues change the user’s trade-offs across situations.
In this view, rehearsal is not merely practice; it is the mechanism by which an avatar internalizes user-specific feedback while remaining safe, auditable, and corrigible.
4.3  Safety
Safety is a prerequisite for Avatar Intelligence because avatars are persistent, stateful, and increasingly entrusted with system access and delegated decision authority. We view avatar safety as two complementary layers distinguished by function rather than agent capability.
Technical safety
continuously enforces delegated authority, reduces the likelihood of failures, and limits their consequences.
Agent Insurance
complements these controls by allocating residual financial risk and compensating covered losses under explicit contractual terms. Both layers support delegation across capability levels: greater capability does not remove the need for technical control, and insurance provides defined financial recourse rather than a guarantee of correct or user-aligned execution.
Layer I: Technical safety for continuous control.
Across capability levels and throughout deployment, safety should be engineered end-to-end around intent fidelity, bounded autonomy, and adversarial robustness:
•
Intent alignment and corrigibility.
Maintain synchronization between the avatar's policy and the user's intent through explicit preference/constraint representations, intent-drift detection, and structured escalation (ask/confirm) at high stakes.
•
Runtime governance (harness-level control).
Enforce least privilege, sandboxing, action preconditions, irreversible-action verification, checkpointing/rollback, and deterministic replanning to constrain the action loop even when the model is wrong.
•
Security and integrity hardening.
Continuously monitor tool usage and environment interactions; detect prompt injection and anomalous behaviors; and protect long-term memory, credentials, and dependencies via sanitization and supply-chain scanning.
Layer II: Agent Insurance for contractually defined loss compensation.
Delegated tasks such as fund-moving, code changes, and account operations can expose users to substantial losses when execution fails. Technical safeguards reduce these risks, but residual uncertainty remains in open-world environments. Inspired by recent work on financial risk management for AI agents
[
30
]
, we argue that
Agent Insurance
, supported by auditable settlement mechanisms, will become a core infrastructure component for delegation at scale. Service fees can be escrowed and released upon verified delivery; providers can post collateral; and users can optionally purchase underwriting for losses arising from specified failures, such as non-delivery, misexecution, or intent misalignment. Coverage must define verifiable failure conditions, compensation limits, exclusions, and claims procedures. Crucially, compensation requires
auditable evidence
, including execution traces and evaluation artifacts, together with dispute processes. These mechanisms make responsibility for covered losses explicit and provide contractual recourse, while technical controls remain necessary to prevent harm, including harms that financial compensation cannot reverse.
Summary.
Taken together, the open problems in personalization, rehearsal-driven specialization, and safety/assurance constitute the missing infrastructure for advancing from L2 (checkpointed delegation) to L3 (full-pipeline autonomy within delegated domains). Identity-continuous personalization provides a stable decision prior, while Rehearsal Engineering supplies user-situated feedback loops to adapt that prior to real environments. Technical safety continuously constrains delegated actions and limits failure propagation. Agent Insurance provides infrastructure for pricing and allocating residual financial risk and compensating contractually covered losses. Together, continuous technical control and defined financial recourse support trustworthy delegation at scale as avatars assume broader responsibilities with less routine human supervision.
5  Conclusion
Avatar Intelligence frames persistent personal agents around a continuing relationship of decision delegation. Its value lies in enabling users to pursue their goals across tasks and over time with less routine supervision and effective control over consequential choices. We outlined a user-centric architecture, a delegation roadmap, and the Agentic Oversight Index to connect this objective with system design and evaluation. The central research agenda is to learn user representations that transfer across contexts, improve decisions through user-situated rehearsal, and support delegation with technical control, accountability, and recourse. Progress should be demonstrated through the decisions users can reliably delegate and the effort required to obtain outcomes they endorse.

article.headline: 把个人智能体做成持续决策代理
article.lede: 论文提出 Avatar Intelligence，主张用持续个人智能体承载目标与决策委托，并以 AOI 衡量监督负担。
article.problem: 长程任务智能体已能跨应用执行，但用户仍需大量设定目标、消解歧义并核验结果。执行负担下降，规格说明、协调与验证的负担并未同步消失。
article.method: 论文以立场文章形式提出 Avatar Intelligence：把智能体视为以用户为中心的操作系统，用持久用户模型与记忆支撑感知、规划、决策、执行的闭环，并通过工作、助理、社交、定制克隆共享同一身份。它给出从 L0 到 L3 的成熟度路线图，主张从人在环内执行走向在授权域内的人在环上监督与端到端自治。评价上提出 Agentic Oversight Index（AOI=U−λP），并将身份连续个性化、基于 Rehearsal Engineering 的用户情境演化、技术安全与 Agent Insurance 列为开放挑战。
article.results: 论文未给出具体实验数字或基准结果；作为立场论文，它给出 L0–L3 四级成熟度路线图和 AOI=U−λP（λ>0）的评价式，并列出三项核心研究挑战。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评价重心从单次任务成功率转向“交付价值减去人类监督负担”，为个人智能体的决策委托与问责提供可讨论的框架。
article.limitations: 论文没有实验验证，也未给出 AOI 的具体参数与校准结果；身份连续性、意图可预测性和 Agent Insurance 的可执行性仍停留在概念与制度设想层面。
article.figure_caption_zh: Avatar Intelligence 作为以用户为中心的操作系统：持久用户模型与记忆支撑感知—规划—决策—执行闭环，工作、助理、社交与定制克隆共享用户身份并连接工具、应用和其他智能体。

figure.caption: Avatar Intelligence as a user-centric operating system. A persistent user model and memory support the inner loop of perception, planning, decision, and execution. The outer ring identifies three system capabilities: work continuity, proactive service, and capability expansion. Work, assistant, social, and custom clones carry the shared user identity into distinct task contexts, connecting the avatar to tools, applications, and other agents. {fig:avatar}

page_papers.title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents
page_papers.abstract: As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on software engineering benchmarks, recent efforts have sought to increase task complexity through longer horizons and more extensive code modifications. However, real-world software development often spans multiple interdependent repositories, introducing additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and interface consistency. Rather than further increasing complexity within individual repositories, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. CrossSWE verifies the necessity of coordinated changes by testing whether partial repository modifications are insufficient to achieve the intended behavior. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. Furthermore, cross-repository inconsistencies emerge as the most prevalent failure mode (44.2%), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.

Abstract
As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on software engineering benchmarks, recent efforts have sought to increase task complexity through longer horizons and more extensive code modifications. However, real-world software development often spans multiple interdependent repositories, introducing additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and interface consistency. Rather than further increasing complexity within individual repositories, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. CrossSWE verifies the necessity of coordinated changes by testing whether partial repository modifications are insufficient to achieve the intended behavior. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. Furthermore, cross-repository inconsistencies emerge as the most prevalent failure mode (44.2%), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.
Figure 1:
Comparison of single-repository SWE tasks and cross-repository SWE tasks.
Figure 2:
Real-world example of cross-repository joint development involving oauth2-proxy and Higress.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) and coding agents
(
Lin et al., 2024
;
Lin et al., 2026
;
Ma et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Chen et al., 2026c
;
Chen et al., 2026d
;
Pan et al., 2026
;
Lyu et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026f
)
have made rapid progress on repository-level software engineering. Benchmarks such as
SWE-bench
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
)
have established issue resolution in real-world repositories as a standard evaluation setting, while subsequent work has expanded this paradigm toward broader language coverage
(
Zan et al., 2025
)
, larger codebases
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, longer-horizon tasks
(
Deng et al., 2025
)
, and more complex software changes
(
Shi et al., 2026b
)
. As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on established issue-resolution benchmarks, increasing task complexity has become an important direction for evaluating their capabilities.
However, existing efforts primarily pursue this direction within individual repositories.
No matter how large the codebase or how long the task, the context an agent needs to understand and the scope of changes it needs to consider are still bounded by a single repository, which limits how much further such tasks can grow in complexity.
Some recent benchmarks, such as
BeyondSWE
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
and
DepBench
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
, have started to bring multiple repositories into the picture.
However, the other repositories in these settings merely serve as context.
The agent reads them to understand an API, a dependency, or a change history, but the patch it writes and the tests that check it still stay within one repository.
To introduce greater complexity, we propose cross-repository SWE tasks for agent evaluation, which requires an agent to change multiple repositories together to complete a single task (Figure
1
).
It is a common real-world practice, as changes to APIs, libraries, or protocols in one repository can propagate to other dependent repositories, requiring corresponding modifications across repository boundaries. Such dependencies arise in API evolution, dependency migration
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
, compatibility fixes, and feature rollouts, where modifying only one repository may be insufficient to achieve the intended behavior.
Figure
2
illustrates a real-world example involving two repositories:
oauth2-proxy
and
Higress
. During session refresh, multiple cookies are incorrectly merged into a single HTTP header, causing authentication failures. Resolving this issue requires changes to both repositories:
oauth2-proxy
must preserve cookies as a list, while
Higress
must process and emit each cookie separately. Modifying only one repository leaves the shared interface inconsistent or the cookies improperly handled. Only the coordinated changes restore the intended behavior, illustrating the cross-repository joint necessity.
Figure 3:
Distribution of reference-patch sizes across CrossSWE, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-Bench ProMax.
Unlike conventional repository-level repair, cross-repository joint development requires agents to reason about dependencies and implementation constraints across multiple codebases
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
. Beyond understanding the implementation within each repository, agents must identify the relevant cross-repository interfaces, determine how changes affect dependent components, and produce mutually compatible modifications. Even when individual repository patches appear correct, inconsistencies between them can prevent the overall task from being resolved. These requirements introduce additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and cross-repository consistency that cannot be fully captured by single-repository evaluation.
To address this gap, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances
spanning 165 distinct repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. Among these instances, 165 involve two repositories, five involve three repositories, and one involves five repositories. As shown in Figure
3
, CrossSWE exhibits a broader reference-patch scope than SWE-bench Pro and SWE-Bench ProMax, with 56.1% of instances modifying more than ten files and 66.7% changing over 200 lines of code.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark comprising 171 real-world cross-repository joint-development tasks spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. (2) We evaluate five frontier LLMs, revealing substantial challenges in cross-repository joint development, with the strongest model achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. (3) We identify cross-repository inconsistencies as the most prevalent failure mode, highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.
2
Related Work
2.1
Repository-Level Software Engineering Benchmarks
Recent software engineering benchmarks have progressively expanded coding agent evaluation
(
Chen et al., 2026e
;
Zeng et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Zeng et al., 2026a
;
Zeng et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Chen et al., 2026f
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Shi et al., 2026a
;
Sun et al., 2026
)
from repository-level issue resolution to broader languages, task scales, and development stages.
SWE-Bench
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
)
established repository-level issue resolution as a realistic benchmark for coding agents, requiring agents to modify real GitHub repositories to complete tasks and pass corresponding test suites.
SWE-bench Pro
(
Deng et al., 2025
)
targets more challenging and longer-horizon software engineering tasks, emphasizing realistic development scenarios that often require substantial reasoning and modifications across multiple files.
SWE-Bench ProMax
(
Shi et al., 2026b
)
further expands the scope toward expert-curated, large-scale software engineering tasks across multiple programming languages, including complex refactoring and code transformation.
FEA-Bench
(
Li et al., 2025
)
and
FeatureBench
(
Zhou et al., 2026
)
extend repository-level evaluation beyond issue fixing to feature implementation, with the former constructing tasks from real-world pull requests and the latter targeting complex feature development spanning multiple commits and pull requests.
However, these efforts primarily increase complexity within individual repositories, leaving cross-repository coordination largely unexplored. CrossSWE explores this complementary dimension by benchmarking real-world development tasks that require jointly necessary changes across multiple interdependent repositories.
Figure 4:
Overview of the CrossSWE benchmark construction framework.
2.2
Multi-Repository Software Engineering
Recent benchmarks
(
Wang et al., 2026a
;
Chen et al., 2026a
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
have begun to move beyond single-repository issue resolution by considering software-engineering tasks that involve multiple repositories or external development contexts.
BeyondSWE
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
broadens coding-agent evaluation beyond single-repository bug fixing along both resolution scope and knowledge scope, covering settings such as cross-repository reasoning, dependency-driven migration, domain-specialized problem solving, and full-repository generation.
DepBench
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
further studies dependency breaking changes as a cross-repository repair problem, where upstream release notes and API changes provide evidence for repairing a downstream consumer after a dependency update. However, the upstream repository primarily serves as a source of repair evidence, while the generated patch and executable validation remain confined to one repository.
Although these efforts extend the scope of repository-level evaluation, incorporating cross-repository information or dependencies does not necessarily require multiple repositories to be modified together. In contrast, CrossSWE introduces
cross-repository joint development
as a complementary dimension of task complexity, where the solution itself spans multiple interdependent repositories. By explicitly verifying the joint necessity of repository changes, CrossSWE evaluates whether coding agents can implement mutually compatible modifications across repository boundaries rather than merely reason about cross-repository dependencies.
3
CrossSWE
This section describes how the benchmark is constructed, verified, and composed.
3.1
Task Formulation
Each instance in CrossSWE consists of four components:
(1) a pre-configured execution environment containing two or more participating repositories at their respective base commits, with all required dependencies installed;
(2) a problem statement describing a single software-engineering task that spans these repositories;
(3) a test suite that validates the target cross-repository behavior as well as required existing behavior; and
(4) repository-specific gold patches recording the original developers’ coordinated solution.
Given the environment and the problem statement, an agent must autonomously inspect and modify the participating repositories so that all required tests pass.
An instance is considered
resolved
if and only if the resulting joint repository state satisfies the complete evaluation suite.
Unlike conventional repository-level tasks, the solution in CrossSWE is not confined to a single codebase: the intended behavior requires coordinated changes across multiple repositories, such that modifying any repository in isolation is insufficient.
3.2
Benchmark Collection
Figure
4
illustrates the construction pipeline of CrossSWE, which progresses from broad candidate discovery to source-grounded validation and reproducible environment construction.
We adopt a multi-stage filtering and validation pipeline that progressively improves source validity, reproducibility, and task quality.
Figure 5:
Diversity of CrossSWE in terms of task intents, technical domains, and programming languages.
Stage 1: Candidate collection.
We use the GitHub API to identify active repositories and search their development histories for candidate cross-repository changes from January 2025 through September 2026.
We mine merged pull requests, issues with reconstructable changes, commits, and release or compatibility discussions using cross-repository relationship cues such as API evolution, dependency migration, provider–consumer, and client–server relations. We further identify candidates through explicit references to issues, pull requests, commits, or repositories in other codebases, which serve as signals of potential cross-repository coordination.
Stage 2: Human screening.
Since the discovery stage is intentionally designed for high recall, we next manually screen the collected candidates to remove cases that do not represent genuine cross-repository development. We inspect each candidate together with its source pull request or issue, development timeline, referenced repositories, and corresponding commits. A candidate is retained only when the source evidence identifies a concrete software change and at least two repositories contain substantive implementation changes that are causally, dependently, or coordinately related to the same task. We exclude candidates in which the additional repository involvement is limited to documentation, release notes, changelogs, or other non-implementation changes. Candidates with insufficient or ambiguous evidence are discarded. The remaining candidates proceed to multi-repository environment construction.
Stage 3: Environment construction and joint-necessity verification.
For each retained candidate, we construct a dedicated Docker image containing all repositories involved in the task. Each repository is checked out at its verified base commit, and all dependencies required to build and execute the repositories are installed in the same environment. We require every checkout to remain in a clean Git state and exclude fixed checkouts, gold patches, hidden tests, and artifacts produced from the fixed versions from the agent-facing image. This gives each instance a single, reproducible execution environment from which all subsequent evaluations are performed.
We then reconstruct a repository-specific gold patch for each participating repository and use these patches to verify whether the task genuinely requires coordinated cross-repository changes. For an instance involving

Stage 4: Problem statement construction.
The development artifacts associated with a candidate—such as pull requests, issue discussions, commit messages, and release notes—are often fragmented and implementation-oriented. Following SWE-Bench ProMax
(
Shi et al., 2026b
)
, we transform each verified candidate into a self-contained natural-language task specification. Drawing on source issues, pull requests, and repository changes, we describe the observable failure, expected behavior, and cross-repository requirements from the pre-fix perspective without prescribing implementation details. We further remove solution-specific information, including gold patches, fixed commits, and evaluator metadata, and manually verify consistency among the problem statement, source evidence, and tests.
In particular, we explicitly specify the required cross-repository behavior to avoid ambiguity about the intended task scope and ensure that hidden tests evaluate observable behavior rather than gold-patch-specific implementation details, such as function names, field names, or file paths.
3.3
Benchmark Composition
CrossSWE contains 171 verified instances spanning diverse cross-repository development scenarios. We characterize the benchmark along three dimensions: task intents, technical domains, and programming-language diversity.
Task complexity.
Figure
3
compares the reference-patch sizes of CrossSWE with SWE-bench Pro and SWE-Bench ProMax. In CrossSWE, 56.1% of instances modify more than ten files, compared with 6% in SWE-bench Pro and 30% in SWE-Bench ProMax. Similarly, 66.7% of instances involve more than 200 modified lines, compared with 13% and 32%, respectively. These results highlight the broader aggregate solution scope of CrossSWE, where coding agents must implement changes across multiple repositories rather than within a single repository.
Task and ecosystem diversity.
Beyond the scale of required modifications, we further examine the diversity of software-engineering scenarios covered by CrossSWE.
Figure
5

The benchmark covers eight task-intent categories, including feature development, API/schema/protocol evolution, security and observability coordination, migration, and compatibility maintenance. These tasks span 20 technical domains and 13 programming languages, covering heterogeneous software ecosystems and cross-language development scenarios. This diversity enables CrossSWE to assess coding agents across different development objectives, technical stacks, and language boundaries, providing a broader evaluation of cross-repository coordination capabilities.
4

Implementation Details.
We use

mini-SWE-agent
is a lightweight repository-level coding-agent framework that enables language models to inspect, modify, and test codebases through iterative shell-based interactions. We evaluate five representative frontier models: GPT-6.1 Sol

, Claude Sonnet 5.5

, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

, GLM-5.3 Flash

Qwen Team (2026)

reasoning-effort setting and keep the agent configuration fixed across experiments. Each run is limited to at most 300 interaction steps and a maximum model cost of $10.
Evaluation Metrics.
We evaluate each model on the same set of CrossSWE instances and report
Pass@1
as the primary effectiveness metric, where an instance is counted as resolved only when the final repository state satisfies the complete evaluation suite. We additionally report
Avg. Input Tokens
,
Avg. Output Tokens
,
Avg. Steps
, and
Avg. Cost ($)

5
Results
5.1
Main Results
CrossSWE remains challenging even for the strongest evaluated coding agents.
Table
1
summarizes the overall performance and resource usage of the evaluated coding agents on CrossSWE. Even the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieves only 58.48% Pass@1 on CrossSWE, substantially below its reported 75.2% performance on DeepSWE v1.1. This gap suggests that cross-repository joint development introduces substantial challenges beyond conventional repository-level software engineering tasks. Among the remaining models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash achieves 52.63%, followed by Claude Sonnet 5.5 (50.29%), GLM-5.3 Flash (43.86%) and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (45.03%). Performance also varies across language settings. GPT-6.1 Sol leads on single-language tasks with 60.34% Pass@1, compared with 54.55% on multi-language tasks. Notably, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash remains competitive on multi-language tasks, achieving 52.73% Pass@1. These results reveal distinct model capabilities when cross-repository development spans programming-language boundaries.
Closed-source models achieve competitive costs despite higher token prices.
Despite its higher per-token pricing, GPT-6.1 Sol achieves the highest Pass@1 with an average cost of $0.3496 per instance, close to GLM-5.3 Flash ($0.3411) and moderately higher than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.2881) and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ($0.2939). This cost competitiveness is consistent with its substantially shorter interaction trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 require only 32.9 and 29.2 steps on average, respectively, compared with 152.7 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 141.7 for GLM-5.3 Flash, and 182.1 for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. These results highlight GPT-6.1 Sol’s favorable effectiveness–cost trade-off, achieving the highest task success rate while offsetting its higher per-token pricing through substantially shorter interaction trajectories.
5.2
Joint vs. Independent Development
To investigate the additional challenges introduced by joint cross-repository development, we derive 330 single-side modification tasks from the 165 two-repository instances in CrossSWE. Each derived task retains both repositories in the execution environment but requires modifications to only one repository, allowing us to examine agent performance when cross-repository context is preserved but joint modification is no longer required.
Joint cross-repository development is more challenging than single-side modification.
As shown in Table
2
, both models achieve higher Pass@1 with fewer actions under the single-side setting. GPT-6.1 Sol improves from 58.48% to 64.55% (+6.07 percentage points), while its average steps decrease from 32.90 to 18.54. Similarly, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash improves from 52.63% to 61.81% (+9.18%), with average steps decreasing from 152.70 to 126.94. These results indicate that cross-repository joint development poses additional challenges beyond accessing multiple repositories, as agents must implement mutually compatible changes across repository boundaries.

5.3
Agent Behaviour Analysis
Figure
6
compares the distributions of input tokens, output tokens, final source lines changed, and interaction steps across the five coding agents on CrossSWE. We further examine their trajectories to understand how different agents approach cross-repository development tasks.
Fewer interaction steps do not imply proportionally smaller code modifications.
Although GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 require substantially fewer steps, the differences in final source lines changed are much smaller than those in interaction length. This suggests that their shorter trajectories are not simply the result of making fewer modifications, but may reflect a greater concentration of code changes within fewer interactions. In contrast, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 Flash perform substantially more interactions without a proportional increase in the size of their final patches.
Coding agents exhibit distinct exploration and modification strategies.
Our manual inspection of agent trajectories reveals different problem-solving patterns. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 tend to identify relevant code locations and begin modifying repository source code earlier, often making larger, more concentrated edits. In contrast, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 Flash tend to spend more interactions exploring repository structures and dependencies, followed by frequent alternation between incremental code modifications and testing.
Such differences may help explain why longer interaction trajectories do not consistently yield better cross-repository task performance.
5.4
Failure Patterns Analysis
To investigate why coding agents fail on cross-repository joint-development tasks, we manually analyze unsuccessful trajectories and classify their primary failure causes into five categories: (1)
Cross-repository inconsistency
, involving incompatible interfaces, protocols, or artifacts across repositories, including related compilation and build failures; (2)
Incomplete implementation
, where the agent fails to implement all required functionality; (3)
Compatibility regression
, where modifications break previously correct behavior; (4)
Logic/state errors
, involving incorrect program logic or state management; and (5)
Boundary handling
, involving unhandled edge cases or exceptional inputs.
Cross-repository inconsistencies dominate agent failures across all five models.
As shown in Figure
7
, cross-repository inconsistency is the most prevalent failure category across all five models, accounting for 44.2% of GPT’s unsuccessful trajectories, 41.2% of Claude’s, 29.2% of DeepSeek’s, and 40.7% of GLM’s. Incomplete implementation is another major failure mode, particularly for Claude (29.4%), DeepSeek (25.0%), and GLM (25.4%). Meanwhile, DeepSeek exhibits a more distributed failure profile, with relatively higher proportions of compatibility regressions (18.8%) and boundary-handling errors (14.6%). These findings suggest that, although models differ in their failure patterns, maintaining consistency across repositories remains a common challenge for current coding agents.
6
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark that extends software-engineering evaluation beyond single-repository task complexity to cross-repository joint development. It comprises 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages, with executable verification of jointly necessary repository changes. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model achieving only 58.48% Pass@1.
Comparisons with single-side modification tasks further reveal higher success rates when only one repository requires changes, highlighting the additional challenges of joint development.
Failure analysis further identifies cross-repository inconsistencies as the dominant failure mode, highlighting the limitations of current coding agents in maintaining consistency across repository boundaries. CrossSWE provides a foundation for evaluating and improving cross-repository development capabilities.
Limitations
Despite its contributions, CrossSWE has several limitations. First, although the benchmark contains 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories and 20 technical domains, its coverage of large-scale multi-repository development remains limited. Specifically, 165 instances involve two repositories, while only six involve three or more repositories. Future work could extend the benchmark to larger networks of interdependent repositories.
Second, CrossSWE provides agents with the participating repositories to focus evaluation on cross-repository dependency reasoning and coordinated code modifications rather than repository discovery. However, real-world development may require agents to identify relevant repositories from a broader software ecosystem. Future extensions could introduce irrelevant repositories to assess repository discovery and selection capabilities.
Third, we adopt a unified mini-SWE-agent scaffold and consistent configurations to ensure fair comparisons across models. Since mini-SWE-agent primarily relies on Bash-based interactions, which are widely supported by coding-agent harnesses, our findings may also provide insights into other shell-based frameworks, although direct validation remains necessary. We additionally impose limits of 300 interaction steps and $10 per instance.
Ethical Considerations
Our benchmark is constructed from publicly available GitHub repositories and development histories. Potential risks include the redistribution of personal information, sensitive data, or offensive content contained in source artifacts, as well as the computational resources required for agent evaluation. To mitigate these risks, we reviewed the benchmark artifacts before release to identify personal identifiers, sensitive information, and potentially offensive or objectionable content. We focus on technical information necessary for task reconstruction and evaluation rather than developers’ personal identities or unrelated content, minimizing unnecessary exposure of such information. Additionally, evaluating coding agents may incur substantial computational and monetary costs, which should be considered when reproducing or extending our experiments.

Appendix A
Appendix
A.1
Data Availability
We publicly release CrossSWE to support future research on cross-repository software engineering:
https://huggingface.co/datasets/CrossSWE/CrossSWE-Bench
.
A.2
Task-Intent Taxonomy
The eight high-level task-intent categories are mutually exclusive and cover all 171 instances in the formal evaluation subset. The definitions shown in table
3
describe the primary cross-repository behavior represented by each high-level category.
Table 3:
High-level task-intent taxonomy used for the formal 171-instance benchmark composition analysis.
Category
Instances
Definition
Feature development

Implement a new user-facing capability whose coordinated behavior spans multiple repositories.
API / schema / protocol evolution

Bug fixing

Appendix B
Data Licensing and Release
CrossSWE is constructed from publicly available GitHub repositories and development histories. The benchmark dataset is hosted on Hugging Face, with source references and patch provenance preserved for attribution. We reviewed the upstream licenses of all 165 repositories and documented their applicable terms in the dataset release. Original non-code benchmark materials are licensed under CC-BY-4.0, while third-party source-code contributions remain subject to their respective upstream licenses. For instances involving commercially licensed MUI X components, official licensing documentation permits qualifying non-production benchmark use.
Appendix C
Use of AI Assistants
AI assistants (such as ChatGPT) were used to draft basic code and refine the language of the manuscript. All experimental designs, data analyses, and conclusions were conducted and verified by the authors themselves. The role of AI was limited to generating general code and optimizing language; it did not influence the research results or their reproducibility.

article.headline: 跨仓库联合开发基准：最强模型通过率 58.48%
article.lede: CrossSWE 收录 171 个真实跨仓库协同任务，覆盖 165 个仓库、20 个领域、13 种语言，并验证只改单仓库
article.problem: 编码智能体在 SWE-bench 一类的单仓库问题上成功率越来越高，后续工作主要靠加长任务时间跨度和扩大代码改动量来继续提升难度，但任务范围始终被限制在一个仓库内。即便 BeyondSWE、DepBench 等基准引入了其他仓库，那些仓库也只作为理解 API 或依赖的上下文，智能体写的补丁和用于验证的测试仍留在单一仓库。然而在真实开发中，一处 API、库或协议的变更往往需要向依赖它的其他仓库传播，只改一侧无法实现预期行为。
article.method: 作者从 GitHub 上 2025 年 1 月至 2026 年 9 月的历史中挖掘跨仓库候选变更（如 API 演进、依赖迁移、provider–consumer 关系等），再经过人工筛选，剔除只涉及文档或发布说明的案例，并为每个任务构建包含全部参与仓库的 Docker 环境。核心验证是联合必要性检验：对涉及 N 个仓库的实例，穷举 2^N 种「基线状态与打补丁状态」的组合，并运行 FAIL_TO_PASS 测试，只有当全部基线状态以及所有只改部分仓库的配置都失败、所有补丁同时应用才通过时，该实例才会被保留。随后用统一的 mini-SWE-agent v2.4.6 脚手架评测五个前沿模型，每个实例最多 300 步、成本上限 10 美元，并人工归类失败轨迹。
article.results: 最强的 GPT-6.1 Sol 仅取得 58.48% Pass@1，明显低于论文提到的其在 DeepSWE v1.1 上的 75.2%；DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 为 52.63%，Claude Sonnet 5.5 为 50.29%，Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 为 45.03%，GLM-5.3 Flash 为 43.86%。从 165 个双仓库实例衍生出的 330 个单侧修改任务上，GPT-6.1 Sol 升至 64.55%（+6.07 个百分点），平均步数从 32.90 降到 18.54；DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 升至 61.81%（+9.18），步数从 152.70 降到 126.94。跨仓库不一致是最主要的失败模式，占 GPT 失败轨迹的 44.2%、Claude 的 41.2%、GLM 的 40.7%、DeepSeek 的 29.2%。参考补丁规模上，56.1% 的实例修改超过十个文件、66.7% 修改超过 200 行，而 SWE-bench Pro 分别为 6% 和 13%，SWE-Bench ProMax 为 30% 和 32%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评测维度从「单仓库内更难」转向「跨仓库协调一致」，对应 API 演进、依赖迁移、兼容性修复等真实工程场景，说明单纯拉长任务时间跨度并不能覆盖这类能力缺口。失败模式分析也给出了可操作的改进方向：智能体更常失败于跨仓库接口与协议不一致，在逻辑推理上较少失败。
article.limitations: 171 个实例中有 165 个只涉及两个仓库，仅 6 个涉及三个及以上仓库，且参与仓库已预先给定，不考察从更大生态中自行发现相关仓库的能力。所有实验共用 mini-SWE-agent 这一 Bash 交互脚手架，并受 300 步、10 美元上限约束，结论能否迁移到其他智能体框架仍需直接验证。

page_papers.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
page_papers.abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.

Abstract
Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present

Introduction
The digital computing environment has become the primary interface through which users interact with software, supporting a wide spectrum of tasks ranging from simple actions (e.g., website logins) to complex workflows (document editing). Recent advances in large (vision) language models
(
Bai et al., 2025
;
Singh et al., 2025
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Anthropic, 2026
)
have made it possible to automate such workflows through
computer-use agents
, which act in digital environments via fine-grained keyboard and mouse inputs
(
Gur et al., 2023
;
Furuta et al., 2023
;
Sager et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 1:
Comparison of error-handling strategies in computer-use agents. (A) Reflection proceeds from the erroneous state, (B) rollback requires often-infeasible environment resets, while (C) recovery restores a prior intact state and resumes the task.
However, computer-use agents remain fragile in long-horizon and sophisticated tasks, where early mistakes accumulate and propagate across subsequent steps
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
, and where executed actions may leave unintended side effects that should not have occurred (e.g., an agent organizing a directory may complete the task but silently overwrite files that the user wanted to keep). As a result, the ability to revert the environment to a previously intact state is critical for reliable operation. To address this, prior work explores two directions: inducing self-reflective behaviors through textual feedback or parameter updates from reward signals that refine forward actions
(
Chae et al., 2025a
;
Chae et al., 2025b
;
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Xue et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026c
)
, and explicit test-time rollback through full environment resets followed by re-executing all prior actions (i.e., action replay)
(
Koh et al., 2024b
;
He et al., 2025
)
or API-based undo operations in web environments (e.g., browser back)
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
, utilized as a heuristic component within an inference pipeline rather than subjected to systematic study.
Yet, these heuristic remedies fall short of providing general-purpose recovery. Environment resets are often infeasible in proprietary settings such as production websites and operating systems
(
Regatti et al., 2021
;
Nguyen and Cheng, 2023
;
Wang et al., 2026b
)
, action replay
(
Koh et al., 2024b
;
He et al., 2025
)
inherits this requirement and becomes costly over long horizons, and API-based rollback
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
is largely confined to web environments, leaving broader desktop settings uncovered. Consequently,
autonomous model-level recovery
, in which the agent itself restores a prior state without relying on such ad hoc mechanisms, emerges as an essential capability. However, whether current agents possess recovery capabilities, and how it affects overall agent performance remain largely unexplored. Therefore, we investigate several fundamental research questions:
RQ1.
Is recovery necessary to unlock models’ latent capabilities?
RQ2.
Do current computer-use agents possess recovery capabilities under erroneous conditions, and are such capabilities latent or entirely absent?
RQ3.
Does accurate model-level recovery translate into measurable improvements in task completion?

Results and Analysis
We now present and analyze the recovery evaluation results across both benchmarks and all agents.

Our results in Figures

This suggests that current forward policies lack both the intrinsic capability and the behavioral tendency to autonomously perform restorative actions under failure
(Finding 2)

The results in Figures

In addition, the largest improvements are observed for generalist computer-use agents, such as Claude-Sonnet-4.6, GPT-5.4-CUA, and Qwen-3.5-9B.
These results suggest that the recovery capability of current computer-use agents is latent rather than absent, but such capabilities are not effectively elicited during standard forward task execution
(Finding 3)
. In contrast, the gains are considerably smaller for post-trained open-source agents, suggesting that
extensive post-training on one-directional task-completion trajectories may weaken their inherent recovery capability
(Finding 4)
. Figure
7
shows the same trend in long-horizon settings: generalist agents exhibit substantially greater recovery potential, whereas post-trained specialists consistently struggle with explicit recovery. Nevertheless, even the most capable models combined with basic explicit recovery strategies still fail to achieve complete recovery under our evaluation settings, suggesting that substantial research remains in developing more robust recovery mechanisms
for computer-use agents.

Results and Analysis
Potential Gains from Model-Based Recovery
To validate the potential benefits of model-based recovery, we analyze its performance gains across diverse recovery settings. As shown in Table
2
, model-based recovery improves Qwen3.5-9B over the no-recovery baseline under every recovery setting, with an average gain of 2.12% in the end-to-end setting. Notably, these gains hold despite the suboptimal recovery success rates observed in Figures

and

indicating that even imperfect recovery can begin to unlock the latent capabilities of current computer-use agents, and that more reliable recovery mechanisms hold substantial promise for improving the overall performance and robustness
(Finding 5)

Recovery Performance Effects on Task Completion

The results in Table
3
show that models with weaker recovery capabilities (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, EvoCUA-32B) suffer performance degradation during end-to-end inference, underscoring the importance of accurate recovery behavior. In addition, Figure
8
demonstrates that allowing more recovery attempts yields further gains for models with comparably better recovery performance (Qwen-3.5-9B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B). EvoCUA-32B, in contrast, exhibits severely limited explicit recovery capability: while even a single successful recovery can substantially improve downstream task performance, its consistently low recovery success rate means that additional attempts more often derail the trajectory into increasingly erroneous states. This suggests that
accurate model-level recovery delivers performance gains, while weak recovery can actively derail the trajectory
(Finding 6)

article.headline: 计算机使用智能体的恢复能力仍不足
article.lede: ReTrace 通过扰动与目标导向动作回放系统评估计算机使用智能体的恢复行为，发现能力潜伏但难以稳定调用。
article.problem: 长程计算机使用任务中错误会累积，动作还会留下非预期副作用，因此智能体需要把环境恢复到先前完好状态。已有做法依赖环境重置、完整动作回放或网页 API 回滚，在专有环境、长程任务和桌面场景中分别不可行、昂贵或受限。模型自身能否恢复、这种能力是否影响任务完成，此前缺乏系统研究。
article.method: 作者提出 ReTrace：先收集成功轨迹，并将每个动作序列重复回放 N 次以构建转移一致的数据集；再通过扰动选定恢复目标并把智能体推入错误状态。随后从恢复状态回放剩余动作，检验智能体能否复现原任务结果，并在 OSWorld 与 WindowsAgentArena 上比较隐式与显式恢复。
article.results: 在 OSWorld 和 WindowsAgentArena 上，最强模型 Claude-Sonnet-4.6 与 GPT-5.4-CUA 的恢复能力仍有限，开源 EvoCUA-32B 平均恢复率低于 1%；显式模型级恢复平均比隐式恢复高 17.86%。在端到端设置中，模型级恢复让 Qwen3.5-9B 在每种恢复设置下都优于无恢复基线，平均提升 2.12%；但即使最强模型配合基本显式恢复策略，也未达到完全恢复。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明当前智能体并非完全缺乏恢复能力，而是标准前向执行没有有效激发它；系统评估恢复行为可为长程任务可靠性提供可度量基准。
article.limitations: 评估集中在 OSWorld 与 WindowsAgentArena，论文未给出向更多专有桌面和网页环境泛化的具体数字；恢复机制设计本身也超出本文范围。
article.figure_caption_zh: ReTrace 概览：(A) 在策略轨迹 rollout 中收集成功轨迹并重复回放动作序列 N 次以构建转移一致数据集；(B) 通过扰动选择恢复目标并将智能体推入错误状态；(C) 从恢复状态回放剩余动作，检验是否复现原任务结果。

figure.caption: Overview of {ReTrace}. (A) On-Policy Trajectory Rollout collects successful trajectories and replays each action sequence $N$ times to build a transition-consistent dataset. (B) Trajectory Drift via Perturbation selects a recovery target and perturbs the agent into an erroneous state. (C) Goal-Oriented Action Replay replays the remaining actions from the recovered state to test whether the agent reproduces the original task outcome.

page_papers.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
page_papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
