Abstract
Abstract:
Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the
agent harness
: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions.
First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development.
Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization.
We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.

just a finished clip
[
gao2026lingbotworld2
]
.
These requirements motivate a transition from video generation
to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results
inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference,
select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes
[
li2026videogenagent
]
.
Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator
architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions,
while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities.
Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots
[
chen2026cinecrew
]
,
actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt
temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a
narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality
score alone rarely specifies what to do next
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
,
ding2026playworld
]
. Effective control
requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining
project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.
The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a
foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an
LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation,
as demonstrated by ReAct
[
yao2023react
]
. Planning and memory extend
this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions
[
weng2023agents
]
.
Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness:
the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context,
exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions
and budgets
[
weng2026harness
,
ning2026code
]
(Section
).
For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an
interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors,
and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good
clip to reliably completing a video
task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two
concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks
can improve the system that will perform future tasks.
Figure 2:
Agent involvement across three directions of video generation.
Representative works branch from a shared video generation foundation into
agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development toward
recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video models to
sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the improvement of
models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects increasing agent
involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and Agent Guided
Improvement to Self Improvement.
Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision
or take replacement targets the current artifact
[
vista2025
]
;
retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
;
updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model
versions
[
liu2025videoalign
]
. These outcomes
should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by
itself establish improvement in future capability.
Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers
how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are
selected and organized for subsequent decisions
[
weng2026harness
]
.
Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a
structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model
weights
[
zhang2025ace
]
. Such work shifts attention from a current
response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the
mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.
Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model
development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments,
and reporting
[
lu2024aiscientist
]
;
autoresearch
runs a bounded
loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based
acceptance
[
karpathy2026autoresearch
]
. These workflows connect proposals
to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the
same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents,
exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive
Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the
agent’s own code or harness
[
zhang2025dgm
,
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate
subsequent improvements.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve
the procedures that produce further improvements
[
chen2026surveyr04
,
duan2026surveyn21
]
.
Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection,
supervision construction, update
selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training
pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally
allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers
and addresses weaknesses.
An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction.
Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing
workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized,
revised
[
weng2026harness
]
. This does not make every harness
self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on
later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints
[
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can
revise reusable production skills
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
, uncertainty can
guide data acquisition for adaptation
[
savov2025autoexplore
]
, and
validation can govern critic renewal for later training
[
yang2026dualipo
]
. These are
building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full
RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses
organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction,
and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first
two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines
persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it.
Figure
2
maps representative work from a shared video
generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions
below.
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness
on video generation (Figure
1
), each corresponding to
one core chapter.
How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation?
Agentic Video Generation (Section
) studies
how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and
watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such
systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes
generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency,
and efficiency.
How can the agent harness be integrated into video
world models?
Agentic World Modeling
(Section
) locates where a harness can intervene in
observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management,
and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state
while the video model renders it.
We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control
fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this
question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world
model.
How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement?
Toward RSI in Video Generation
(Section
) examines how advances in video
generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces
subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement,
agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through
which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data
curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms
and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that
can support next-generation video generation models.
These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction
can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into
changes deployed in later tasks. Section
compares the shared
agent capabilities that support all three settings.
Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys
Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation.
Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models,
representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the
mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences
[
yin2025spatiotemporal
]
.
Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video
generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation,
preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation
[
li2026videoposttraining
]
.
Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and
alignment with user instructions
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
]
.
Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved,
and assessed.
More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation
surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions
available to a controller across visual modalities
[
huang2026agenticvisual
]
,
or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of
stateful artifacts
[
xu2026ags
,
wang2026artifactcreation
]
. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single
capability ladder of visual generation
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
.
World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities
across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness
in sustained interaction
[
chu2026agenticworldmodel
,
liu2026interactiveworldmodel
]
,
or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to
continually improving agents
[
yang2026quovadis
]
.
Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding
agents
[
ning2026code
,
guo2026harnessdesign
]
.
Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets,
adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI
systems
[
gao2025surveyr02
,
chen2026surveyr04
,
wu2026rsisurvey
]
.
These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent
control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the
unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.
Table
1.2
compares related surveys and
adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design.
Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on
video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video
model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as
the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness:
agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide
interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model
development. Where capability ladders treat agentic
generation and world modeling as successive stages of the
generator
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
, we take the agent harness around the
generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production,
interaction, and development.
Our contributions are threefold.
•
A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness
execution loop (Section
) and apply it to
production, organized by workflow function
(Section
), and to world-model interaction,
organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes,
including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world
state (Section
).
•
An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current
output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and
evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels
through which an improvement could re-enter video development.
No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and
validates the generator (Section
).
•
Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness
supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and
world models (Section
), what the
evaluation of agentic production must separate
(Section
),
which capabilities video imposes on agents
(Section
), and which challenges remain
(Section
).

article.headline: 智能体外壳连接视频生成、世界模型与自改进
article.lede: 一篇综述提出以智能体外壳为分析单元，连接视频生成、世界模型交互与递归自改进。
article.problem: 视频生成模型能产出片段，但单模型不负责把创作简报拆成镜头、维持跨场景引用、检查素材并做局部编辑，也难以控制生成成本。交互视频还要求系统基于观察持续行动，而不只是输出一段成品。现有综述多分别讨论生成模型、世界模型或智能体，缺少以视频生成器外围可执行运行时为统一分析单元的视角。
article.method: 作者把 agent harness 定义为围绕模型构建上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈并执行预算的可执行运行时，并沿三条方向组织材料：智能体视频生成、智能体世界建模、面向视频生成的递归自改进。文章按工作流功能与交互接口分析生产与交互，并区分当前输出修复、harness 状态/生成器参数/评估器更新，以及开发流程改变。
article.results: 综述将材料组织为三条主线，对应三个核心问题：智能体视频生成、智能体世界建模，以及面向视频生成的递归自改进。作者区分当前输出修复、harness 状态/生成器参数/评估器更新和开发流程改变，并提出四条改进重新进入视频开发的通道。文中明确称，所调查系统中尚无系统修改训练与验证生成器的流程；论文未给出具体实验数字，图示缩略图也不是实验结果。
article.why_it_matters: 这个框架把评估从单段视频质量扩展到任务完成、状态连续性和改进是否被保留，可能推动视频生成从一次性合成走向可审计的长期工作流。
article.limitations: 这是综述与立场文章，未提供统一基准或实验验证。作者也承认尚无被调查系统完成修改训练与验证流程的完整 RSI 闭环，框架的实用性仍需实证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从视频生成到智能体外壳介导的世界交互：外壳围绕生成器完成观察、决策、控制翻译、调度与反馈整合，图中缩略图仅为示意而非实验结果。

figure.caption: {From video generation to harness-mediated world interaction.} Conditional visual generation remains the shared core. In a video world model, one-shot conditioning becomes sustained control, temporal context must support continuing state, and output frames become observations for the next decision. Around this core, the harness observes, decides, translates controls, schedules generation, and incorporates returned feedback and relevant history. The central interfaces translate controls, coordinate execution, and interpret returned observations. External memory and tracking are distinct from model-side state or context. The diagram summarizes shared, adapted, and added components; a particular system need not implement every component. page_papers.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
page_papers.abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

Abstract
Robot-use agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training.
To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks.
Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

Introduction
Recent breakthroughs in frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026c
)
, Opus 5.5
(
Anthropic, 2026
)
) have shown surprising zero-shot performance in robotic manipulation, highlighting robot-use agents (RUAs)
(
Isola, 2026
)
as a promising approach for robotics
(
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Qu et al., 2026
)
.
This approach effectively transfers the models’ generic problem-solving capabilities, such as task decomposition and failure recovery, which are hard to learn from limited robotics data alone, yet extremely useful for robotics
(
Isola, 2026
;
Chu et al., 2026
;
Jia et al., 2026
)
.
However, because these frontier foundation models are proprietary, research on RUAs has been limited to using the models as-is, such as harness design
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Si et al., 2026
)
.
Without access to their weights, researchers cannot directly explore how further training of these models can advance RUA capabilities.
Moreover, API dependence makes large-scale interaction costly
(
OpenAI, 2026c
)
and restricts model-level optimization, such as efficient caching, despite inference speed being a major bottleneck for RUA
(
Isola, 2026
)
.
The main challenge in adapting open-weight models for robot use is the capability gap between open-weight and closed-weight foundation models. Robot use demands strong spatial understanding and agentic capabilities, which existing open-weight models often lack. Consequently, prior work has focused on ad-hoc improvements, including leveraging privileged information such as ground-truth simulator states or oracle task-success feedback
(
Fu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, or incorporating task-specific skills
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
.
Before attributing these limitations to the models themselves and pursuing ad-hoc improvements, we argue that we must first establish a generalizable and effective robot-use harness to systematically understand and maximize their existing capabilities, laying the foundation for future RUA training.
In this paper, we take a first step toward democratizing robot-use agent research by laying this foundation for both competitive open-weight agents and future robot-specific training. We introduce uni-robot-agent, a general-purpose RUA harness. It provides
Unified
tool interfaces and feedback formats across models, embodiments, tasks, and environments, supporting joint training on simulation and real-world interaction data.
For future large-scale training, we emphasize
Efficiency
by overlapping model reasoning with tool execution to accelerate interaction, and
Modularity
through interchangeable agent runtimes, tools, and robot backends.
Together, these designs provide a scalable, extensible foundation for RUA research.
The proposed uni-robot-agent enables competitive manipulation performance with open-weight models, including Qwen and DeepSeek, in both simulation and physical environments.
A key finding is that well-structured information, such as camera calibration and robot descriptions, together with reliable tool interfaces that provide informative feedback, are
sufficient
for effective robot use. As a result,
without privileged inputs
, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent achieves a Score of
31.39
, surpassing GPT-6 Astra’s result (
28.97
) on RoboDojo
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
from the RoboDojo team
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system to outperform closed-weight foundation models on RoboDojo using open-weight models, without privileged informations or distillation from those closed-weight models.
In real-world experiments on 19 tabletop manipulation tasks, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent achieves a Score of
49.50
, outperforming Dream-1 (
35.50
;
Dream Labs, 2026
) and matching fine-tuned
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
47.75
;
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
).
Having established the competitiveness of open-weight RUAs, we further compare models across generations, families, and sizes to investigate the capabilities underlying robot use.
Trajectory analysis reveals four common failure patterns involving visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning.
Based on these findings, we posit that current robot-use capability emerges from a combination of these general-purpose capabilities and identify them as key areas for improvement in future RUA training.
Finally, we provide an analysis of the effect of privileged information, cost, and execution efficiency.
Figure 2
:
Five logical layers of uni-robot-agent.
Requests flow from agent runtimes through orchestration and shared tools to domain services and native backends. Context policies and concrete backends are replaceable components; arrows summarize logical interactions rather than individual network connections.
2
uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
In this section, we introduce the key mechanisms of uni-robot-agent. We describe how the harness connects diverse agents, robot environments, and embodiments through shared tools and supports interaction based on information only available in real-world deployments.
2.1
System Overview
uni-robot-agent connects different agent runtimes to a shared toolkit for simulation and physical robots. The agent selects operations using task instructions and observations, while the harness executes them and returns feedback. We organize this interaction around four principles:
•
Unified.
Shared tools give operations and feedback a common meaning across environments, with adapters handling native APIs (Section
2.2
). The resulting interaction records can also be combined for subsequent training.
•
Efficient.
Reasoning should overlap physical execution, while operations that share a resource retain their required order (Section
2.3
).
•
Realistic.
Agents and tools should rely on information available in physical deployments, without simulator-provided depth or task-verifier feedback (Section
2.4
).
•
Modular.
Explicit interfaces should allow researchers to replace runtimes, tools, and perception models independently. We introduce this architecture below.
These principles guide how we organize the system, but reliable interaction also requires care in how observations, actions, and feedback are handled. We first describe the architecture, then examine these practical design choices in Section
2.5
.
Modular Architecture.
A tool call passes through five layers with explicit interfaces (Figure
2
). The
agent layer
manages model interaction and context, passing tool requests to the
orchestration layer
for scheduling and dispatch. The
tool layer
implements shared robot operations and accesses environment, perception, and action-model capabilities through the
service layer
, which manages their runtime resources. The
backend layer
supplies the concrete simulator, robot, and model implementations used by these services. Results return through these interfaces to the agent, completing the interaction.
2.2
Unified Interaction Interface
Moving a gripper to a target pose should mean the same thing in simulation and on a physical robot, even when their control APIs differ. We give agents a shared set of tools for motion, perception, skills, and episode control, with common arguments, units, and feedback formats. Environment descriptions identify the available arms, cameras, and optional capabilities. This lets the agent use familiar operations while accounting for the robot and sensors available in each environment.

:
Tool reuse across environments.
Shared tools avoid

To make these operations work across environments, shared tools access observations, robot state, and primitive actions through a common interface implemented by environment adapters.
For example, the shared
move
tool generates intermediate targets and monitors progress; the adapter translates those targets into native commands and returns the resulting state.
Adding an environment therefore requires an adapter and its configuration rather than a separate implementation of every tool.
As Figure
2.2

The common request and feedback formats also make the experience collected across environments easier to combine for subsequent training.
2.3
Efficient Execution
The orchestration layer determines how agent interaction proceeds while tools are running. Waiting for every movement to finish delays reasoning that could proceed independently, yet successive movements may still need to execute in order. We combine background tool calls with resource-aware scheduling to satisfy both requirements, forming a pipeline between agent reasoning and tool execution.
Two Levels of Concurrency.
The agent need not wait for every tool, but its next call may still need to wait for a resource:
•
Between agent and tools.
A
background
call returns a job handle, allowing the agent to continue independent reasoning and retrieve the result later; an
immediate
call waits for completion. Decisions that depend on the result must still wait.
•
Among tool calls.
Calls sharing an exclusive resource execute in submission order; parallel calls run outside that queue. Two
move
calls on the same resource therefore run sequentially, while reading an existing snapshot can overlap movement.
Two-Stage Pipelining.
These mechanisms enable a two-stage pipeline comprising agent reasoning and tool execution (Figure
2.3
). The agent can submit successive calls while previously submitted calls execute in resource order. Reasoning and execution thus overlap even when the tools themselves execute sequentially. When observations or execution feedback require a change of plan, the agent can use
flush_queue
to cancel calls that have not started for a specified resource. Where supported, a single model response can submit multiple tool requests, and a batched wait can retrieve multiple results.

2.4
Interaction Without Privileged Inputs
Efficient execution alone does not ensure that simulation performance carries over to physical robots: the information supporting each action also matters. Existing systems provide depth-based geometry and completion checks
(
Li et al., 2026
)
, or construct object models to maintain a virtual scene
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. In physical settings, depth measurements can vary or be missing even in a static scene, and simulator task-verifier feedback is unavailable. These differences motivate testing whether agents can infer spatial relationships and assess progress from more limited observations.
2.5
Key Design Choices
Effective robot use requires careful design of how observations reach the agent, how commands are executed, and how outcomes inform subsequent decisions. We introduce six practical design choices spanning observation and execution consistency, coordinated motion control, progress monitoring, actionable feedback, and visual context management.
Figure 5
:
Key design choices.
Each column pairs two designs for physical consistency, action precision, or context management.
Keeping Observations and State Consistent.
When a robot moves after an image is captured, interpreting a selected pixel using a newer camera pose mixes two physical states. We bind images, camera calibration, and robot state to an immutable snapshot and use that snapshot for localization (Figure
5
). The agent and tools thus work from the same recorded state.
Preventing Repeated Actions After Communication Failures.
The agent must also know which actions have occurred: a missing reply may mean lost feedback, so retrying could repeat a physical action. We record request identities and execution status to reject duplicates (Figure
5
). If completion is uncertain, further actions are blocked while the session attempts to recover the execution record; unresolved requests remain explicitly marked as uncertain.
Coordinating Motion and Gripper Control.
Separate movement and gripper commands prevent the agent from adjusting the opening during a movement. Our
move
tool accepts a target pose and an optional gripper opening together, allowing the arm and gripper to act simultaneously (Figure
5
).
Detecting When Motion Should Stop.
During execution, a fixed step count may stop motion too early or waste steps on an unreachable target. Our
move
tool generates intermediate targets from measured poses and checks progress after each step (Figure
5
). This lets the tool adjust motion locally, stop on arrival, and return control when motion stalls or reaches an execution limit. Appendix
D
gives the algorithm and stopping criteria.
Making Action Outcomes Diagnosable.
Reaching a target pose does not establish that an object was grasped or placed successfully. We return numerical motion feedback, including pose errors and stopping reasons, alongside images of the outcome (Figure
5
). The numbers distinguish a small residual error from rejected or stalled motion; the images show the effect on the object. Together, they help the agent decide whether to refine the motion or change its manipulation strategy.
Managing Growing Visual Histories.
This feedback accumulates, but old images may lose relevance while task instructions and action records remain useful. Our sliding window replaces old images with text placeholders, preserving recent images and the surrounding text (Figure
5
). We evict images in batches to keep the prompt prefix stable between evictions and support cache reuse. If the context still exceeds budget, we compact the history with the same model that we use for the policy, using the compaction prompt of the codex CLI
(
OpenAI, 2026a
)
.
3
Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
Effective robot use has largely been the preserve of frontier, closed-source models. In this work, however, we show that open-weight models can also achieve competitive performance in simulation and on physical robots. In particular, on RoboDojo, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next surpasses most fine-tuned VLA and WAM baselines in a zero-shot setting without privileged information, and also the GPT-6 Astra’s result reported by the RoboDojo team.
On real robots, a less-explored setting in prior works, open-weight models also achieve competitive performance, showing their real-world applicability.
These results highlight the viability of open-source robot-use agents and the importance of a properly designed harness for supporting these models.

3.1.1
Setup
We evaluate 42 RoboDojo
(

We report the success rate and the score (incorporating partial success, scaled to 0–100) following the RoboDojo’s evaluation protocol. 4.3
Four Major Failure Modes
Our trajectory analysis identifies four major failure types:
general visual understanding
, such as misinterpreting objects or action outcomes;
fine-grained pointing and spatial grounding
, such as selecting inconsistent corresponding points across views;
localization and pose computation code
, involving errors in geometric calculations, coordinate transformations, or orientation construction; and
embodied reasoning
, such as proposing physically inappropriate grasp poses. Figure
7
summarizes these four failure types across thirteen models.
General visual understanding.
Perhaps the most straightforward reason for failures in earlier Qwen Flash and Plus models is basic visual misunderstanding. Such errors, including mistaking zero for nine or inverted cups for upright ones, occur in
12.2–23.8%
of trials. In contrast, these kinds of errors occur in
3.2%
of Qwen3.8-27B trials and none of the trials from more performant models such as Qwen3.8-Flash or GPT-5.6 Sol. These observations suggest that general visual understanding is closely associated with its performance.
Spatial grounding.
In addition to coarse scene understanding, we find that models struggle to pinpoint the same physical feature across camera views. Selecting inconsistent pixels for the same feature leads to large reprojection errors, causing the triangulation tool to reject the result. We therefore use the fraction of calls rejected for this reason to measure difficulty in pinpointing corresponding features. Task performance tends to be negatively associated with this failure rate: Qwen3.8-Flash and DeepSeek have lower failure rates than models with zero task success, including Qwen3.5–3.7 Flash and Qwen3.7 Plus. GPT-6.1 Sol achieves the lowest spatial-grounding failure rate among the evaluated models (31.5%), but this substantial remaining error rate highlights precise spatial grounding as a common challenge for further improvement (Figure
7
b).
Coding in geometry
Coding skill is also closely correlated with task performance, as illustrated by geometry computations involving coordinate transformations and orientations. Earlier Qwen models frequently reverse coordinate transforms or mix quaternion conventions, with such errors affecting
47.3–81.8%
of executed calculations across the earlier Flash and Plus cohorts. In contrast, the error rates are
8.2%
for Qwen3.8-Flash,
1.5%
for DeepSeek, and
0.7%
for GPT-5.6 Sol, with no errors in GPT-6.1 Sol’s calculations. The pattern suggests that reliable robot-specific computation is another capability associated with effective robot use (Figure
7
c).
Embodied reasoning.
Beyond perceiving and computing a target pose, robot use requires embodied reasoning to propose appropriate interactions, including grasp poses. Because this broad capability is difficult to measure, we restrict our analysis to pick-and-place and use GPT-6 Astra to assess whether proposed grasp poses are physically reasonable. We report the rate at which the model proposed unnatural or infeasible grasping poses and failed to correct them in these tasks (Figure
7
d). To our surprise, even recent models can lack this capability: GLM repeatedly fails to reorient its wrist for grasping, contributing to many unsuccessful trials and a
26.2%
error rate. Such errors are less frequent in newer Qwen and GPT models, which more often select appropriate grasp orientations. However, grasp-pose proposal is only one instance of embodied reasoning. GPT-6 Astra still struggles with other skills, including bimanual coordination, where inappropriate interaction plans limit performance. Embodied reasoning therefore appears to improve across model generations, but remains a substantial bottleneck beyond this narrow grasping analysis.
In conclusion, these failure patterns suggest that effective robot use draws on a combination of visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning, rather than a single robot-specific capability. This suggests that general model capabilities provide a substantial foundation for robot use. We therefore argue that future RUA training should develop these capabilities jointly – for example, by using robot data to construct training tasks targeting each capability – rather than focusing solely on fitting action outputs.

Related Work
Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend robot policies beyond task-specific demonstrations by transferring pretrained visual-language representations and learning from diverse robot data
(
Brohan et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
)
. Training on heterogeneous sources has further improved generalization:
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
performs manipulation in previously unseen environments by combining robot experience with semantic supervision and web data
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
. World-action models (WAMs) explore a complementary route through predictive modeling. Joint video and action generation enables DreamZero to generalize to unseen tasks and environments
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, while Cosmos Policy uses predicted future states and values to support test-time planning
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
. These advances broaden where learned policies can operate and what behaviors they can perform. Reliable use of past observations and recovery from failures over extended interactions nevertheless remain important areas for further investigation.
Tool-Using Agents for Robot Control.
Tool use allows language models to organize decisions around observations and feedback. In computer environments, agents operate graphical interfaces through repeated observation and action, combining visual grounding with planning and context management
(
Anthropic, 2024
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Agashe et al., 2025
)
. Robotics research has explored related ideas through skill selection and programmatic composition of perception and control APIs
(
Ahn et al., 2022
;
Liang et al., 2022
)
. Environment feedback enables replanning
(
Huang et al., 2022
)
, while spatial representations connect language instructions to physical motion
(
Huang et al., 2023
)
. Together, these studies establish ways for general-purpose models to direct interaction through tools. In robotics, this interaction must also account for a world that changes while actions are running, making the coordination of observation, reasoning, and execution a central concern.
Robot-Use Agents and Harnesses.
Recent studies show that general-purpose multimodal models can operate robots through tools without task-specific robot training
(
Isola, 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. This has prompted efforts to design the harness through which a model observes the scene, issues actions, and receives feedback. RoboDawn and Robo-Harness K1 provide motion and geometric perception tools
(
Guo et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
)
, while OpenRUA gives coding agents access to native ROS 2 interfaces through a terminal
(
Chu et al., 2026
)
. Beyond these interfaces, Harness VLA and GAP investigate how agents can guide learned policies through memory-based planning and corrections to policy-generated actions
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Su et al., 2026
)
. ORA also demonstrates robot use with open-weight models, combining robot tools with environment information and context management
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
. As robot use expands to more models and environments, reusing these components becomes an important system-design question. We develop uni-robot-agent around this need, separating shared robot tools from model runtimes and environment adapters so that changing one does not require rebuilding the others. We also coordinate tool execution and feedback to let agents continue reasoning while physical actions are underway.
8
Conclusion
We presented uni-robot-agent, a unified and modular harness with efficient execution and reliable tools for robot-use agents. Evaluations demonstrate strong performance with GPT-6 Astra in both simulation and real-world manipulation. More importantly, our results show that an open-weight model can also achieve strong robot-use performance: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, exceeding the published Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97. These findings support further investigation of open-weight models that can be deployed locally and adapted through training on robot experience. Precise manipulation and reliable long-horizon execution remain challenges in our evaluations. By providing shared interaction interfaces, replaceable components, and structured execution feedback, uni-robot-agent offers a unified foundation for collecting robot interaction data, developing training methods, and evaluating their effects on agent behavior and task performance.

(
Dream Labs, 2026

B.2
Training Task Catalogue and Collection Protocol
The accompanying training catalogue lists 30 task templates and 1,550
trajectories: 27 templates specify 50 trajectories each, while bag zipping,
coin insertion, and tissue extraction specify 100, 80, and 20, respectively.
The templates span stacking and sorting, object transfer and handover,
container loading, cloth manipulation, surface wiping, and operation of
buttons, switches, drawers, and a microwave door. Collection protocols vary
object placement, material, color, container arrangement, and table appearance
at task-specific intervals. For example, paper-cup stacking uses four to six
inverted cups at different positions, changes cup material every five
trajectories, and changes the table mat every ten. Test-tube transfer uses three
to four tubes of different sizes and reverses the transfer direction every
five trajectories. Cloth folding includes two folds per trajectory, changes
cloth orientation every three trajectories, and changes the cloth every six.
These collection settings establish the reference operations and variations
against which the test catalogue defines new objects, instructions, and action
combinations. The catalogue is collected to fine-tune end-to-end embodied
policies such as
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
, whereas uni-robot-agent does not use any of these
demonstrations; for uni-robot-agent, every entry is therefore evaluated zero-shot, and
the five dimensions characterize the type of variation that each entry
introduces.
B.3
Evaluation Dimensions
Spatial understanding.
This dimension includes one simple entry (fruit transfer), two intermediate
entries (cloth folding and plate extraction), and two complex entries
(test-tube transfer and mug hanging). Fruit transfer moves cherries, bananas,
apples, oranges, and melons from bowls or plates into a basket. Cloth folding
varies size and orientation. Plate extraction requires one arm to lift a
bottle while the other removes and stacks the plate beneath it. Test-tube
transfer and mug hanging further distinguish acquiring an object from
completing the subsequent placement.
Object generalization.
The operation remains bottle handover or bowl stacking while the manipulated
objects change. Handover introduces tea, coconut-water, and bottled-water
containers, together with handled stainless-steel and plastic cups. Bowl
stacking introduces stainless-steel bowls, small and large paper bowls,
ceramic bowls, and large salad bowls. These variations probe differences in
shape, size, material, and available grasp geometry.
Instruction following.
Three tests separate color, object, and spatial-language grounding.
Color-conditioned cup stacking places two or three differently colored cups
on the table and specifies which color should be stacked onto which other
color. Object-conditioned pick-and-place uses a toy car, five fruit types,
blocks, and three tableware types, with bowls, plates, and baskets as target
containers. Direction-conditioned bowl stacking requests left-to-right or
right-to-left arrangements. These tests evaluate whether a physically
feasible operation is directed toward the requested object, destination, and
spatial relation.
Compositional generalization.
Four entries recombine familiar operations, objects, and semantic constraints.
Tissue extraction followed by disposal chains two actions into one objective.
Stacking upward-facing cups changes the object configuration relative to the
inverted-cup training template. Wiping a whiteboard with a rag combines the
wiping operation with an object used elsewhere in the task catalogue, replacing
the whiteboard eraser specified for training. Arranging cubes by color changes
the criterion from the size ordering specified in the training catalogue.
Together, these cases test action sequencing, object substitution, and
semantic recombination.
Unseen tasks.
The final dimension organizes transfer by its relation to the training
catalogue. Closing the microwave door isolates a sub-action of the microwave
loading routine. Taking a bowl out of the microwave and unfolding a rag
reverse the corresponding loading and folding operations. Stacking books is
listed as a combined action, while building a three-level Tower of Hanoi is
listed as a new action.

B.5
Scoring Protocol
Before each trial, the evaluator resets the scene and randomizes object
placements and goal regions. Each task provides a pool of paraphrased
instructions; the evaluator selects one per trial and passes it to the method
as the only task specification. All methods, including
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
and
uni-robot-agent, receive the same task-level instruction, without task-specific
demonstrations, subtask plans, or hints. After each trial, the evaluator
records whether each scoring criterion is satisfied, and all methods are

Appendix E
Spatial Grounding Through Agent-Written Code
Figure 15
:
Agent-written triangulation in
insert_tubes
.
Matching pixels marked A define viewing rays, illustrated schematically above the executed code excerpt. Recorded coordinates and reprojection errors connect the calculation to its output; the final frame follows subsequent grasping and insertion.
The depth ablation in Section
5.1
raises a practical question: how does an agent obtain usable spatial coordinates when its observations contain no depth? We examine two successful Qwen3.8-Flash-Next episodes from the no-depth, no-skill configuration. In both, the agent writes and executes geometry code using RGB observations and the supplied camera intrinsics and extrinsics, rather than calling the built-in triangulation operation. The cases illustrate different ways of constructing localization estimates: matching features across views and testing geometric assumptions against image evidence.
E.1
Recovering Tube Positions Across Views
In
insert_tubes
, the agent must place three tubes into a rack. After obtaining image-space segmentation boxes, it captures additional camera views and writes a Python function to intersect viewing rays in a least-squares sense. It then selects corresponding tube-cap pixels and computes their world coordinates. Figure
15
follows one cap: the calculated position reprojects within 0.46 and 1.94 pixels of the selected points in the two views. This gives the agent a way to check whether its chosen correspondences agree geometrically.
The cap positions are only the beginning of the manipulation sequence. The agent subsequently estimates tube axes, chooses grasp poses, and uses observations and action feedback to guide lifting and insertion. The episode ends with all three tubes in the rack. Here, code execution turns image correspondences into coordinates that the agent can inspect and use in its action planning.
Figure 16
:
Geometric hypothesis testing in
cover_blocks
.
The agent varies a candidate table height and computes cup dimensions from selected pixels. The schematic illustrates the ray–plane intersections computed by
hit()
in the code excerpt; the right-hand frame shows a later placement over the red block.
E.2
Exploring Geometry Before Moving a Cup
In
cover_blocks
, the agent must cover three colored blocks from left to right, then uncover them in a specified color order. Locating the cups requires reasoning about their extent as well as their image centers. The agent extracts colored image regions and writes code that tests candidate table heights, intersects pixel rays with each candidate plane, and compares the resulting cup dimensions (Figure
16
). The height sweep exposes how an assumed scene parameter changes the inferred geometry, rather than treating a single image estimate as fixed.
The agent continues by projecting candidate object shapes into the images and refining its scene estimates. It then uses the estimated cup positions to approach, grasp, and place the cups, checking the scene as the task proceeds. The recorded episode completes the required covering and uncovering sequence. This case shows a more exploratory use of code: the agent constructs and tests geometric hypotheses before committing to physical actions. Together, the two cases illustrate how RGB-based localization can support successful execution, while requiring correspondence selection, geometric assumptions, and verification that depth access can simplify.
Appendix F
Planning During Physical Execution
The overlap measurements in Section
6.2
show when model requests and physical actions run concurrently, but not what the agent prepares during that time or how it uses the result. We follow longer excerpts from two recorded trajectories to connect this preparation to subsequent actions and feedback. Each figure pairs key observations with the recorded execution timeline and enlarges one interval in which the model generates a concrete calculation while a physical tool is running. The annotations summarize recorded outputs; the bars denote model requests, not a measurement of internal reasoning time.
Figure 17
:
Grasp adjustment and supported sliding in
align_blocks
.
The upper row summarizes four stages, each illustrated by a representative observation; a stage may contain multiple tool calls. Green and blue bars show physical tools and model requests; shading marks overlap. The marked interval is enlarged below, where the model prepares a clearance check during release. Image timestamps and the main axis are relative to the first displayed observation.
F.1
From Regrasping to Supported Sliding
In
align_blocks
, the agent must align three blocks with a set square while keeping the blocks on the table. Figure
17
follows the trajectory from an uncertain grasp through contact adjustments to the final aligned row. While a background
release
opens the gripper, the model generates a Python check for a lower grasp pose. Using the finger geometry and table height, it checks that the proposed pose leaves clearance even after a 2 mm uncertainty allowance. The program runs after the release finishes, and the agent then moves to the checked pose, grasps, and tests retention with a short lift.
The lift does not retain the set square. The agent explicitly changes its approach: it will keep the square supported and use sliding contact instead. It lowers the hand, closes the gripper, and issues a sequence of small rotations and translations, then inspects the scene and adjusts contact again. The final observation shows the blocks in a row with the arms clear. This longer sequence shows both the use of preparation during background execution and the need to revise that preparation when subsequent physical evidence contradicts it.
Figure 18
:
Orientation preparation during digit transport.
The upper row summarizes four stages rather than individual tool calls; the lanes below show recorded execution. The enlarged interval shows a model request preparing rotation candidates while transport continues. The later divergence is retained to show how execution feedback affects the prepared plan. Colors and time conventions match Figure
17
.
F.2
Preparing Reorientation During Transport
In
arrange_largest_number
, the agent must place digit-shaped objects on pads to form the largest number. The excerpt in Figure
18
follows one digit from localization and grasping through transport and reorientation. While the arm moves toward a raised target, the model generates a program that composes candidate
90
∘
90^{\circ}
and
180
∘
180^{\circ}
world-axis rotations with the current orientation and converts them to Euler angles. This prepares later orientation commands without waiting for the transport result.
The transport first exhausts its step budget, so the agent continues toward the same target before attempting the prepared rotation. The first orientation target is reached, but the next rotation stops for divergence. The agent then raises the hand while retaining its measured orientation and captures a new observation. The sequence illustrates why advance preparation and execution monitoring are complementary: a candidate action can be prepared during an earlier movement, while its application still depends on the state returned by the robot.

article.headline: 开源模型零样本用机器人，统一框架是关键
article.lede: 清华等提出 uni-robot-agent 统一框架，Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 在 RoboDojo 得 3
article.problem: 机器人操作智能体（RUA）此前主要依赖闭源前沿模型，权重不可得，研究者既无法通过继续训练提升其能力，也难以做缓存等模型级优化，而大规模 API 调用成本高昂。开源权重模型在空间理解与智能体能力上存在差距，已有工作常靠真值深度、任务验证器反馈等特权信息或任务专用技能绕过。作者主张先建立通用、有效的 harness，系统弄清并释放开源模型的现有能力，再谈机器人专用训练。
article.method: uni-robot-agent 分 agent、orchestration、tool、service、backend 五层，共享工具在多个环境与本体间复用，新增环境只需一个适配器，避免 N×M 套实现。编排层用后台调用加资源感知调度，让模型推理与物理执行形成两段流水线，共享独占资源的动作仍按提交顺序执行。交互只使用 RGB、相机标定、本体状态与指令，不接触仿真深度和任务验证器反馈，并配合快照一致性、重复请求去重、带停止判据的运动监控、数值化执行反馈和滑动窗口图像淘汰。
article.results: 在 RoboDojo 42 个任务、252 个 episode 上，Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 取得 25.00% SR 与 31.39 Score，超过 GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe 的 22.48% SR 与 28.97 Score；DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 为 21.39% SR、27.11 Score，换用 GAP 等 harness 则损失 8.89% SR 与 10.38 Score。自建 19 项真实桌面任务中，Qwen 得 49.50 分，优于 Dream-1 的 35.50、接近微调 π0.5 的 47.75，GPT-6 Astra 配该 harness 为 75.50。去掉深度后 Qwen 由 35.89 降至 31.39（保留 87.5%），Astra 由 55.83 降至 55.04；连相机参数也去掉时 Qwen 跌至 9.13。关闭技能库仍有 30.31 分（保留 96.6%）。成本上 Qwen 每 episode 约 1.09 美元，Astra 约 21.29 美元；流水线使 episode 时长缩短 4.8% 至 73.7%，执行与模型请求重叠 84.5% 至 93.8%。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一个可复现、可替换组件的开源基线，证明不靠特权信息与闭源蒸馏也能在仿真和真机上做出有竞争力的机器人操作智能体，为后续用机器人交互数据继续训练提供了统一接口和数据来源。作者还通过跨代际、跨家族、跨规模的对比，把有效机器人操作归结为视觉理解、空间定位、几何代码与具身推理四类通用能力的组合。
article.limitations: 真实世界对比并不完全同条件：uni-robot-agent 额外使用 RealSense D405 深度，而 π0.5 与 Dream-1 只用 RGB，且真实评测是自建、以评分细则计分的基准，部分得分不等于完整任务成功率。此外部分模型对比只跑 1 个 seed、1 种布局，Qwen 在精密操作（10.21）与长程任务上仍落后于 Xiaomi-Robotics-1、OpenWAM-α，去掉相机参数后性能大幅下滑也说明方法仍依赖标定。

page_papers.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present

Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments
Yao et al. (2023)
;
Zhou et al. (2024)
. As these tasks grow more complex, multi-agent systems (MAS) offer a way to divide work among agents with complementary roles. Instead of asking one agent to plan, gather information, act, and verify every step, MAS can organize these activities through specialization, parallel exploration, and iterative feedback. Systems such as AutoGen, MetaGPT, ChatDev, and Magentic-One demonstrate how agents can coordinate their contributions toward a shared task
Wu et al. (2023)
;
Hong et al. (2024)
;
Qian et al. (2024)
;
Fourney et al. (2024)
.
However, the collaboration that makes MAS useful also reshapes LLM serving demand; its diverse, framework-specific patterns hinder reusable workload construction. Conventional serving treats model requests as independent arrivals, while a single-agent workflow typically follows one evolving interaction. In MAS, requests may depend on other agents’ progress and outputs: parallel branches may release several calls together, synchronization may delay downstream calls, and refinement or debate may trigger repeated exchanges. Agents may inherit histories, share intermediate results, or build new contexts for later calls, changing opportunities for reuse
Bian et al. (2026a)
;
Bian et al. (2026b)
. Thus, even tasks with similar request counts and token lengths can differ in request readiness, batching opportunities, and memory demand (Fig.
1
). These differences arise from task structure, not merely scheduling decisions; request traces record the realized work, not the collaboration rules generating it.
Collaboration shapes serving demand in two distinct ways.

Work generation
determines which model calls, inputs, and token lengths emerge as agents coordinate and exchange results.

Figure
2

4
describes its realization and replay.
3.1

Experimental Setup
We use vLLM and vLLM-Ascend on the GPU/NPU platforms in Table
4
, with BF16, tensor parallelism one, and one exposed accelerator per serving instance. Qwen3.5 combines recurrent linear and full attention; Qwen3-8B
Yang et al. (2025)
provides full-attention workloads.
Seven structures cover the four templates, two compositions (Spawn–Fork–Join–Refinement and Fork–Join–Debate–Refinement), and a research–review–writing Sequence. Thirty shared task bindings retain generated artifacts and natural output lengths across code, reasoning, finance, evidence processing, and science.
Three-block native runs use 32/64/128 users, each issuing one ordinary call or executing a MAS workflow. Three paired Qwen3-8B/910C blocks fix work and arrivals for release/resource interventions. The GPU composition study limits requests to 64. Fixed-work serving evaluations use length-locked replay unless stated otherwise.
Table 4:
Application and operator coverage.
910C applications use one logical chip per dual-chip card; operator probes are separate from application runs.

Discussion
Reuse-aware compute and tiered KV memory.
The GPU reversal motivates SRAM/L2 retention for reusable weights and cache bypass with HBM streaming for rotating weights; Gather motivates programmable SIMT with access-aware path selection. A page-managed HBM pool could asynchronously extend KV into DRAM when migration and remote access cost less than saved prefill. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) could hold cold, read-mostly weights with low update traffic; 3D near-memory attention could benefit long contexts when saved data movement exceeds transfer overhead. These hypotheses must advance timely task completion; dependency hints and input-prefix reuse could guide retention and prefetch.
Multi-replica and disaggregated serving.
Consider a production MAS whose agents invoke model APIs backed by replicas across machines or clusters. Prefix affinity can save prefill but concentrate demand on a contended replica, making routing and load balancing affect complete-task latency and SLOs even with fixed dependencies. MAServeBench separates logical collaboration from physical placement; an API-facing replay adapter could preserve recorded work and arrivals while exposing per-replica routing and queueing, including delays before submission.
At the phase level, systems such as Mooncake
Qin et al. (2025)
separate prefill and decode
Zhong et al. (2024)
;
Patel et al. (2024)
. Parallel MAS stages create prefill bursts, while refinement and debate repeatedly release dependent calls. Phase specialization must offset KV/state-transfer costs and cross-pool queueing, especially for long contexts and hybrid-model recurrent state. Replay extensions that associate phase placement and state transfers with each operation could evaluate these designs through complete-task SLOs.
7

Conclusion
MAServeBench provides a source-grounded, extensible benchmark for multi-agent serving. Composable stages vary collaboration and context construction under shared task bindings, generating distinct workloads through native execution. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for controlled comparisons of legal release and serving resources at fixed work. Task-linked measurements reveal how collaboration shapes parallelism, locality affects compute efficiency, and KV pressure impacts task completion. Decoupling workflow semantics from backend execution lets Semantic Traces serve as workloads for serving backends and architecture simulators, supporting MAS serving and hardware evaluation.

Acknowledgments
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to Jianming Tong for his insightful discussions, thoughtful suggestions, and valuable feedback throughout the development of this work. His perspectives and constructive comments helped
us refine our understanding of the research challenges and improve the presentation of this study. We greatly appreciate his generous support
and encouragement.

Execution demand varies within this quality range. For example, GPT Researcher’s realization invokes more tools, while OWL’s realization uses fewer input tokens with nearly the same call counts. article.headline: MAServeBench：多智能体服务基准
article.lede: 新基准把多智能体协作规则变成可复现的服务负载，用语义轨迹比较不同释放与资源条件下的表现。
article.problem: 多智能体系统把一次用户请求拆成相互依赖的模型调用与工具操作，这些操作在不同时刻就绪、携带演化上下文，带来变化的并发、计算和内存需求。传统服务基准把请求视为独立到达，而执行轨迹只记录已发生的工作，不记录生成这些工作的协作规则。
article.method: MAServeBench 用可组合阶段在共享任务绑定下改变协作与上下文构建，并通过原生执行生成负载。它引入分层语义轨迹，保留实际操作与依赖关系，从而在固定工作下控制释放时机和资源条件进行比较。实验在 vLLM 与 vLLM-Ascend 上运行，覆盖七种结构、30 个任务绑定和 32/64/128 用户规模。
article.results: 配对实现与源工作流在任务质量上接近：成功/准确率指标的绝对差异为 1.2–3.8 个百分点，RACE 至多 0.019，但执行需求仍有差异，例如 GPT Researcher 调用更多工具，OWL 在几乎相同调用数下输入 token 更少。在 27 个目标中，首调用驻留均短于第二调用，后者在 GSM8K 与 PubMedQA 超过前者，在 Science 仅部分抵消。
article.why_it_matters: 它把工作流语义与后端执行解耦，使语义轨迹可作为服务后端和架构模拟器的负载，便于用完整任务指标评估 MAS 服务与硬件设计。
article.limitations: 当前实验限于 vLLM/vLLM-Ascend、单加速器与 TP=1，且模型主要覆盖 Qwen3.5/Qwen3-8B，结论对其他后端和硬件的可迁移性仍待验证。论文把多副本与分离式服务列为后续方向，说明真实跨副本路由、排队和端到端 SLO 尚未纳入评测。
article.figure_caption_zh: 协作重塑服务需求：独立请求到达与多智能体任务引发的依赖请求、产物交换和同步不同，MAServeBench 提供可控、可复现的评测。

figure.caption: {Collaboration reshapes serving demand.} (a) Independent request arrivals. (b) A multi-agent task induces dependent requests with artifact exchange and synchronization. Both can use continuous batching. (c) MAServeBench enables controlled, reproducible evaluation of collaboration-induced serving demand and hardware resource behavior.

page_papers.title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
page_papers.abstract: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

Abstract
Robot agents built on vision–language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher’s harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost?
We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher’s trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness.
On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher’s success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%.
Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining.
On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors’ harnesses.
It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher’s accelerator time.

We connect these approaches by asking:
can we first improve a large teacher’s harness, then transfer the resulting decision-making capability to a small model?
This would allow the improved system to run with substantially less inference compute.
We present
TinyAstral
, a family of 0.8B–4B manipulation agents built in two stages (
Fig.
2

First, we freeze the weights of an open-weight teacher, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
[
34

, and improve its harness through a master-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. Humans specify the rules and budget in advance. Frontier LLM agents then inspect failures and propose harness edits, which the system automatically accepts or rejects according to pre-registered paired statistical tests.
Second, we freeze the final harness and collect teacher trajectories containing reasoning, tool calls, and recovery from injected failures. Together with auxiliary offline real-robot supervision, these trajectories train a compact student to interpret feedback, choose actions, recover from failure, and decide when to finish. At deployment, the student replaces the teacher in the same frozen harness.
We evaluate both stages and the connection between them. Harness evolution raises the frozen teacher’s RoboTwin success from 33.4% to 63.6%, and distillation produces a 4B student at 62.8%.
To test whether this connection holds beyond the final endpoint, we distill students at four harness versions. The four students score 36.2%, 49.8%, 60.0%, and 62.8%, each close to its corresponding teacher.
The same evolved harness also improves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the untrained 4B initialization, showing that its gains are reusable across planners. On identical episodes the student outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses (93.6% vs. 78.9% on Guava; 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% on LIBERO-PRO), and on unseen benchmarks the small 4B student scores close to a 552B planner in the same harness.
Our contributions are:
•
Harness evolution followed by distillation.
A two-stage approach first improves a frozen teacher’s manipulation harness, then trains a compact planner from that teacher’s reasoning and recovery trajectories for deployment in the same harness.
•
Evidence that evolution gains transfer.
The harness improves other frozen planners, and distilled students at four harness versions track the performance of their corresponding teachers, showing that system improvements carry into compact models.
•
Compact agents with lower inference compute cost.
A single TinyAstral-4B model covers six benchmarks: on identical episodes it outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses, scores close to its teacher on the three training benchmarks and close to a 552B planner on unseen ones, and uses about one fifth of the teacher’s accelerator time per episode in our deployment measurement.

2. Propose edits.
For a target cluster of failing tasks, the master writes candidate components: new tools or primitives, more honest tool returns, perception fixes, failure handling, or local corrections to the task memory.
Edits must be general.
Code may not branch on the task name. In the final integration phase, the system prompt and existing tool descriptions must remain byte-identical to the parent. Memory may change only for the targeted tasks.
In addition, every new component must fire through an explicit trigger that writes a component-specific marker to the log.
A separate code audit verifies that, whenever the trigger does not fire, the candidate behaves step-for-step like the parent.
3. Test and accept edits.
Candidates are compared with the current harness on the same task/seed pairs. Training, selection, and evaluation seeds occupy disjoint ranges. The pre-registered gate requires positive evidence of improvement on targeted or triggered pairs and checks for regressions elsewhere; unsuccessful candidates are rejected or stopped early. The final integration phase accepted three of seven candidates.
Evaluation seeds are excluded from acceptance tests. The acceptance rules and capability ledger are in
Appendix
E
.

e.g

The other five benchmarks, including all zero-shot ones, use no task memory.

Successful episodes rarely show how to recover from failure, so we add

Starting from a successful teacher episode, we replay its first

Comparison with other agents.
On the same evaluation episodes, TinyAstral-4B outperforms the tested open agents, including Guava-4B, PyRUA-Lean-4B, and SenseNova-RoboRSI-27B (

5
Conclusion
TinyAstral first improves a frozen teacher through harness evolution, then distills its reasoning and recovery behavior into a compact student deployed in the final harness. Across four harness versions, students trained from later versions perform better and stay close to their corresponding teachers, showing that harness improvements carry into compact agents. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners.
The final 4B student outperforms every open competitor we ran on identical episodes, stays close to its teacher on three training benchmarks, scores close to a 552B planner on unseen benchmarks, and uses about one fifth of the teacher’s accelerator time in our deployment measurement. These results support harness evolution followed by distillation as a route to capable robot agents with lower inference compute cost.
Future work will extend the approach to more RSI environments.

PyRUA-Lean-4B

finish

Same teacher in alternative systems.
Guava harness with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses the official prompt and parser with medium reasoning effort and default sampling, whereas our teacher uses its default xhigh reasoning and temperature 0. Both allow 25/30 calls per task. MotorMind with this planner uses its official stop-on-success protocol and uncapped calls (median 77, compared with 8 for our student on LIBERO-PRO). PyRUA-Lean with this planner uses benchmark-trained VLA executors and allows 30/40 calls on RoboTwin/LIBERO-PRO; it runs on all 500 RoboTwin episodes (91/500) and our 300 LIBERO-PRO episodes, and its reported success requires

article.headline: TinyAstral：先进化再蒸馏的紧凑机器人智能
article.lede: 华为等提出两阶段方法：先在冻结教师上进化执行框架，再把教师推理与恢复轨迹蒸馏到 0.8B–4B 学生，4B 学生在 Ro
article.problem: 基于视觉语言模型的机器人智能体，其表现不仅取决于规划模型本身，也取决于围绕它的执行框架——工具接口、反馈、记忆与失败恢复逻辑。已有工作分别证明框架进化能提升冻结规划模型、智能体蒸馏能把强智能体轨迹迁移到小模型，但能否先改进大教师的框架、再把收益迁移到小模型以降低推理成本，尚未得到验证。
article.method: TinyAstral 分两阶段。第一阶段冻结教师（Qwen3.8-Flash-Next）权重，由前沿 LLM 智能体读取教师轨迹、提出框架修改（新工具、更诚实的工具返回、感知修正、失败处理、任务记忆），每次修改都要在预注册的配对 A/B 统计检验中通过才被接受，模型权重自始至终不变。第二阶段冻结最终框架 H*，采集教师含推理与失败恢复分支的轨迹，与离线真实机器人监督混合，蒸馏到 0.8B–4B 的 Qwen3.5 学生模型；部署时学生在同一个冻结框架中替换教师。
article.results: RoboTwin 500 个评测回合上，教师随框架演化从 H1 的 33.4% 升到 H* 的 63.6%，最终 4B 学生达 62.8%；在 H1、H7、H16、H* 四个框架版本上分别训练的 4B 学生为 36.2%、49.8%、60.0%、62.8%，各自接近对应的教师。在 Guava 和 LIBERO-PRO 上，4B 学生分别为 93.6% 与 78.3%，教师为 94.7% 与 80.0%。三个零样本基准上，学生与教师差距在 5.0 个百分点内，与同一框架下的 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 差距在 2.4 个百分点内。20 个共享 SimplerEnv 回合上，4B 学生每回合 25.3 加速器·秒，教师为 123.8（4.9 倍），DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 为 249.6（9.9 倍）。消融显示去掉教师推理文本会使 LIBERO-PRO 下降 19.3 个百分点、SimplerEnv Google VM 下降 11.2 个百分点、VLABench 下降 10.0 个百分点；加入真实机器人数据把离线下一调用准确率从 0.235 提到 0.923。
article.why_it_matters: 结果说明，对冻结教师做框架进化所得到的系统级改进可以被蒸馏进小模型，让紧凑智能体以约五分之一的加速器时间接近大模型乃至 552B 规划器的表现。
article.limitations: 真实机器人闭环只在 SO-ARM101 上演示了三个任务，推理成本仅基于 20 个共享 SimplerEnv 回合测量；RoboTwin 上框架还读取了每个任务一句话的终止状态注释（其余五个基准没有），且部分回合结果不确定被计为失败。0.8B 学生在 LIBERO-PRO 上降到 54.7%，明显落后于 4B 学生的 78.3%，说明小模型容量在扰动基准上仍有代价。
article.figure_caption_zh: TinyAstral 总览：第一阶段冻结教师，由前沿 LLM 智能体提出框架修改并通过配对统计门控接受；第二阶段冻结最终框架 H*、采集教师含推理与恢复分支的轨迹，蒸馏出 0.8B–4B 学生，部署时在相同框架中替换教师。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} Stage~1: humans specify the rules and budget in advance. A master of frontier LLM agents reads trajectories of the frozen teacher acting through the harness (tools, feedback, memory, recovery) and proposes harness edits, which are accepted only if a paired A/B test on selection seeds passes a pre-registered statistical gate; model weights never change. Stage~2: after evolution ends, we freeze $H^*$ and collect teacher trajectories, including reasoning and recovery branches. These are mixed with offline real-robot supervision to train tiny students (0.8B--4B), which replace the teacher in the same harness. Evaluation covers three training domains and three unseen benchmarks, plus three closed-loop real-robot tasks on an SO-ARM101 arm.

page_papers.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.

Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
Guizhen Chen
