Abstract
Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations.
Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance.
These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.
Our data and code are available at
https://regap-bench.github.io
.
1
Introduction
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become increasingly capable at recognizing objects, shapes, and spatial relations in single-step perceptual tasks
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Team et al., 2026
)
, yet they often struggle to maintain and use that information across multiple reasoning steps. For example, a model may detect every object in a scene but still miscount them. Much of the field’s response to such failures has focused on perception, pursuing higher-resolution encoders and finer-grained visual features
(
Tong et al., 2024b
)
. However, the missing capability may instead lie between perception and reasoning: models lack a stable mechanism for referring to objects, regions, or locations while reasoning. Figure
1
shows an example of a counting problem. The model refers to shapes by vague locations such as “on the left side” and counts one ellipse twice; when every shape carries a number, it lists the ellipses by label and answers correctly.
Following
Lu et al. (2026)
, we call this the
reference gap
: the failure to maintain stable bindings between language-based reasoning and the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Recent work addresses it either by training a model to produce coordinates within its reasoning
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
, or by drawing lines on the image and instructing the model to scan along them
(
Izadi et al., 2025
)
. Two questions remain open. First, neither isolates the effect of the reference itself.
Lu et al. (2026)
compare a newly trained model with other models, so part of the gain may come from training data or architecture.
Izadi et al. (2025)
varies both the image and the prompt together, so it is unclear if MLLMs can perform systematic scanning of the image without additional instructions from the prompt. Second, each applies the same reference to every task, although tasks might need different visual operations. It thus remains unclear which reference a task needs, and whether any added structure would help equally.
Figure 1:
The same question to GPT-5.4 mini about the same scene, without and with numbering reference. In the plain setting (left), the model refers to shapes by vague locations and double counts. With numbering (right), it lists the ellipses by label and answers correctly.
To design such a diagnostic framework, we identify visual routines used for complex visual reasoning, such as marking visited items, activating bounded regions, and tracing boundaries
(
Ullman, 1984
)
. We hypothesize that MLLMs lack internal reference frames for reliable execution of these visual routines, and that external references such as numbering, shading, or grid lines can support them, with each reference helping most on tasks that demand its visual routines.
To test this hypothesis, we introduce
ReGap-Bench
, a controlled benchmark of paired reference interventions across five tasks: shape counting, angle ranking, size ranking, clock ranking, and transformation prediction. Each underlying scene is rendered with and without explicit visual references, while its task-relevant objects, geometry, question, and gold answer remain fixed.
Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy on all five tasks. Numbering yields gains of up to 17.5% on shape counting and 25% clock ranking; shading improves angle and size ranking; and grids improve size ranking and transformation prediction. Next, we show that the gains depend on matching the reference to the task, not on adding marks. Additionally, model scale across six Qwen3-VL models from 2B to 235B does not remove the reference gap.
Building on these findings,
we introduce a
training-free visual skill
that enables an agent to dynamically identify the required visual routine and select the corresponding reference scaffold. Evaluated on CartoMapQA
(
Ung et al., 2025
)
, this skill enables autonomous reference selection and improves complex map understanding without finetuning.
We summarize our contributions as follows:
•
We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired evaluation framework that measures the reference gap. It spans five visual reasoning tasks and three reference systems, with scene semantics, questions, and answers held fixed across reference conditions.
•
We show that task-matched references improve all evaluated models on all five tasks. Mismatched, incomplete, and model-scale analyses provide evidence that the gains come from supporting the visual routine a task requires, and that they persist from 2B to 235B parameters.
•
We introduce a training-free visual skill that enables an agent to identify the visual routine required by a task and dynamically construct a corresponding visual reference at inference time.
2
Diagnosing the Reference Gap with Visual Interventions
2.1
The reference gap
We use the reference gap to describe the failure to maintain a stable link between language and the relevant visual entity, region, or location that the language corresponds to. Models might perceive the relevant visual information, yet struggle to identify, revisit, or distinguish from other visual elements as reasoning proceeds. Consider shape counting. A model may correctly recognize individual triangles when asked about them separately yet still miscount them (see preliminary analysis in Appendix
A
). The model needs to repeatedly select an object, determine whether it belongs to the target class, keep track of counted objects, and then move to the next. Without a stable internal reference, it can lose track of which objects have been counted, resulting in omissions or duplicates. The reference gap is therefore distinct from a perception failure, and it should matter most in visual reasoning that spans multiple steps.
Most benchmarks do not reveal whether the model failed to perceive the relevant content or failed to maintain reference to it during reasoning. To address this, we diagnose the reference gap by testing whether performance changes when the underlying visual problem is held fixed but the model is given explicitly external reference to refer to its visual elements.
2.2
External references for visual routines
To choose useful visual references, we draw on Ullman’s theory of visual routines
(
Ullman, 1984
)
, which describes complex visual reasoning as a sequence of elementary operations such as shifting the processing focus, bounded activation, boundary tracing, indexing, and marking. We propose three types of visual references that externalize intermediate visual states to support these routines.
Numbering.
Numbering supports marking and indexing. It turns description-dependent visual elements into addressable entities. For instance, instead of using ambiguous phrases like “the upper-left triangle”, the model can refer to “shape 7”. This makes it easier to find an item again and to track which items have already been processed.
Shading.
Shading supports bounded activation by making a region explicit. For example, shading the interior of an angle makes the angular region itself visible. Filling a shape similarly emphasizes its bounded area rather than only its outline.
Grid lines.
Grids provide spatial marks that can support systematic focus shifts and boundary tracing. They divide the image into regular grid intervals and can provide a reference for position, width, height, displacement, and alignment.
These scaffolds provide different kinds of reference information. Therefore, we do not expect every scaffold to help every task. Our main hypothesis is that: a reference scaffold helps most when the type of reference it provides matches the visual routines that the reasoning process needs.

We introduce

2.3

3.1
Tasks
We design five tasks that share a common requirement: the model must shift its focus across different parts of an image and repeatedly bind reasoning steps to particular visual elements. For each task, we identify the visual routine it relies on most and the reference scaffolds we expect to support that routine, which we call
matched
.
Shape counting.
The scene contains outlined shapes such as triangles, quadrilaterals, and pentagons, arranged in rows and columns at random orientations. We annotate the shapes with standard geometry marks, such as tick marks on equal sides and small squares at right angles, to make each shape’s class unambiguous. The question asks for the count of a specific shape. The model must select each shape, classify it, and record it as counted without skipping or repeating any. The task therefore relies on indexing and marking. Numbering could be a matched reference because it assigns each object a stable address that can be used throughout the counting process.
Angle ranking.
The scene contains several angles, each formed by two rays from a vertex, and marked by a red arc. The model is tasked to rank the angles by size, from smallest to largest, or the reverse. The main difficulty is keeping the correct angular region active: looking at the wrong side of the rays turns an angle into its conjugate angle. Shading the angular wedge could be helpful in making the region being compared explicit and thus supports bounded activation.
Size ranking.
The scene contains several shapes of one class. The model is asked to rank the shapes according to their visual size. This requires estimating the size of each shape and maintain these estimates while shifting the focus to other shapes. We expect two references to help: shading makes each shape’s area explicit as a bounded region, and grid lines provide a common scale for comparing width and height across locations.
Clock ranking.
The scene contains several analog clocks, each with twelve tick marks, an hour hand, a minute hand, and an “AM” or “PM” label. The task is to rank the clocks from earliest to latest, or the reverse. The main reference challenge is mapping hand positions onto a stable circular reference frame. We expect dial numbering to help, because it marks positions on that frame directly.
Transformation prediction.
Given a source figure and a chain of transformation steps, the model needs to determine which of the four given options is the final figure. Transformation operations include translation, reflection, rotation, and dilation. To solve the task, the model must trace the shape through each step and shift focus across panels to compare final positions.
We expect grid lines to help, because they provide a common frame for position and scale.

4.2
Analysis on Matched Versus Mismatched References
The positive scaffold results establish that each reference method can help in matched settings. However, it is unclear whether these gains simply come from adding more visual marks. We test this by applying numbering, shading, and grid lines to the same shape counting and clock ranking scenes. If improvements were caused merely by additional visual information, then numbering, shading, and grid lines should help similarly. If the reference gap exists, then the operation-matched scaffold should produce the largest gain. Figure
6
supports the second explanation. In shape counting, numbering improves accuracy by 11.3% on average, compared to only 1.7% for shading, while grid lines reduce accuracy by 4.1%. The same separation appears in clock ranking.
These results show that added visual structure is not always beneficial: a scaffold can be neutral or harmful when it does not provide the kind of reference the task needs.
The effectiveness of a scaffold therefore depends on its alignment with the visual routine needed for solving the task.
4.3
Analysis on Incomplete References
Figure 7:
Performance improves as dial numbering becomes more complete.
Next, we test whether references help because they provide complete reference structure, or whether partial reference is sufficient. We test this on clock ranking by varying how many dial numerals are shown while keeping the clocks themselves fixed. The four conditions contain zero, two, four, or all twelve numerals. If numbering helps because it provides stable addresses, then a more complete reference system should be more useful than a sparse one.
Figure
7
confirms this, mean accuracy rises from 23.9% with no numerals to 25.3% with two, 31.8% with four, and 38.0% with all twelve. The trend is non-decreasing for every evaluated model. Sparse numbering therefore provides only a small benefit, whereas a complete reference system produces a substantially larger gain. This result is consistent with a reference-based mechanism: a scaffold is most useful when it supplies stable addresses that the model must repeatedly identify during reasoning.
Partial references can still help, but they leave a larger portion of the task dependent on the model’s own spatial descriptions or implicit object bindings.

Analysis of Model Scale
The final question is whether the reference gap is primarily a limitation of small models. We evaluate six Qwen3-VL Thinking models ranging from 2B to 235B parameters on shape counting. Figure
8

a larger model size improves the task performance but does not eliminate the benefit of an explicit reference system

5
Task-matched references as training-free visual skills
In Section
4
, we show that models that lack an internal reference system can benefit from task-matched references
without any training
. One implication is that agents can add these references on their own using a visual skill when a task requires such reference. Unlike most skills that are text-only, we package the three references as a visual skill that can refer to visual examples and overlay the reference onto the image similarly.
We test the skill on CartoMapQA
(
Ung et al., 2025
)
that contains street-level OpenStreetMap renderings with icons for points of interest (POIs), road labels, markers, and a scale bar. We use stratified sampling to draw 100 tasks across the eight subtasks, and run the Codex GPT-5.5 agent on the same tasks with and without the skill, using the BenchFlow framework
(
BenchFlow Team, 2026
)
.
The skill contains three components: First, written rules specify which reference to use for each type of visual operation: numbering for counting, listing, or matching discrete map elements, as well as tracking junctions along a route; grid lines, calibrated using the map’s scale bar, for measuring distances or comparing positions; shading for isolating bounded regions; and no overlay when the answer can be obtained from a single clearly labeled element.
Second, a pair of before-and-after example images demonstrating how to draw each reference. Third, a script draws the chosen reference on a copy of the map and leaves the original unchanged.

identify the
reference gap
as a failure to ground verbal reasoning in precise visual entities and locations. Such failures can propagate across reasoning steps in dense counting, spatial deduction, and path tracing. 7
Conclusion
We identify the
reference gap
as a distinct bottleneck in multimodal reasoning: models may perceive the relevant visual content yet fail to maintain stable references to it during multi-step reasoning. Using ReGap-Bench, we show that task-matched visual references consistently improve performance, whereas mismatched references provide little benefit or can be harmful, and that this gap persists even at larger model scales. These results suggest that improving multimodal reasoning requires
mechanisms that support the visual routines needed by the task. Finally, our training-free visual skill demonstrates that an agent can dynamically construct such references at inference time, offering a simple way to improve visual reasoning without additional model training.

Appendix A
Preliminary Check: Can Models Perceive the Shapes?
Section
2.1
claims that a model can perceive the shapes in a scene yet still fail to count a target class. As a preliminary check of this claim, we run two simpler probes on the plain shape-counting scenes with Claude-Opus-4.7.
Finding the shapes.
We ask the model how many shapes the image contains, regardless of class. It answers correctly in 193 of the 200 scenes (96.5%; Table
3
). The errors grow with the number of shapes.

Recognizing single shapes.
For each scene, we crop one shape from the plain image and ask whether it belongs to the scene’s target class, with the same inclusion rules as in the counting prompt. For example, the scene question “How many parallelograms are there?” becomes “Is this shape a parallelogram?”. If the scene contains the target class, we crop a random target shape (answer Yes); otherwise, we crop a random shape (answer No). The model answers correctly for 95.9%.
Summary.
The model counts all shapes correctly in 96.5% of scenes and recognizes the single shape in 95.9%, but counts the target class correctly in only 72.0%. Most counting errors therefore do not come from missing or misreading individual shapes.

B.2
Task Generation
We pre-define shapes from 11 classes: square, rectangle, trapezium, parallelogram, regular pentagon, equilateral triangle, isosceles triangle, right triangle, right isosceles triangle, circle, and ellipse.
Shape counting.
We randomly sample shapes from the 11 classes to fill the cells. Some cells are left empty. We add marks as follows: squares and rectangles have right-angle marks at all corners; squares, pentagons, and equilateral triangles have one tick on every side; rectangles and parallelograms have one tick on one pair of opposite sides and two ticks on the other; isosceles triangles have one tick on each equal side; right triangles have a right-angle mark; right isosceles triangles have a right-angle mark and one tick on each leg; circles have two dotted radii, each with one tick. Trapezia and ellipses have no marks. Each shape has a random orientation and a random size, and classes with free proportions (e.g., rectangles, isosceles triangles, ellipses) also get random proportions. The target class is drawn from all 11 classes, not only those present, so the answer can be zero. The gold count follows class inclusion: a square also counts as a rectangle, parallelogram, and trapezium; a rectangle also counts as a parallelogram and trapezium; a parallelogram also counts as a trapezium; equilateral and right isosceles triangles also count as isosceles triangles; a right isosceles triangle also counts as a right triangle; and a circle also counts as an ellipse. The question uses one of five templates, such as “How many parallelograms are there?” and “What is the total number of circles in the image?”

article.headline: 多模态推理的参考缺口：视觉标记并非万能
article.lede: 配对基准ReGap-Bench显示，任务匹配的编号、阴影或网格可提升多模态推理，错配则可能有害。
article.problem: 多模态大模型能识别视觉内容，却常在多步推理中丢失对同一对象的稳定指代，例如计数时重复或漏数。作者认为这不只是感知失败，而是“参考缺口”：语言推理未能稳定绑定到对应的视觉实体、区域或位置。
article.method: 作者提出ReGap-Bench配对基准，覆盖形状计数、角度排序、尺寸排序、时钟排序和变换预测五个任务，每个任务200个场景，仅改变编号、阴影或网格等外部参考，题目与答案保持不变。实验评估五个多模态模型，并测试2B到235B的六款Qwen3-VL模型；随后把任务匹配的参考封装成免训练视觉技能，在CartoMapQA上验证。
article.results: 任务匹配的参考带来提升：编号使形状计数提升6.0%到17.5%、时钟排序提升8.5%到25.0%；阴影使尺寸排序提升4.0%到11.0%；网格使尺寸排序提升2.0%到8.0%、变换预测提升2.0%到5.5%。在形状计数中，编号平均提升11.3%，阴影仅1.7%，网格为-4.1%；时钟数字从0个增至12个时，平均准确率由23.9%升至38.0%。六款Qwen3-VL上编号增益为9.0%到23.5%，未随规模消失；CartoMapQA上智能体在100题中为57题绘制覆盖层，编号子集由63.7%升至70.1%。
article.why_it_matters: 把参考缺口视为独立于视觉感知的瓶颈，并给出免训练的干预方式，可能比单纯堆高分辨率编码器更直接地改善多步视觉推理。
article.limitations: 基准场景为合成渲染，任务与参考类型有限；CartoMapQA验证仅100题，阴影子集只有3题，外部有效性仍待检验。规模分析也只覆盖Qwen3-VL的形状计数。

page_papers.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
page_papers.abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5times faster on TREC DL and 16.7times faster on BRIGHT.

DecisionRank: effective and efficient single-token reranking through distillation.
All methods rerank the same BM25 top-100 candidates on TREC DL19–23. (a) Distillation substantially improves ranking accuracy across all three student sizes, with each student outperforming the 27B generative teacher (62.91). Arrows indicate absolute gains in nDCG@10 × 100 over zero-shot scoring. (b)
DecisionRank
students achieve favorable accuracy–latency tradeoffs compared with other rerankers. The gray triangle shows Jev, using median server-reported latency. Qwen3-RR denotes Qwen3-Reranker.
1
Introduction
Figure 2:
Training
DecisionRank
with offline rankings and on-policy feedback. A frozen generative teacher supplies offline rankings for RankNet (left) and conditional feedback along the student’s current ranking (right). One teacher-forced forward pass provides the teacher’s choice distributions, which are aligned with the student’s scores renormalized over the remaining documents. Both objectives supervise the same first-token scores. The student’s scoring procedure is the same during training and inference: a single forward pass produces the first-token scores used to rank all candidates.
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in document reranking, particularly through listwise methods like RankGPT
(
Sun et al., 2023
)
that autoregressively generate candidate identifiers in descending order of relevance. However, this multi-step decoding incurs substantial inference latency. Decision models address this latency by directly predicting choices or scores without generating text, as illustrated by Jev
(
Almeida, 2026
)
and AnyJev
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. In document reranking, single-token methods such as FIRST
(
Gangi Reddy et al., 2024
)
follow the same principle: they sort first-token document-ID logits to obtain the ranking. Training these scores to capture the ranking preferences of capable generative teachers is therefore critical to effective single-token reranking.
Conventionally, ranking knowledge is transferred by training the student on static rankings generated offline by the teacher
(
Sun et al., 2023
;
Gangi Reddy et al., 2024
;
Schlatt et al., 2025
)
via learning-to-rank objectives. However, such fixed supervision cannot adapt to the student’s evolving predictions, leaving the teacher unable to provide feedback on the student’s current ranking decisions. While on-policy distillation (OPD) provides dynamic, state-aware feedback and has demonstrated notable success in autoregressive generation
(
Agarwal et al., 2024
;
Gu et al., 2024
)
, effectively enabling it to complement offline ranking supervision in single-token rerankers remains challenging due to the structural mismatch between sequential feedback and single-pass scoring.
Specifically, standard token-level OPD relies on autoregressive rollouts to obtain conditional teacher feedback, whereas a single-token reranker represents the entire ranking through a static score vector in a single forward pass. Given this discrepancy, naive distillation strategies are insufficient: matching only the teacher’s first-token distribution captures initial preferences but leaves subsequent conditional choices unused, while training the student to generate full ranking sequences creates a mismatch with the first-token scores used at inference. This raises our core question:
How can we distill the sequential ranking preferences of an autoregressive teacher into a student that ranks all candidates in a single forward pass?
To address this question, we propose
DecisionRank
, a decision reranking model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (Figure
2
). Rather than relying on autoregressive student rollouts, we sort the student’s first-token scores to construct ranking prefixes from its current top-
K
K
candidates. A frozen generative teacher evaluates these prefixes in a single teacher-forced forward pass, providing conditional choice distributions over the remaining candidates at each ranking step. We obtain the corresponding student distributions by normalizing its first-token scores over the same remaining candidates, and align them with the teacher distributions using reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence in item space. This directly supervises the student’s first-token scores used for inference, while allowing teacher feedback to adapt as the student’s ranking evolves. Because the alignment operates over candidate identities rather than vocabulary tokens, the teacher and student need not share a vocabulary or model architecture. We jointly optimize this on-policy objective with offline RankNet supervision derived from teacher-generated rankings, combining global ordering preferences with conditional feedback on the student’s current ranking. At inference, the student preserves its single-pass efficiency, ranking the full candidate set without autoregressive generation.
We conduct extensive experiments across four benchmarks covering both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks. Our method achieves a strong effectiveness–latency tradeoff compared with existing LLM-based rerankers. As shown in Figure
1
, all three distilled students (1.7B, 4B, and 8B) outperform the 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19–23
(
Craswell et al., 2020
;
Craswell et al., 2025
)
. Notably, our 8B student also surpasses the listwise DirectRank-8B while running
24.5
×
24.5\times
faster on TREC DL under the same input length settings. Our method consistently improves ranking effectiveness over offline RankNet supervision across all four benchmarks and outperforms alternative training objectives, including Offline KL, autoregressive SFT, autoregressive OPD, and Listwise GRPO
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
Prabhakar et al., 2026
)
. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary benefits of offline RankNet supervision and on-policy distillation, with their combination achieving the strongest performance. Beyond ranking effectiveness, our 8B students yield lower pairwise calibration error than their Qwen3.8 and Gemma teachers on TREC DL and BRIGHT, without a calibration-specific training objective (Section
3.2.3
).
The contributions of this paper are threefold:
•
We introduce item-space on-policy distillation and combine it with offline ranking supervision to distill the ranking ability of generative LLM teachers into
DecisionRank
, a decision model for document reranking.
•
We show that
DecisionRank
achieves competitive performance across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, with substantially lower inference latency than generative listwise rerankers.
•
We demonstrate generalizability across teacher families and student sizes, with consistent improvements over zero-shot students across all 4 benchmarks.
2
Method
DecisionRank
is a decision model for document reranking that learns from a generative teacher. It combines offline ranking supervision with on-policy feedback (Figure
2

First-Token Ranking and Item-Space Alignment
uses first-token document-ID logits as ranking scores and aligns teacher and student choice distributions over the same candidate items.
On-Policy Conditional Feedback
uses the student’s current ranking as a sequence of document selections. The teacher evaluates the remaining documents given those already selected, providing feedback to supervise the student’s scores.
Offline Supervision and Joint Training
combines this feedback with global ordering preferences from offline teacher rankings.

RQ1: How does our method compare with existing rerankers?
We compare our method with pointwise and listwise rerankers. Pointwise methods score each query–document pair independently, while listwise methods consider multiple documents together. We evaluate ranking effectiveness across all 4 benchmarks, then examine inference efficiency and score calibration on TREC DL and BRIGHT.

Ranking Effectiveness

General retrieval.
All three student sizes outperform the compared baselines on both TREC DL and BEIR.
Our 8B student improves over the strongest baseline, listwise DirectRank, by 1.42 points on TREC DL and 2.20 points on BEIR. The advantage already appears at 1.7B: our smallest student exceeds every compared baseline on both benchmark averages, including models with up to 32B parameters.
Reasoning-intensive retrieval.
Our 8B student achieves the highest average score on BRIGHT, and both 4B and 8B students outperform all open-weight pointwise baselines on BRIGHT and R2MED.
The 8B student reaches 36.86 on BRIGHT, improving over listwise DirectRank by 0.99 points. On R2MED, it achieves 43.55, compared with 44.50 for listwise DirectRank. With just 16,000 training queries, our method distills the teacher’s ability to rerank reasoning-intensive queries and transfers this ability to out-of-domain medical retrieval.

RQ2: Which training objective works best for ranking with first-token logits?
Here, we ask which form of teacher supervision best improves the first-token reranking scores used at inference. We compare five additional objectives on top of a common RankNet loss: offline logit distillation (Offline KL), autoregressive supervised fine-tuning (AR SFT), autoregressive on-policy distillation (AR OPD), Listwise GRPO, and our item-space on-policy distillation (Item-space OPD).
RankNet.
RankNet is a classic pairwise learning-to-rank loss
(
Burges et al., 2005
)
. Following FIRST
(
Gangi Reddy et al., 2024
)
, we use a weighted RankNet objective (Equation
6
) as the foundation for distillation. The following objectives each add a different form of supervision to this common foundation.
+ Offline KL.
Offline KL matches the student’s first-token distribution to a fixed teacher distribution. Before training, we run the teacher on the full candidate set and cache its first-position distribution over candidate IDs. We then minimize forward KL,

+ Autoregressive SFT (AR SFT).
AR SFT teaches the student to generate the teacher’s ranking as an autoregressive sequence. We apply teacher-forced cross-entropy to the ranking tokens, following the joint ranking and language-model supervision in FIRST
(
Gangi Reddy et al., 2024
)

We therefore only generate the first 20 candidate IDs from the teacher’s offline ranking and use them as the SFT target. The student learns to generate this ranking sequence while RankNet loss supervises the full candidate set on the first token logits.
+ Autoregressive OPD (AR OPD).
AR OPD applies distillation at each candidate-ID position in a student-generated ranking, following the GKD paradigm
(

We provide the teacher with the query and the selected candidates, and append the student-generated ranking as a teacher-forced response. We design Item-space OPD to obtain corrective teacher feedback on the student’s ranking decisions. At each training step, the student’s first-token logits select and order its top-
K
K

A single forward pass yields the teacher’s conditional next-item distributions along these prefixes. As shown in Table
2
,
our method is the only method that consistently improves RankNet across all four benchmarks.
Offline KL
improves BRIGHT but degrades general retrieval and R2MED, suggesting that the teacher’s first-token distribution does not adequately capture ranking preferences beyond the initial selection.

improve reasoning-intensive retrieval but hurt general retrieval, consistent with a mismatch between sequence-generation training and first-token-score inference.

provides ranking-level scalar rewards without explicit feedback on individual selections. In contrast,
our method

4
Related Work
4.1
Efficient LLM-based Reranking
Generative listwise rerankers, such as RankGPT
(
Sun et al., 2023
)
and RankZephyr
(
Pradeep et al., 2023
)
, produce rankings autoregressively, incurring decoding latency and repeated model calls for long candidate lists. TourRank
(
Chen et al., 2025a
)
and GroupRank
(
Long et al., 2026
)
improve efficiency through grouped comparisons and parallel processing. In contrast, FIRST
(
Gangi Reddy et al., 2024
)
eliminates ranking-sequence generation by sorting first-token document-ID logits, with subsequent work extending this approach
(
Chen et al., 2025b
)
. Our work builds on first-token ranking and focuses on learning these scores from a generative teacher.
4.2
Knowledge Distillation for Reranking
Knowledge distillation transfers ranking knowledge from powerful teachers to smaller models. RankZephyr
(
Pradeep et al., 2023
)
and LiT5-Distill
(
Tamber et al., 2023
)
train generative rerankers on teacher-generated rankings, while Rank-DistiLLM
(
Schlatt et al., 2025
)
distills teacher rankings into cross-encoders using learning-to-rank objectives. DeAR
(
Abdallah et al., 2025
)
further incorporates reasoning-based supervision. Beyond offline distillation, GKD
(
Agarwal et al., 2024
)
and MiniLLM
(
Gu et al., 2024
)
leverage teacher feedback on student-generated sequences. Unlike these autoregressive approaches,
DecisionRank
applies on-policy teacher feedback directly to first-token ranking scores.
5
Conclusion
We introduced
DecisionRank
, a decision reranking model that combines offline ranking supervision with item-space on-policy distillation. Conditional teacher feedback on the student’s current ranking directly trains the first-token scores used at inference. This approach improves ranking across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval and generalizes across teacher families and student sizes. On TREC DL and BRIGHT, our 8B model outperforms its generative listwise counterpart with substantially lower latency.
DecisionRank
learns from a generative teacher’s sequential ranking decisions while reranking the full candidate set through single-token scoring, offering a promising path to distilling efficient decision models for broader applications.

Score questions are batched using the same passage-length limits as our students. Choice presents all 100 candidates as options in one question and ranks them by their returned probabilities. Passages are shortened uniformly when needed to fit the API context. Both modes break ties using retrieval order. To make the latency comparison fairer, we use server-reported time to exclude client-side network and connection delays. Latency measurement.
For the local models in Section
3.2.2
, we use each method’s original inference configuration with passages truncated to 128 tokens for TREC DL and 384 tokens for BRIGHT, measuring both effectiveness and latency under these settings. We rerank 100 candidates from BM25 and ReasonIR-8B, respectively, using one vLLM worker per NVIDIA B200. After warm-up, queries are processed individually; we take the median latency per worker, then the median across 8 workers. Pointwise rerankers process all 100 query–document pairs concurrently; timing ends when all scores are available. Listwise timings include all required model calls and decoding steps. Student timings cover the forward pass and exclude score sorting.

article.headline: 单token重排器用在线蒸馏学习生成教师
article.lede: Meta与普渡大学提出DecisionRank，将生成式教师的排序偏好蒸馏进单token决策重排器，以单次前向完成重排。
article.problem: 生成式listwise重排器靠自回归逐项生成排序，精度强但解码延迟高；单token重排器用首token文档ID logits一次排序，却难以继承教师的序列排序偏好。
article.method: DecisionRank把学生当前首token分数排出的top-K候选当作选择前缀，让冻结生成教师在一次teacher-forced前向中输出每一步对剩余候选的条件选择分布。学生把同一批剩余候选上的首token分数归一化成分布，用reverse KL在候选项目空间对齐教师分布，并与离线教师排名上的RankNet损失联合训练。
article.results: 在Qwen3-8B学生上，TREC DL、BEIR、BRIGHT、R2MED的平均nDCG@10×100分别为64.34、57.98、36.86、43.55；相对listwise DirectRank-8B，TREC DL高1.42、BEIR高2.20、BRIGHT高0.99，但R2MED低0.95（43.55对44.50）。在TREC DL和BRIGHT上，8B学生比该生成式listwise对照分别快24.5倍和16.7倍。1.7B学生在TREC DL19–23平均63.89，超过其27B生成教师。
article.why_it_matters: 这意味着检索系统可在不逐token解码的情况下获得较强的排序质量，并显著降低在线延迟；跨教师家族和1.7B–8B学生规模的增益也提高了部署灵活性。
article.limitations: 方法依赖强生成教师提供离线排名与在线条件反馈，训练仅用16,000条查询，候选集上限为100且学生仅使用100个单token文档ID，尚未验证更大候选集或开放域扩展。R2MED上8B学生为43.55，仍低于listwise DirectRank-8B的44.50。
article.figure_caption_zh: 离线RankNet与在线项目空间蒸馏共享同一首token分数：冻结教师一次前向给出条件选择分布，学生按候选身份对齐并用于单次前向排序。

figure.caption: Training with offline rankings and on-policy feedback. A frozen generative teacher supplies offline rankings for RankNet (left) and conditional feedback along the student's current ranking (right). One teacher-forced forward pass provides the teacher's choice distributions, which are aligned with the student's scores renormalized over the remaining documents. Both objectives supervise the same first-token scores. The student's scoring procedure is the same during training and inference: a single forward pass produces the first-token scores used to rank all candidates.

page_papers.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

Real-time streaming video generation must sustain playable output with consistent appearance and natural motion.
Chunk-wise autoregressive methods such as Self Forcing (SF) and Causal Forcing (CF) denoise each chunk conditioned on preceding content
(
Huang et al., 2025a
;
Zhu et al., 2026b
)
.
Under the clean-history caching convention adopted in this work, an additional forward pass, termed
store
, refreshes the key/value (K/V) history from the clean result.
Sequential execution places denoising and store between consecutive outputs, yielding
NF1C (N Forward Rounds, 1 Chunk Output)
.
Thus, even one-step denoising requires two forward passes when store is included.
We target
1F1C
: one completed chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill, while retaining every denoising update.
Inspired by wavefront scheduling
(
Jin et al., 2016
)
, earlier chunks execute later denoising stages while newer chunks execute earlier ones.
These staggered tasks form a moving
wavefront
(Fig.
1
a).
Assigning a full-model replica to each denoising stage and the store stage creates a bounded-width pipeline (Fig.
1
c).
To advance chunks before their predecessors finish, we use
chunk-wise causal context
: full attention within each chunk, cached history, and live context from earlier, cleaner chunks, with no dependence on later chunks.
This directional conditioning accommodates differences in stage-wise progress and enables overlapped execution (Fig.
1
b).
Our staged training builds on mixed-noise joint denoising
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
, uses teacher videos to supervise motion and framing, and adapts the model to causal inference with self-generated history.
This generation structure and its training recipe together constitute
Wave Forcing (WF)
.
To turn this scheduling potential into shorter output intervals,
Wave Runtime (WaveRT)
implements
Wave Parallelism (WP)
.
Following GPU software-pipelining principles
(
NVIDIA, 2026b
;
NVIDIA, 2026a
)
, WP exploits differences in stage-wise progress for early layer-wise K/V delivery and communication–computation overlap, reducing exposed dependency waits.
Data placement, kernel optimization, and load-balanced VAE pipeline parallelism complete the execution path from concurrent denoising to
sustained video output
.
On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
, 5-step WF achieves overall quality comparable to 5-step Rolling Forcing (RF), with VBench Total scores of 81.64 versus 81.15 and VBench-Long Quality scores of 81.26 versus 81.18
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2026b
)
.
Dynamic Degree increases from 51.39 to 94.44 on short videos and from 36.63 to 91.45 on 100-second videos.
These gains are accompanied by better Subject Preservation (97.10 versus RF’s 92.75) while maintaining low Camera Drift
(0.37 versus RF’s 0.17)
.
In terms of system performance, 4-step WF with the BF16/FA3 backend achieves
147.6 DiT FPS
and
134.8 end-to-end FPS
on eight H200 GPUs, yielding a
7.07
×
\mathbf{7.07\times}
end-to-end speedup over the 19.06-FPS single-GPU baseline (Table
4
).
At this denoising speed, residual output-path overhead remains visible even with three-stage VAE pipelining, as discussed in Section
7
.
Across six model scales from 1.3B to 14B, WP outperforms the faster context-parallel (CP) baseline at five scales under BF16 and all six under Sage+W8A8, achieving
1.025
–
2.530
×
\mathbf{1.025\text{--}2.530\times}
its throughput under Sage+W8A8.
System ablations and profiling further analyze how communication overlap, K/V placement, compute backends, and VAE stage balance affect runtime performance.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
Causal wavefront generation.
We introduce Wave Forcing, allowing newer chunks to condition on earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising completes. By pipelining denoising and clean-history cache refresh across full-model replicas, WF enables one completed chunk per concurrent forward round (1F1C) after pipeline fill while retaining all denoising updates.
•
Training for continuous generation.
We develop a staged training recipe combining mixed-noise initialization, teacher-guided motion supervision, and causal adaptation with self-generated history. This adapts the model to wavefront inference, enabling strong motion and subject preservation over long rollouts at overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing.
•
Efficient streaming execution.
We build Wave Runtime to realize wavefront concurrency through early layer-wise K/V delivery, communication–computation overlap, and direct placement into attention buffers. With optimized local computation and load-balanced VAE decoding, the runtime translates stage concurrency into sustained end-to-end throughput, with efficiency validated across 1.3B–14B models.

Local computation and K/V delivery require joint optimization. SageAttention
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
and W8A8 target faster local operators but alter producer–consumer progress. K/V quantization reduces payloads, and paged writes reduce receiver-side context assembly. The goal is K/V readiness before each layer’s attention, reducing exposed communication and
synchronization waits
.
Asynchronous decoding overlaps VAE and DiT, but the slower pipeline limits E2E throughput. We use profiled streaming times to balance contiguous VAE partitions across dedicated GPUs while preserving request-local causal caches (Fig.
4
). Decoding and inter-stage transfers must sustain DiT’s output rate. The first decoded output still incurs pipeline fill latency (Appendix
B.5
).
WP uses full-model replicas, with execution width determined by the denoising-step count. Logical K/V fan-out remains quadratic in the number of stages, while attention workloads vary across stages. Appendices
B.8
and
B.4
quantify communication traffic and pipeline fill/drain costs, respectively.

Related Work
Efficient streaming video generation.
Self Forcing
(
Huang et al., 2025a
)
reduces exposure bias by training autoregressive video diffusion on self-generated histories. SGF
(
Zhuang et al., 2026
)
restores gradient supervision for historical K/V through two-pass replay, while SGF+
(
Su et al., 2026b
)
separates context-writing and denoising parameters to reduce gradient conflict. Other approaches include few-step causal distillation
(
Yin et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2026b
)
and mixed-noise denoising
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
. AnyFlow
(
Gu et al., 2026
)
learns two-time flow maps with on-policy distillation for variable sampling budgets; Mask Forcing
(
Zhao et al., 2026b
)
perturbs DMD self-rollouts with dual-noise masking to improve teacher-mode coverage. For long-horizon streaming, Helios
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)
compresses historical and noisy context and simulates drifting during training. Vidu S1
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
uses stage-aware noisy and clean history caches for real-time, voice-controlled character generation. Vidu S2
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
introduces Self-Replay Forcing and supports dynamic references and streaming editing. These methods motivate studying training objectives together with the context available during streaming inference.
Multi-chunk generation.
Blockwise diffusion also appears in language modeling and action generation. D2F
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
conditions language generation on partially denoised predecessors, while MBD-LMs
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
align training with concurrent decoding of a bounded set of blocks at heterogeneous noise levels. In vision-language-action models, BlockVLA
(
Wang et al., 2026c
)
adapts pretrained autoregressive models through block diffusion finetuning, and TBD-VLA
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
organizes actions into temporal blocks and supports asynchronous chunk execution through temporal inpainting. Multimodal Diffusion Forcing
(
Huang et al., 2025c
)
assigns noise levels across time and modalities to model dependencies within multimodal robot trajectories. These approaches illustrate different choices of block dependencies; WF specifically trains video chunks to consume cleaner intermediate context through a directed causal wavefront.
Parallel execution.
Ulysses
(
Jacobs et al., 2023
)
and Ring
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
partition individual forward passes, using all-to-all exchange and K/V circulation, respectively. Live Avatar and HiAR
(
Huang et al., 2025b
;
Zou et al., 2026
)
explore pipelined execution with fixed-timestep or matched-noise designs. WP instead schedules chunk–stage tasks on full-model replicas (Sec.
5.5
), adapting wavefront scheduling
(
Hou et al., 2018
;
Jin et al., 2016
)
alongside optimized attention and runtimes
(
Dao et al., 2022
;
Dao, 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Zheng et al., 2024
)
.
Video evaluation.
VBench
(
Huang et al., 2024
)
provides standardized quality, semantic, and motion measures. Our long-video comparisons (Sec.
5.1
) show that high Quality and Dynamic Degree can coexist with subject loss and camera drift. We therefore supplement benchmark scores with targeted stability diagnostics; their scope and future alternatives are discussed in Secs.
7
and
8
.
These lines frame WF’s joint design of causal conditioning, training, and execution, together with the evidence used to assess it. Section
7
examines the remaining methodological and system limits; Sec.
8
connects them to better evaluation, interactive generation, and world modeling.
7
Limitations
Our evaluation establishes streaming generation under fixed conditioning and the tested model, sampling, and hardware configurations. The following limits of the training and execution design discussed in Sec.
6
motivate the agenda in Sec.
8
.
Quality evaluation and diagnostic coverage.
VBench-based scores do not fully characterize long-stream quality: in our comparisons, high Quality and Dynamic Degree coexist with subject disappearance and camera drift (Sec.
5.1
). Subject Preservation and Camera Drift expose these failures, but rely on a 100-prompt subject-focused subset, tracking and identity association, and geometric heuristics (Appendix
C.1
). Their sensitivity to thresholds and missing observations, coverage of intentional scene changes, and agreement with human judgments remain to be established. They provide targeted diagnostics, with broader perceptual and semantic quality still requiring assessment.
Output-path capacity and attribution.
VAE pipelining overlaps and partitions decoding but does not remove its finite service capacity. The 1.3B BF16 configurations reach 147.58/134.81 DiT/E2E FPS at four steps and 104.82/96.46 at five steps (Tab.
1
), with three and two VAE GPUs under the eight-GPU budget, respectively. These gaps are consistent with residual decoder/output-path limits. Aggregate timings, however, do not isolate VAE compute, transfers, queueing, or backpressure, and system DiT timing may reflect decoder interference. For 14B BF16, the gap narrows to 28.74 versus 28.64 DiT/E2E FPS (Tab.
4
). Matched VAE-on/off runs and stage-level measurements are needed to identify bottlenecks and guide end-to-end resource allocation.
Training complexity.
WF currently uses a complex multi-stage training procedure. An important direction is to simplify this procedure while preserving generation quality and long-video stability.
Scalability at a fixed sampling budget.
For
S
S
DiT denoising steps, WP uses
S
S
denoising stages and one cache-refresh stage, each with a full-model replica. Stage parallelism is therefore bounded at a fixed step count, limiting the scale of a single pipeline. Our experiments also show that WP’s throughput advantage over CP narrows for larger models. These constraints motivate studying finer-grained or hybrid parallelism and resource sharing across streams.
Interaction and serving scope.
High steady-state throughput alone does not establish low input-to-visible-output latency. Online condition changes require deciding when inputs take effect in active chunks and how cached state is refreshed; the fixed-context equivalence argument in Appendix
B.6
does not cover these updates. Prompt switching, camera/action control, closed-loop tasks, and multi-stream deadline guarantees require dedicated evaluation beyond the present fixed-conditioning experiments.
8
Future Work
The limits in Sec.
7
define our research agenda: strengthen end-to-end streaming execution, enable online interaction, and then extend toward interactive world models. Serving research and richer quality evaluation support these capability extensions throughout. Appendix
E
develops the task-specific questions.
End-to-end execution and scalability.
We plan to profile decoder stages, transfers, queues, and backpressure to guide DiT/VAE resource allocation. To address WP’s fixed-step scaling limit, we will study finer-grained execution and combinations with context parallelism, checking communication costs and causal dependencies under each design. Simplifying WF’s training recipe while preserving motion and long-horizon stability remains a parallel objective.
Serving concurrent streams.
StreamDiffusion’s image-stream batching
(
Kodaira et al., 2025
)
and StreamDiffusionV2’s video-stream scheduling
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
motivate latency-aware batching. SlackServe
(
Xia et al., 2026
)
uses playout slack for resource and quality decisions, while PhysisServe
(
Physis AI Infra Team, 2026
)
explores fine-grained stage pipelining. Building on these directions, we aim to study admission control, batching, and resource allocation for concurrent WF streams while respecting their context dependencies. Evaluation should include startup delay, output jitter, playback stalls, fairness, and quality alongside throughput.
Interactive streaming generation.
The next capability is updating prompts during generation. LongLive’s KV recaching
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
provides a starting point for coordinating new conditions with visual history. Extending WF requires defining which active chunks receive each update, refreshing affected state, and adapting training to condition changes. We will assess prompt-to-visible-output latency, prompt adherence, and visual continuity, rather than inferring responsiveness from output FPS.
Interactive world models.
Camera and action inputs further introduce feedback-dependent state evolution. We aim to explore both learned world prediction
(
Zhao et al., 2026a
;
Su et al., 2026a
)
and systems in which code or an engine maintains world state while a video model renders observations
(
Chen et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. The latter motivates adapting WF for structure-conditioned streaming rendering. Both routes require training under the corresponding control interface and evaluating control alignment, state consistency, and closed-loop behavior. They build on the execution and interaction work above and remain prospective extensions of WF.
Richer quality evaluation.
To address the metric limits above, we plan to incorporate streaming-interaction benchmarks such as StreamEval
(
StreamEval Team, 2026
)
, which evaluates task execution and state consistency under timed inputs alongside visual quality. Long-video understanding methods such as StreamMeCo
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
could help organize temporal evidence for an auxiliary quality judge. We aim to combine automatic diagnostics, understanding-based judgments, and human assessment, with explicit criteria for subject continuity, intended motion, and instruction execution. Such judges require timestamped evidence, calibration against human annotations, and checks for missed failures before their scores can support model comparisons.
9
Conclusion
We present Wave Forcing, which jointly designs causal context, training strategies, and multi-GPU pipelining to denoise multiple video chunks concurrently. WF uses cleaner intermediate states of preceding chunks as context for subsequent chunks, with three-stage training adapting the model to mixed-noise contexts and self-generated histories. A pipeline of full-model replicas then produces one video chunk per concurrent forward round after fill, while WaveRT overlaps K/V delivery with computation to reduce dependency waits. Experiments show that WF improves motion while maintaining overall generation quality and achieves high-throughput streaming video generation. These results demonstrate that jointly designing generation context, training, and execution can translate cross-chunk parallelism into practical gains in video generation efficiency.

B.6
Same-graph semantic preservation
Wave Forcing changes the model graph relative to RF. Once the WF graph is fixed, synchronized and asynchronous execution can be compared at the operator level.
Proposition 1
(Same-graph scheduling)
.
Fix the model parameters, denoising schedule, initial noise, per-update re-noising draws, text conditioning, positional embeddings, and history/store rules. Assume each local operator evaluates the same mathematical function and every attention operation receives the ordered K/V context in Eq. (
5
), after the corresponding K/V production and delivery have completed. Then dependency-respecting asynchronous execution and synchronized execution produce the same mathematical latent sequence.
Proof.
At the first tick, both executions start from identical inputs and empty history. At each layer, local Q/K/V projections depend only on that rank’s current hidden states and fixed conditioning. The synchronized execution gathers all projections before consuming them. The asynchronous execution may publish and consume them at different times, but the readiness condition guarantees the same legal K/V values and sequence order at attention. Consequently each attention result and the remaining local layer outputs agree. Induction over layers gives identical clean-latent predictions, from which the fixed scheduler and noise draws produce identical stage outputs. Store receives the same clean latent, runs the same cache-refresh computation, and promotes the same pages after the tick. Induction over ticks establishes identical histories and emitted latents through fill, steady state, and drain.

Evaluation details
VBench protocol.
We follow the standard VBench benchmark
[
Huang et al., 2024
]
with the original prompts, normalization, and weights, and scale scores to 0–100. For detailed metric definitions, we refer readers to the VBench paper. All metrics are computed with the official standardized evaluation scripts.
VBench-Long protocol.
We report the VBench-Long Quality score and Dynamic Degree, scaled to 0–100. Each method uses the same 200 MovieGen prompts and seed 42, generating 399 latent frames and saving 1593 frames (about 100 seconds) at 16 FPS per video. Causal Forcing (Full Attn.) uses the EMA generator of the released
chunkwise/longvideo.pt
checkpoint with its native 4-step schedule and full attention, for both standard VBench and VBench-Long.
Quality-generation setup.
Rolling Forcing and Causal Forcing are evaluated in their own code repositories. RF with the causal mask and Wave Forcing use WaveRT with causal KV context, paged exchange, and a time-partitioned VAE. The 4-step and 5-step models use 4+1+3 and 5+1+2 GPUs, respectively, ordered as denoising + Store + VAE. Checkpoint quality is evaluated with SDPA for standard inference and SageAttention for fast inference. Execution performance is measured separately using FA3 and dummy DiT weights.

Appendix E
Extended Future Work
This appendix develops the interaction, serving, and world-model extensions in Sec.
8
, following the training and execution limits in Sec.
7
. These extensions have not been evaluated with WF.
Online interaction and condition changes.
LongLive
[
Yang et al., 2026
]
uses KV recaching to align visual context with an updated prompt; EditStream and LPM
[

,

]

B.6

Serving under streaming deadlines.
StreamDiffusion’s image-stream batching
[
Kodaira et al., 2025
]
and StreamDiffusionV2’s video-stream scheduling
[
Feng et al., 2026
]

[

]
relates scheduling and quality choices to buffered playback time, while PhysisServe’s technical blog
[
Physis AI Infra Team, 2026
]
describes pipelining over transformer blocks and denoising steps, together with GPU time sharing. Future WF serving should study admission control, stream priorities, resource allocation, and finer-grained placement under its live-context dependencies. Changing sampling budgets also changes WP’s available stage parallelism (Sec.
7
); adopting another system’s batching or state-reuse rules would therefore require checking WF’s conditioning graph. Startup delay, output jitter, stall rate, and fairness should accompany throughput and quality measurements.
Learning controlled world evolution.
One route extends video prediction with structured controls. minWM and ForgeWM
[
Zhao et al., 2026a
,
Li et al., 2026
]
study controllable few-step video generation; SolarWM
[
Huang et al., 2026a
]
emphasizes data standardization and causal adaptation; SANA-WM
[
Zhu et al., 2026a
]
explores hybrid linear attention for long-horizon generation; and OneWM
[
Su et al., 2026a
]
jointly learns world prediction and action generation. Integrating WF would require specifying when new camera or action inputs become available to in-flight chunks, validating state dependencies for each architecture, and assessing control fidelity, prediction consistency, and policy performance in closed-loop tasks.
Executable world state and generative rendering.
A complementary route delegates persistent state, rules, and dynamics to code or an engine. Code World Model and Matrix-Game 4.0
[
Chen et al., 2026
,
Zhang et al., 2026a
]
connect such state to video generation through visual proxies. StreamRender-H3
[
Lu et al., 2026
]
and SolarRenderer
[
Fang et al., 2026
]
further motivate structure-conditioned streaming rendering. Here WF could supply an execution foundation for a renderer trained to follow incoming structure, rather than taking responsibility for the engine’s dynamics. This would require aligned structure/video training and validation of temporal conditioning: StreamRender-H3 uses bidirectional attention within a streaming window, whereas SolarRenderer includes a block-causal variant. Neither establishes compatibility with WF’s wavefront. Evaluation should check whether rendered observations preserve the underlying state and expose action effects quickly enough for feedback.
Understanding-assisted quality evaluation.
Following the metric limits in Sec.
7
, a future evaluator could combine local defect checks with long-horizon, instruction-aware judgments. StreamEval
[
StreamEval Team, 2026
]
evaluates timed requests and retained state alongside visual quality. StreamMeCo
[
Wang et al., 2026a
]
addresses efficient streaming video understanding, while MemForest
[
Wang et al., 2026b
]
provides event-centric memory compression and retrieval. These mechanisms could help a video-understanding judge retrieve temporal evidence about entities, actions, and failures. Adapting them to quality judging requires human-calibrated validation: we should report supporting timestamps and unscorable intervals, assess agreement with human annotations, and test whether compressed memory loses brief defects or earlier facts. The goal is to complement our targeted diagnostics with broader, auditable quality assessment.

article.headline: 把去噪排成波前：流式视频生成提速 7 倍
article.lede: Wave Forcing 让不同 chunk 的去噪阶段错峰流水，8 张 H200 上 4 步模型端到端达 134.8
article.problem: 现有的 chunk 级自回归流式视频方法（如 Self Forcing）把去噪与历史 K/V 刷新串行执行：每个 chunk 需要 S 次去噪前向再加一次 store 前向，即使在一步去噪的情况下也要两次前向，作者称之为 NF1C。这种串行结构使输出间隔被两段前向时间锁死，而更长的 rollout 还会带来质量退化与镜头漂移。
article.method: Wave Forcing 让新 chunk 通过 chunk 级因果注意力读取更早、更干净但尚未去噪完成的 chunk 的中间状态，并把各去噪阶段与 store 分配到整模型副本上，形成宽度为 S+1 的有界波前流水线，填充后实现每个并发前向轮输出一个 chunk（1F1C）。为适配这种混合噪声上下文，作者设计了混合噪声初始化、off-policy DMD（含 LPIPS）与自生成历史因果适配的三阶段训练；执行侧 WaveRT 用提前发布 K/V、计算通信重叠、直接写入注意力槽位与负载均衡的 VAE 流水把阶段并发转成吞吐。
article.results: 在 Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B 上，5 步 WF 的 VBench Total 为 81.64（Rolling Forcing 81.15），VBench-Long Quality 81.26（RF 81.18），Dynamic Degree 从 RF 的 51.39 提升到短视频 94.44、100 秒视频 36.63 到 91.45，Subject Preservation 97.10 对 92.75，Camera Drift 0.37 对 0.17。系统侧 4 步 WF 在 8 张 H200 上达到 147.6 DiT FPS 与 134.8 端到端 FPS，相对单卡基线 19.06 FPS 为 7.07 倍；在匹配 SageAttention+W8A8 后端、步数与 GPU 数的 DiT-only 测试中，WP 在 1.3B–14B 六个尺度上最高达较快 CP 基线（Ulysses/Ring）的 2.53 倍（区间 1.025–2.530 倍），但 9B BF16 下为 0.985 倍，略逊于 Ulysses。
article.why_it_matters: 它把生成上下文、训练目标与多 GPU 执行放在一起设计，说明跨 chunk 的流水线并发可以转化成实际的流式吞吐，而不必牺牲去噪步数。这为实时长视频生成提供了一条「图结构—训练—运行时」协同优化的工程路线。
article.limitations: 系统吞吐数字全部来自随机初始化的 dummy DiT 权重（只测执行成本、不测质量），14B 模型也未训练，因此这些加速尚未在真实权重上验证。质量侧的主体保持与镜头漂移指标依赖 100 条筛选 prompt 子集与几何启发式，阈值敏感性和与人类判断的一致性仍待确认；此外阶段并行受去噪步数限制，模型变大时对上下文并行的优势明显收窄。
article.figure_caption_zh: 因果波前与连续输出（S=4）：去噪与 store 沿反对角线推进，五轮之内单个 Self Forcing 副本只输出 1 个 chunk，而 5 个 WF 副本在填充后输出 5 个。

(b) One later-layer K/V edge arrives before use. Other edges and initial waits are omitted. (c) Both schedules retain four denoising forwards plus store per chunk. Over five rounds, one SF replica emits one chunk, whereas five WF replicas emit five after fill. Wall-clock gains depend on stage costs and overlap.

page_papers.title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
page_papers.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards:
Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
Minju Gwak
Affiliation:
Georgia Institute of Technology

Abstract
Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in reasoning post-training have strengthened small language models
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Guo et al., 2025
)
, but further improvement under limited supervision requires making better use of available training problems. Self-improvement offers one route: models generate reasoning traces and learn from feedback on their own responses
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
;
Haluptzok et al., 2023
;
Yuan et al., 2024
)
. Answer-level feedback, such as the checkable outcomes used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)
(
Guo et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025
)
, provides a practical training signal but cannot distinguish responses with equally correct final answers. Such responses may differ in the soundness of their reasoning, the completeness of their justification, and the amount of unnecessary repetition; they may also differ in their value as training examples. Auxiliary preferences over these traces could provide additional supervision without requiring new problems or step-level annotations. We therefore ask:
when answer-level rewards cannot distinguish successful solutions, can auxiliary trajectory preferences improve learning and downstream transfer?
Figure 1:
Correct answers leave room for preference. We investigate whether these trajectory preferences improve learning and downstream transfer.
We investigate two auxiliary signals derived from the model’s own predictive token distributions. Self-Certainty (SC)
(
Kang et al., 2025
)
favors trajectories with greater predictive confidence. The second signal, inspired by uniform information density (UID)
(
Meister et al., 2021
)
, favors trajectories that combine global entropy variation with local smoothness, following observations of locally smooth but globally non-uniform information flow in successful reasoning
(
Gwak et al., 2026
)
. These signals define alternative preferences among responses receiving the same answer-level reward.
The central hypothesis of our study is that auxiliary preferences provide useful learning signals beyond answer-level feedback, improving task performance under limited supervision. To test this hypothesis, we compare training with and without auxiliary preferences while retaining the underlying answer-level supervision. Specifically, we adopt test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL)
(
Zuo et al., 2026
)
for only 2 epoch of training to adapt the model on a small set test time without reference answers, therefore using only 30 AIME2026 problems. Within TTRL, we augment majority-agreement rewards with auxiliary preferences among responses supporting the majority answer, preserving the reward between agreeing and disagreeing responses.
Results show that auxiliary trajectory preferences can improve self-improvement from answer-level feedback. After adaptation on just 30 AIME2026 problems without reference answers, TTRL augmented with a Self Certainty and UID Conjunction metric (UID-Conj.) improve Qwen3-1.7B’s macro-average accuracy across four mathematics and science benchmarks by 2.03 and 2.08 percentage points, respectively. The benefits extend to critique-verdict prediction and evidence-conditioned scientific reasoning. UID-Conj. improves CriticBench verdict accuracy by 1.24 points, incorrect-class F1 by 1.58 points, and LabBench2 accuracy by 0.76 points, without task-specific training. Complementary offline extensions show that UID-Conj. also improves Qwen3-1.7B’s macro-average by 1.25 points over random correct–correct DPO preferences and by 1.93 points over uniform SFT.
To summarize, our contributions are:
∘
\circ
An independent assessment of whether auxiliary signals distinguish reasoning quality among correct responses.
∘
\circ
A controlled study of auxiliary trajectory preferences for small-model self-improvement with limited training data, spanning online and offline settings with controls matched within each objective.
∘
\circ
An evaluation of transfer from mathematical self-improvement to critique and research-level reasoning.

Best-of-
N

selection.
Selection methods exploit different properties of sampled reasoning. Self-consistency aggregates agreement across final answers
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, whereas Self-Certainty (SC) scores responses using statistics of predictive distributions
(
Kang et al., 2025
)
. The uniform information density hypothesis concerns how information is distributed across language
(
Meister et al., 2021
)
; its application to LLM reasoning associates successful trajectories with local smoothness and global non-uniformity
(
Gwak et al., 2026
)
. These findings leave two questions unresolved: whether the scores identify useful differences among already-correct responses, and whether reinforcing those improves generation.
Self-improvement with outcome, process, and internal feedback.
Self-improvement methods use feedback on model-generated responses to refine reasoning. STaR learns from its own rationales that yield correct answers
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
)
, while DeepSeek models use RL with outcome feedback
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
Guo et al., 2025
)
. Process supervision provides finer-grained feedback on intermediate steps
(
Lightman et al., 2023
)
, while there have been research on preferring answers by length
Arora and Zanette (2025)
. Closest to ours, Intuitor uses SC as the sole reward in GRPO and reports generalization from mathematics to out-of-domain tasks
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
, and
Agarwal et al. (2025)
minimizes entropy during training. This establishes internal confidence as a self-improvement signal and raises a specific question: does entropy-trajectory structure add useful supervision beyond confidence when correctness feedback is available?
Transfer beyond verifiable training tasks.
Math datasets with known answers provide accessible supervision for reasoning models
(
Hendrycks et al., 2021
;
Shao et al., 2024
)
, but the intended applications may exceed this supervision in both difficulty and scope. Easy-to-hard generalization studies whether supervision from simpler problems can support harder math reasoning
(
Sun et al., 2024
)
, while scientific question answering exposes the difficulty of evaluating outputs that require specialized expertise
(
Rein et al., 2023
)
. Open research problems often lack gold answers for outcome-based rewards, even when proposed solutions can be checked. This gap motivates testing both transfer to harder math and transfer beyond verified answer generation.

3.2
Auxiliary Rewards with Answer-level Aggregation
Direct selection using auxiliary scores does not reveal how the selected reasoning traces differ (Table
1
). We therefore compare trace quality while holding final-answer correctness fixed. Averaged across rollout budgets, SC and UID-Conj achieve 25.4% and 25.7% accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B, compared with 25.9% for majority voting; for Qwen3-4B, the corresponding accuracies are 33.8% and 34.2%, versus 33.9%. However, incorporating answer-level agreement through Borda aggregation yields improvements, with UID-Conj + Borda achieving the highest accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B at 27.0% and SC + Borda performing best for Qwen3-4B at 34.7%. These gains vary across rollout budgets and model size (Figure
3
). For Qwen3-1.7B, auxiliary scores with Borda aggregation improve selection most clearly at smaller budgets. For Qwen3-4B, gains remain modest on MinervaMath, while results on HMMT and AIME depend on both the scoring method and rollout budget. Thus, auxiliary rewards provide complementary signals to answer-level agreement, but their selection benefits are context-dependent rather than uniform.

Training with Auxiliary Trajectory Signals
We mainly investigate auxiliary trajectory signals using post-training methods for reasoning models in online TTRL
(
Zuo et al., 2026

, where scores refine majority-vote feedback without reference answers. We also extend our setup to offline training, where scores define DPO

These settings let us examine the usefulness of auxiliary preferences under different forms of supervision and optimization. Together, these settings test whether trajectory-level distinctions provide useful supervision beyond answer-level feedback.

Models, training data, and benchmarks.
We use Qwen3-1.7B as base model, and additionally test on Qwen3-4B as well. Trainings are done for only 2 epochs for RL and 1 epoch for offline training. For online training, we perform test-time adaptation on AIME2026 without reference answers. For offline extensions, we use historical AIME problems gathered until 2025. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME2026, HMMT2026, and MinervaMath, and science reasoning on GPQA’s Diamond subset for verifiable tasks, and use CriticBench and LabBench2 for research-level reasoning. We also further evaluate on instruction following tasks to explore the different effects of different auxiliary rewards.
Comparison methods.
We compare UID-Conj. and SC within each training objective. Online comparisons include the base model, original TTRL, and a random auxiliary-score control. For DPO, we compare auxiliary-score preferences against randomly selected and oriented correct vs. correct pairs. For weighted SFT, uniform weighting provides the control on the same correct response pool.
Evaluation.
For verifiable mathematical benchmarks, we report mean accuracy across five sampled responses per question. For CriticBench, we report verdict accuracy and incorrect-class F1, which assess verdict correctness rather than critique quality. For IFBench, we report prompt-level loose accuracy using the official verifiers. For IHEval, we use the official task-specific metrics and aggregation procedure, reporting results separately for reference, aligned, and conflicting instruction settings.
