Abstract
Activation steering offers training-free and dynamic control of target behaviors in large language models, but existing methods can impair general capabilities and require domain-specific intervention designs. We introduce
Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS)
, a unified framework that balances target-behavior control with capability preservation. To make target-behavior improvement and general-capability preservation tractable, we introduce two proxies: log-probabilities of target tokens in model generated responses, and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining the local approximation of the two proxies yields a
closed-form solution
, enabling
lightweight steering
without iterative model training or additional inference-time computation. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients
achieve effective steering while limiting general-capability loss
. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure supports adaptation across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on Qwen and Llama models, CANS achieves comparable or better steering while better preserving MMLU, BBH, and IFEval performance than SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduces HarmBench attack success from
15.50
%
15.50\%
to
1.75
%
1.75\%
with a
1.11
1.11
-point decrease in average capability. These results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.
https://github.com/Eric-Arya/CANS-Steer
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications
(
OpenAI, 2023
;
Grattafiori et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
.
Despite their broad capabilities, they can produce unsafe or toxic
content
(
Gehman et al., 2020
;
Wei et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
)
and hallucinate factually incorrect statements
(
Ji et al., 2023
;
Manakul et al., 2023
)
.
The predominant countermeasure is training to control target behavior, including
supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
(
Bianchi et al., 2024
)
,
reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
, and direct preference optimization (DPO)
(
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
.
However, these approaches require additional training cost,
and do not inherently support dynamic, continuously adjustable control.
These limitations motivate lightweight methods that control
specific behaviors at inference time.
A prominent family of such methods is
activation steering
, which
modifies model behavior through activation interventions. These include two
widely adopted intervention levels: the vector level, targeting residual-stream hidden states
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Arditi et al., 2024
)
or attention-head outputs
(
Li et al., 2023
)
, and the neuron level,
which modifies individual activations
(
Suau et al., 2024
;
Dai et al., 2022
)
.
We focus on feed-forward network (FFN) neurons, defined as coordinates
of the FFN’s intermediate activations.
Prior work demonstrates their causal role in behavioral control: neuron interventions
can control human value-related behaviors
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
,
restore safety behavior
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
,
and regulate over-compliance with false premises and harmful instructions
(
Gao et al., 2025
)
. These findings motivate neuron-level steering as
a fine-grained mechanism for controlling model behavior.
However, these methods face two central challenges.
First, improvements in target-behavior control
can compromise general capability
.
This loss of capability can partly be attributed to the polysemanticity of LLM neurons:
a single neuron can encode information relevant to both the target behavior
and general-purpose tasks
(
Olah et al., 2020
;
Elhage et al., 2022
;
Gurnee et al., 2023
;
Bricken et al., 2023
)
.
Rescaling neurons associated with a target behavior
can disrupt shared functions needed for general tasks
(
Suau et al., 2024
;
Haider et al., 2026
)
.
Second, cross-domain generalizability is limited
by domain-specific
intervention designs
(
Suau et al., 2024
;
Gao et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
,
so applying them to a new target behavior can require redefining how neurons’ contribution
to a target behavior is scored, which neurons to intervene on, and by what magnitude.
Empirically, we find that transferring these procedures across domains often yields
limited steering gains and/or substantial capability loss.
To this end, we propose
Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering
(CANS), as illustrated in Figure
1
.
The central idea is to assign each neuron a coefficient
that accounts for both its contribution to the target behavior
and its impact on general capabilities.
CANS applies this adaptive scaling across all FFN neurons,
favoring changes that support the target behavior with less
disruption to other capabilities.
To make this objective computationally tractable, we introduce
two practical proxies.
For
target-behavior control
, we estimate how each neuron
affects the likelihood of target word spans in model responses associated with the
behavior we want to promote or suppress.
For
capability preservation
, we measure how much an
intervention changes the model’s output distribution on
general-purpose reference text.
This provides a label-free signal of disruption without
requiring separate evaluations of every capability.
We derive a
closed-form optimal solution
to the resulting optimization problem, yielding a steering coefficient for each neuron.
These coefficients balance estimated target-behavior gains against
output-distribution disruption, supporting effective steering with
limited general-capability loss. CANS also supports
cross-domain
generalizability
through a shared data-construction protocol and steering
procedure: adapting to a new domain requires only sampling responses from the unmodified model, filtering them, and annotating target spans.
We evaluate CANS on safety, toxicity, and hallucination control
using Qwen3-4B and models from the Llama family.
Across the evaluated settings, CANS achieves a more favorable
steering–capability trade-off than the compared neuron-level
steering baselines, with low computational overhead.
For example, on the safety benchmark HarmBench
(
Mazeika et al., 2024
)
,
CANS reduces Qwen3-4B’s attack success rate from
15.50
%
15.50\%
to
1.75
%
1.75\%
with a
1.11
1.11
-point decrease in average capability.
For toxicity, it reduces the same model’s toxic-prompt rate on
RealToxicityPrompts
(
Gehman et al., 2020
)
from
19.17
%
19.17\%
to
1.00
%
1.00\%
with no loss in average capability.
For hallucination, it reduces Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s hallucination rate on
TruthfulQA
(
Lin et al., 2022
)
from
17.75
%
17.75\%
to
0.75
%
0.75\%
with only a
0.06
0.06
-point decrease in average capability.
Figure 1:
Overview of CANS.
CANS uses target-token log-probabilities
for target-behavior control (left) and output-distribution KL on general-purpose
inputs for general-capability preservation (right). Local approximations
of these two proxies yield closed-form adaptive scaling across all neurons
under a shared preservation budget (center), enabling the same steering effect
with minimal general-capability loss.
2
Related Work
Activation steering for behavioral control.
Activation steering controls LLM behavior by modifying internal
activations at inference time, with representative methods including
intervention at vector and neuron levels.
At the
vector level
, methods modify residual-stream hidden states
or attention-head outputs. Fixed-direction approaches use steering vectors
precomputed from reference examples
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2023
)
.
However, a single direction may not capture complex patterns in
behavior-related activation distributions, limiting the expressiveness of
fixed-direction steering
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
.
Adaptive methods vary steering directions with hidden states with additional
training or inference cost
(
Kong et al., 2024
;
Pham and Nguyen, 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
,
whereas CANS steers each activation in a single step by the closed-form
coefficients, avoiding training or iterative activation updates.
At the
neuron level
, methods modify the scalar activations of
individual neurons. Such interventions have been used to reduce hallucinations
(
Gao et al., 2025
)
, mitigate toxicity
(
Suau et al., 2024
)
,
improve safety
(
Zhao et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
and
steer responses toward specified human values
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
.
Although these methods evaluate capability retention, they do not explicitly
incorporate a capability-preservation criterion into their steering objectives.
CANS instead optimizes neuron-wise strengths under a preservation budget
on general-purpose reference inputs.
These methods also rely on domain-specific criteria for locating and modifying
neurons, whereas CANS provides a generalizable framework for steering
target behaviors across domains.
Capability preservation during model behavior control.
Improving a target behavior can impair the model’s general capability.
For example, RLHF can reduce performance on other language tasks
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
, while safety-oriented activation patching can
improve safety at the expense of helpfulness
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
Training-based safeguards include KL regularization against a reference
model
(
Ziegler et al., 2019
;
Stiennon et al., 2020
;
Ouyang et al., 2022
;
Bai et al., 2022a
;
Bai et al., 2022b
;
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
and representation-retention losses
(
Zou et al., 2024
)
,
but require iterative model fine-tuning.
CANS instead optimizes neuron-wise strengths under a preservation budget
on general-purpose reference inputs, with an optimal closed-form solution
to the local proxy and no iterative model fine-tuning.
3
CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering
CANS treats steering as allocating a limited amount of change across
neurons. For each neuron, we ask two questions: how would scaling it
affect the target behavior, and how much would it change
the model’s general capability? We make these questions tractable
through two proxies, and derive a closed-form solution(See figure

for an overview).

Conclusion and Discussion
We introduced CANS, a lightweight, training-free approach to neuron
steering that balances target-behavior improvement with general-capability
preservation. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on the
evaluated Qwen and Llama models, CANS generally achieves a more favorable
steering–capability trade-off than the compared baselines.
The same optimization and intervention procedure applies across the evaluated domains,
using model-generated responses with filtering and target-span annotations.
Sequential steering results (Appendix
C
) further
support its potential as a lightweight, generalizable alternative to SFT for model behavioral control.
Limitations and future work.
Diagonal Fisher approximation.
CANS retains only the Fisher diagonal to avoid quadratic storage costs,
omitting neuron interactions and their joint roles in supporting model functions.
Richer curvature approximations could
capture these dependencies.
Reliance on target-span supervision.
Steering depends on the quality of generated responses, behavior labels,
and span annotations. A single target span may provide incomplete supervision
for hallucination, which is intertwined with the model’s underlying knowledge,
and for other domains involving complex behaviors that are not easily captured by a single target span.

The smaller Qwen and Llama models evaluated in this work generated

Ethics Statement
CANS aims to reduce undesirable model behaviors. However, neuron steering could also be misused to weaken
safeguards. Our preservation criterion provides no guarantee of safety or
fairness, and deployment requires application-specific evaluation.

Appendix C
Sequential Cross-Domain Steering
We compare CANS with sequential supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, applying each method successively to hallucination,
toxicity, and safety. Each stage starts from the model produced by the
preceding stage.
For sequential SFT, we use fixed domain corpora constructed from responses
sampled from the unmodified model, following the same corpus construction
as CANS in the single-domain setting. Each stage uses the SFT supervision
specified in Appendix
G
, and these corpora
remain fixed throughout sequential training.
For CANS, we first sample responses from the unmodified model to construct
the hallucination steering corpus and apply hallucination steering.
We then sample responses from this steered model to construct the toxicity
steering corpus and apply toxicity steering. Finally, we use the model
after both stages to construct the safety steering corpus and apply safety
steering. Each corpus follows the filtering and target-span annotation
procedure in Appendix
D
, and each stage’s steering
gradient is computed on the model entering that stage using the newly
constructed corpus. In contrast, the diagonal Fisher estimate is computed
only once from the unmodified model on the general-purpose reference corpus
and reused unchanged across all three stages; it is not re-estimated after steering.
Figure
10
shows that CANS promotes each
successive target behavior while accumulating less general-capability
loss than sequential SFT in this setting.

Appendix D
Domain-Gradient Corpus Construction
We construct each corpus separately for each model. Gradients in
Eq. equation
5
use teacher forcing with the full prompt
and pre-span response prefix. Only the loss is span-localized; when
computing gradients, we sum activation–gradient contributions over every
non-padding token position, with neuron scaling applied at all such positions.
Input formats.
Raw format
uses prompt and response text directly, without a chat
template;
chat format
uses the tokenizer’s native user–assistant
template. For CANS corpus construction and gradient computation, safety
and toxicity use raw format for both response generation and gradient
computation. Hallucination uses chat format for both stages,
with Qwen3 thinking disabled.
Safety.
From prompts in the Circuit Breakers training corpus,
generate raw-text responses separately for each model and retain 256
refusals using the case-sensitive
llm-attacks
refusal-substring
matcher
(
Zou et al., 2023
)
. Its
REFUSAL_PREFIXES
lexicon
is matched against the full completion;
first_refusal_cue
marks the earliest completed match.
Toxicity.
Use RealToxicityPrompts
(RTP).
Use prompts with stored toxicity at least
0.5
0.5
first,
and generate 25 raw completions per prompt. The
s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier
checkpoint
from ParaDetox
(
Logacheva et al., 2022
)
labels
completions with probability at least
0.5
0.5
as toxic and below
0.05
0.05
as
non-toxic; intermediate scores are discarded. Retain 500 same-prompt
mixed pairs and use their toxic members, with one exact response-local
target span localized individually by GPT-5.6-sol in each response.
The classifier fixes the response label; span annotation does not relabel
or discard a response. The annotation instructions allow contextual

(Section
D.1
).
Hallucination.
From TruthfulQA,
freeze 417 source questions by category-stratified sampling with seed 42,
leaving the other 400 for evaluation. Generate 10 native-chat responses
per source and model, with Qwen3 thinking disabled. The
allenai/truthfulqa-truth-judge-llama2-7B
evaluator
(
Allen Institute for AI, 2024
)
assigns truthfulness labels to the

article.headline: CANS：闭式神经元缩放兼顾行为控制与能力保持
article.lede: CANS 以目标 token 对数概率和通用输入 KL 为代理，闭式求解 FFN 神经元缩放系数，无需训练或额外推理。
article.problem: 现有激活引导方法无需训练即可动态控制 LLM 行为，但可能损害通用能力；神经元的多义性使针对目标行为的缩放干扰共享功能。同时，许多方法依赖领域专用的干预设计，迁移到新行为时往往需要重新定义评分、选点和幅度。
article.method: CANS 为所有 FFN 神经元分配缩放系数，用目标 token 对数概率代理行为收益，用通用输入上的输出分布 KL 代理能力损失。对两个代理做局部近似后，方法在共享保持预算下得到闭式解，并把系数折叠进 down-projection 权重，因而不增加推理时计算。跨域适配只需采样模型响应、过滤并标注目标片段。
article.results: 在 Qwen3-4B 上，CANS 将 HarmBench 攻击成功率从 15.50% 降到 1.75%，平均能力仅下降 1.11 分；将 RealToxicityPrompts 有毒提示率从 19.17% 降到 1.00%，平均能力无损失；在 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 上把 TruthfulQA 幻觉率从 17.75% 降到 0.75%，平均能力下降 0.06 分。在安全、毒性和幻觉控制上，CANS 相比 SFT、CAA 和神经元级基线取得相当或更好的引导效果，同时更好地保持 MMLU、BBH、IFEval。
article.why_it_matters: 它为推理时的行为控制提供了轻量替代方案：无需迭代训练或额外推理计算，同一套数据构建和干预流程可跨安全、毒性和幻觉等域复用。
article.limitations: 局限包括：仅保留 Fisher 对角项，忽略神经元之间的交互；依赖生成响应、行为标签和目标片段标注，对幻觉等复杂行为的监督可能不完整。Qwen3 上的幻觉控制增益有限，且预算增大后出现饱和。
article.figure_caption_zh: CANS 概览：左侧用目标 token 对数概率控制目标行为，右侧用通用输入上的输出分布 KL 保持通用能力，中心由两个代理的局部近似得到所有神经元的闭式自适应缩放系数。

figure.caption: {Overview of CANS.} CANS uses target-token log-probabilities for target-behavior control (left) and output-distribution KL on general-purpose inputs for general-capability preservation (right). Local approximations of these two proxies yield closed-form adaptive scaling across all neurons under a shared preservation budget (center), enabling the same steering effect with minimal general-capability loss.

huangxin25@m.fudan.edu.cn stmatengss@gmail.com {zhuoranli, yibozhao}@stu.pku.edu.cn zhaoshi.li@metax-tech.com
wangbo18@xiaohongshu.com yang_wei@fudan.edu.cn wangchenxi@ict.ac.cn {taoxie, youwei}@pku.edu.cn
*
Corresponding author
Abstract.
KV cache reuse accelerates LLM serving,
but existing systems manage host DRAM and NVMe SSD as a tiered hierarchy
where DRAM acts as an intermediate cache.
Production LLM workloads break both premises of this hierarchy.
First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering,
since workloads are dominated either by one-shot blocks with long reuse distances
or by multi-gigabyte agentic sessions that exceed DRAM capacity,
putting SSD on the critical read path.
Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration.
Holding host staging buffers for in-flight prefixes causes contention under load
that aborts prefetches, while incremental eviction scatters a session’s blocks
across the SSD and prevents large sequential reads.
We present
FlatCake
, a
flat
KV storage architecture that exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD
as peer media in a unified 64-bit address space.
Exploiting the fact that KV blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope,
FlatCake
places each block directly onto its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order
at creation time and never migrates it.
FlatCake
streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage
and decouples DRAM and SSD request queues to prevent head-of-line blocking.
On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
FlatCake
sustains a 94% cache hit rate as load increases (versus 64% for Mooncake),
eliminates Mooncake’s
6.5
×
6.5\times
–
6.7
×
6.7\times
SSD read amplification,
and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by
1.6
×
1.6\times
while improving total token throughput by
1.6
×
1.6\times
.
Across 8K–128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B,
FlatCake
further reduces mean TTFT by up to
2.4
×
2.4\times
over Mooncake
and
1.8
×
1.8\times
over Mooncake-GDS.
Keywords:
LLM serving, KV cache management, memory tiering,

Introduction
Prefix caching is now standard in large language model (LLM) serving,
allowing requests that share a prefix to reuse previously computed key-value (KV) tensors
and avoid redundant prefill computation
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Qin et al., 2025
)
.
As LLM workloads evolve from short, globally shared system prompts
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
to multi-turn conversations
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
and long-context agentic coding sessions
that append tool outputs and retrieved files on every turn (averaging 219K input tokens
per request in a production Claude Code trace
(
SemiAnalysis, 2026
)
),
active KV working sets routinely reach tens of gigabytes per session and span hours.
Because these working sets far exceed GPU HBM and host DRAM capacity,
while recomputing evicted history consumes up to 93% of prefill compute
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
,
NVMe SSDs must serve as a primary KV cache medium on the critical path
(
Qiu et al., 2025a
)
.

placing host DRAM in front of SSD as an intermediate L2 cache and staging layer.
Borrowed from general-purpose memory and storage systems,
this hierarchical design relies on two foundational premises:
(1)
temporal filtering
, namely that recency-based caching in DRAM can capture
the active working set so the slower SSD serves only cold misses off the critical path; and
(2)
staging and coalescing
, namely that because incremental eviction scrambles
on-disk layout relative to read order, staging SSD accesses through host DRAM buffers
is an effective way to reassemble scattered reads and hide device latency.
Profiling eight production traces from Mooncake, Qwen Bailian, and Claude Code (§
2.2
)
reveals that LLM KV cache workloads violate both premises simultaneously.
First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering,
putting SSD on the critical read path.
Across production traces, KV reuse falls into two regimes, and neither fits a DRAM cache filter.
In conversational and API workloads (seven traces), 53–94% of KV blocks are accessed only once,
while reusable prefixes span long reuse distances of hundreds to thousands of intervening requests;
admitting every request into DRAM pollutes it with one-shot blocks
that flush reusable prefixes to SSD before their next turn arrives.
Conversely, in agentic coding (Claude Code), 83.4% of blocks are reused (98.3% ideal hit rate)
with immediate turn-to-turn locality,
but multi-gigabyte session footprints quickly exceed host DRAM capacity across concurrent sessions.
In both regimes, most cache hits must be served from NVMe SSD,
so migrating blocks between DRAM and SSD adds data movement without keeping hot data in DRAM.
Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout turn SSD restoration
into a concurrency and I/O bottleneck.
When SSD must serve the bulk of hits, the tiered mechanisms meant to smooth SSD access
become the bottleneck itself.
Restoring a long-context prefix through host DRAM requires holding host staging buffers
for the entire in-flight hit, scaling memory demand with context length and concurrency.
Even when SSD-to-DRAM and DRAM-to-GPU transfers are pipelined,
concurrent restores contend for bounded staging memory,
delaying or aborting prefetches under load and turning blocks already stored on SSD into recomputed misses.
Worse, even when bypassing host DRAM via batched GPUDirect Storage (GDS),
tiered storage populates and reclaims SSD space in eviction or FIFO-bucket order rather than session order.
As a result, a session’s blocks are scattered across non-contiguous SSD offsets
and coarse bucket reclamation invalidates active prefixes across sessions,

Why does tiered storage fall into this trap?
Tiering is designed for mutable pages whose future access patterns and spatial grouping
are unknown when written.
Our key insight is that LLM KV cache blocks are write-once, immutable,
and reused together at the granularity of a session scope.
Because a block is never modified in place, there is no dirty state to write back;
because blocks generated in a turn belong to a known session prefix
and are always restored together across layers on subsequent turns,
their ideal on-disk spatial grouping is already known at creation time.
Consequently, if blocks are placed directly onto their target medium
in session-contiguous, layer-major order at write time and never migrated,
SSD restores become naturally sequential and no longer need host DRAM for either caching or reassembly.

FlatCake

flat KV storage architecture
that replaces the migratory hierarchy with peer storage media (§

2.
Background and Motivation
2.1.
KV Cache Reuse and Tiered Storage
Once generated during prefill, KV cache
(
Vaswani et al., 2017
)
blocks are write-once and immutable,
and their reuse across requests follows three primary patterns
determined by how the shared prefix is formed.
Prefix caching
(
Zheng and others, 2024
)
reuses KV blocks
across
requests that share a static prefix, such as a system prompt or few-shot template,
so only the uncached suffix requires prefill computation.
Multi-turn conversations
reuse KV blocks
within
a user session,
where each turn appends a new prompt and model response to the accumulated history of prior turns.
Agentic workloads
also accumulate state within a session,
but append tool invocations, retrieved files, and command outputs on every turn
while spawning sub-agents that replay the shared session prefix in parallel.
As a result, per-turn context grows by tens of thousands of tokens,
and a single session’s KV footprint can reach tens of gigabytes.
To accommodate working sets that exceed GPU HBM, existing systems such as
Mooncake
(
Qin et al., 2025
)
, LMCache
(
Cheng and others, 2025
)
, and SGLang HiCache
(
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
)
organize GPU HBM, host DRAM, and NVMe SSD as a three-level
tiered hierarchy
(Figure
1
(a)).
In this design, newly generated KV blocks are admitted into host DRAM first,
evicted incrementally to NVMe SSD under LRU or FIFO policies when DRAM fills,
and staged back through host DRAM buffers when restored to the GPU.
This architecture relies on two premises:
first, that host DRAM acts as an effective
temporal filter
that keeps the active working set in memory;
and second, that
staging and coalescing
SSD reads in host DRAM hides on-disk fragmentation and device latency.

2.2.
Why Tiered Storage Fails on LLM Workloads
Characterizing eight production traces from three providers (Table
1
,
evaluated at each trace’s native block size of 512, 16, and 64 tokens for Mooncake, Qwen Bailian, and Claude Code,
with reuse distance measured in intervening requests)
shows that LLM KV workloads break both premises of tiered storage.
Observation 1: Bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering, putting SSD on the critical read path.
Table
1
shows that ideal hit rates under an infinite-capacity cache
span 36.6% to 98.3% across the eight traces.
The traces fall into two distinct reuse regimes,
and in neither regime can recency-based DRAM caching retain the active working set.
Across the seven prefix-caching and conversation traces, 53.2–94.0% of blocks
are accessed only once, peaking at 94.0% in Qwen to-B API and 78.5% in Mooncake ToolAgent.
While the top 10% of blocks account for 34–65% of all accesses (Figure
2
(a)),
reuse distances exhibit heavy tails, reaching a mean of 2,550 intervening requests
and a P99 of 54,728 in Qwen to-B API (489 and 4,085 in Mooncake ToolAgent).
When every newly generated block is admitted into host DRAM first,
one-shot blocks continually flush reusable session prefixes to SSD before their next turn arrives.
Consequently, replacing the DRAM eviction policy yields little benefit:
even when the fast tier holds 40.1% of total blocks in multi-turn serving,
LRU, FIFO, and queue-enhanced policies all achieve DRAM hit rates near 20%
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
.
The agentic coding trace (Claude Code) exhibits the opposite reuse pattern
but reaches the same storage outcome.
Because each turn extends and replays the session prefix and sub-agent fan-out
reuses prefixes almost immediately (mean reuse distance of 0.85 requests, P99 of 14),
only 16.6% of blocks are one-shot and the infinite-capacity hit rate reaches 98.31%.
However, each request spans an average of 3,421 blocks (218,922 tokens),
compared with 23 blocks in Mooncake Conversation.
Even under DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s compressed FP8 representation (Figure
2
(b)),
a single request requires a median of 0.52 GiB and a mean of 0.80 GiB of history KV state
per GPU rank (4.1 GiB median and 6.4 GiB mean across eight ranks, reaching 16.0 GiB at P90).
Across concurrent multi-turn sessions, the active working set rapidly exceeds host DRAM capacity.
Thus, whether reuse is sparse with long reuse distances or dense across multi-gigabyte contexts,
most cache hits must be served from NVMe SSD,
making cross-tier migration between DRAM and SSD unproductive.
Observation 2: DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration.
Because most cache hits must be served from SSD (Observation
2.2
),
end-to-end prefill performance is governed by the SSD restoration path.
Although storage I/O accounts for 51–98% of TTFT
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
,
raw NVMe bandwidth is not the primary limit:
even when the SSD is emulated in DRAM at 16.9 GiB/s,
KV offloading achieves only 2.0 GiB/s
(
Ren et al., 2025
)
.
Instead, when SSD serves the bulk of hits, the tiered mechanisms meant to smooth SSD access
become the bottleneck itself.
First, staging SSD restores through host DRAM creates a concurrency bottleneck.
In a tiered hierarchy, restoring an SSD-resident prefix copies KV blocks from SSD
into host staging buffers before transferring them layer-by-layer to GPU HBM,
while background promotion separately populates the DRAM cache.

Takeaway.
Tiered storage falls into this trap because it is designed for mutable pages
whose future access patterns and spatial grouping are unknown when written.
In contrast, LLM KV cache blocks are
write-once, immutable,
and reused together at the granularity of a session scope
.
Because a block is never modified in place and its session-prefix grouping is known upon creation,
placing blocks directly onto their target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order at write time
makes SSD restores naturally sequential and eliminates the need for host DRAM caching or reassembly.

FC-GVA: Global Virtual Address Manager
In a tiered hierarchy, the storage layer does not need to decide a block’s long-term home at write time:
every block enters host DRAM first, and LRU eviction reactively pushes cold blocks to SSD.
However, as Observation
2.2
showed, this reactive filtering pollutes DRAM with one-shot blocks
and scrambles session prefixes on disk.
Eliminating cross-tier migration therefore raises
Q1
:
Without reactive LRU eviction, how can
FlatCake
permanently bind KV blocks to DRAM or SSD at creation time
and route accesses in

FC-GVA answers this question by exploiting two domain properties of LLM serving.
First, reuse scope is observable at request arrival:
whether a prefix belongs to a globally shared system prompt, a short-turn chat, or a multi-gigabyte agentic session
is known when the blocks are generated.
Second, flat storage exhibits
asymmetric misprediction cost
:
because both DRAM and SSD are directly accessible peer media and SSD scopes are laid out contiguously (§
3.4

placing a reusable block on SSD does not cause a cache miss or cross-tier migration storm;
it simply serves the hit via coalesced GDS at SSD bandwidth instead of DRAM bandwidth.

Session-Granularity SSD Reclamation.
Write-once scope placement also simplifies storage reclamation.
Because KV blocks are never modified in place, freeing SSD capacity requires zero dirty-block writeback.
FC-GVA tracks active readers per session scope with an atomic reference count;

4.
Implementation
We implement
FlatCake
in approximately 8.8K lines of C++17/CUDA and 7.1K lines of Python,
integrating it into SGLang
(
Zheng et al., 2024
)
behind the standard
HiCacheStorage
interface (
exists
,
get
,
put
)
without modifying model runner or attention kernels.
Pinned DRAM pool and hugepage allocation.
At engine initialization, the local DRAM backend pre-allocates the host KV pool using
mmap
with
MAP_POPULATE
and 2 MB hugepages (
MAP_HUGETLB
),
and registers the arena once with
cudaHostRegister
.
Pre-faulting and pinning hugepages at startup eliminates page-fault traps, TLB thrashing,
and per-transfer pinning overhead on the
cudaMemcpyAsync
path.
Pre-allocated NVMe file pool and GDS alignment.
To prevent filesystem metadata allocation and extent fragmentation on the write path,
FC-CIO pre-allocates a pool of fixed-size single-extent files on the XFS/RAID-0 array at startup using
fallocate
and opens each file with
O_DIRECT
and
cuFileHandleRegister
.
All logical block offsets within a GPU File and all GPU staging buffer slices are aligned to 4 KiB boundaries,
satisfying
libcufile
DMA alignment requirements and preventing driver-internal bounce buffering.
Double-buffered GPU staging and page scatter.
Because calling
cuFileBufRegister
dynamically on per-request GPU buffers incurs millisecond-scale
BAR1 and IOMMU mapping overhead, FC-CIO allocates and registers a fixed per-GPU HBM staging window once at initialization.
Restores pipeline GDS reads across two ping-pong layer buffers within this registered window;
as soon as a coalesced layer read completes on the I/O CUDA stream,
a lightweight CUDA scatter kernel copies each 256-token page from the contiguous staging buffer
into its non-contiguous destination slot in SGLang’s paged KV pool,
synchronizing with the model compute stream via
cudaEventRecord
and
cudaStreamWaitEvent
.
Lock-free Level-1 GVA index.
The Level 1 block-key-to-GVA index is implemented as a concurrent open-addressed hash table
using 64-bit atomic compare-and-swap (
CAS
) operations.
Because GVAs are immutable once published and session reclamation frees entire scopes asynchronously,
scheduler threads querying prefix hits execute wait-free reads without contending with background write-completion workers.

Why Tiered Storage Degrades: Delivered Cache Hit Rate.
Figure

Across all arrival rates,
FlatCake

staying within 0.6 percentage points of the trace’s 94.72% prefix-reuse ceiling.
In contrast, +L2 Host DRAM plateaus at 53.30% across all rates because multi-gigabyte agentic sessions
exceed host DRAM capacity (Observation

More importantly, while +L3 Mooncake achieves an 87.9% hit rate at low load (0.1 QPS),
its delivered hit rate drops to 64.26% at 0.5 QPS and above, recovering only 11 percentage points over DRAM-only caching

3.2

Because a tiered restore must stage an entire in-flight prefix in host DRAM buffers before H2D transfer completes,
concurrent long-context restores exhaust the engine’s bounded in-flight staging budget as QPS rises.
When staging memory saturates, SGLang revokes the blocked prefetch and falls back to recomputing the prefix on the GPU,
turning cached SSD blocks into expensive compute misses.
In contrast,
FlatCake
streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a fixed-size GPU HBM staging window (§
3.4

when the window is fully occupied under high load, incoming restores wait briefly on stream synchronization
rather than aborting prefetches, preserving a 94.16% hit rate at peak load.

6.
Related Work
Prior work has explored paged KV cache management
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Prabhu et al., 2025
)
,
prefix caching
(
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Qin et al., 2025
)
, KV compression
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
,
and prefill-decode disaggregation
(
Patel et al., 2024
)
.
We focus on KV cache placement, scheduling, and I/O across heterogeneous storage media.
Tiered KV Cache Storage and Offloading.
Existing LLM serving systems extend HBM capacity by offloading KV blocks to host DRAM and NVMe SSD
through a tiered hierarchy
(
Sheng et al., 2023
;
Zhao et al., 2024
;
Jeong and Ahn, 2025
;
Gao et al., 2024
;
Qin et al., 2025
;
Cheng and others, 2025
;
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
;
Jeong et al., 2025
)
,
building on general-purpose tiered memory designs
(
Abulila et al., 2019
;
Zhang et al., 2023
;
Jung et al., 2023
;
Shin et al., 2026
;
Ruan et al., 2020
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2023
;
Al Maruf et al., 2023
;
Xiang et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Weiner et al., 2022
;
Duraisamy et al., 2023
)
.
Recent studies characterize production KV reuse
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
and improve tiered hierarchies via workload-aware eviction (Bidaw
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
),
selective token or layer offloading
(
Chen et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2024
;
Zhong et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2021
)
,
joint compression and tier placement (AdaptCache
(
Feng et al., 2025
)
),
or SSD-aware tier coordination (SolidAttention
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, KVDrive
(
Lin et al., 2026
)
).
Despite these optimizations, all of these systems retain a migratory hierarchy in which blocks enter host DRAM first
and reach SSD through incremental eviction or demotion.
In contrast,
FlatCake
exploits the write-once, session-scoped immutability of KV blocks
to bind each block directly to DRAM or SSD at creation time (FC-GVA) and never migrate it thereafter.
Direct Storage I/O and Request Scheduling.
Several systems accelerate the SSD-to-GPU read path using GPUDirect Storage
(
Bergman et al., 2017
;
Bae et al., 2021
;
Qureshi et al., 2023
;
Qiu et al., 2025b
;
Li et al., 2025
)
,
pre-registered GPU buffers with parallel disk workers (LMCache
(
Cheng and others, 2025
)
),
GPU-initiated
io_uring
queues (Tutti
(
Qiu et al., 2025a
)
),
or storage-near execution
(
Pan et al., 2025
;
Luo and Shen, 2026
)
.
However, optimizing the transport primitive alone does not resolve on-disk fragmentation:
when SSD space is populated in LRU eviction order, a session’s prefix remains scattered across non-contiguous LBAs,
preventing NVMe controllers from coalescing reads into single DMA transfers (Observation
2.2
).
FlatCake
co-designs write-time layer-major scope layout within pre-allocated
GPU File
s
and read-time sort-merge coalescing (FC-CIO) so that standard GDS transfers read sequential per-layer extents.
Furthermore, unlike device-level I/O schedulers
(
Woo et al., 2021
)
,
FC-MAS uses the media identity encoded in each 64-bit GVA to decouple DRAM-ready and SSD-preparing queues
while preserving arrival-order fairness across media.
7.
Conclusion
We presented
FlatCake
, a flat KV storage architecture that replaces the migratory DRAM–SSD hierarchy
with peer storage media behind a unified 64-bit address space.
Exploiting the insight that LLM KV cache blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope,
FlatCake
combines FC-GVA, FC-MAS, and FC-CIO to eliminate cross-tier migration and host staging contention.
On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
FlatCake
sustains a 94% delivered cache hit rate under load,
eliminates Mooncake’s
6.5
×
6.5\times
–
6.7
×
6.7\times
SSD read amplification,
and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by
1.6
×
1.6\times
while improving total token throughput by
1.6
×
1.6\times
.
Across 8K–128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B,
FlatCake
further reduces mean TTFT by up to
2.4
×
2.4\times
over Mooncake and
1.8
×
1.8\times
over Mooncake-GDS.

article.headline: FlatCake：DRAM 与 SSD 同级的 K
article.lede: FlatCake 用统一 64 位地址空间把主机 DRAM 与 NVMe SSD 并列为同级介质，KV 块创建即定址、终
article.problem: Mooncake、LMCache、SGLang HiCache 等系统把主机 DRAM 当作 SSD 之前的 L2 缓存与暂存层，依赖「时间过滤」和「暂存合并」两个前提。作者分析来自 Mooncake、Qwen 百炼与 Claude Code 的八条生产 trace 后发现，这两个前提同时失效：七条对话/API trace 中 53.2%–94.0% 的块只被访问一次，复用距离均值可达 2,550 个请求、P99 达 54,728；而 Claude Code 相反，83.4% 的块被复用、理想命中率 98.31%，但单请求平均 3,421 个块（218,922 token），单会话足迹达数十 GB。两种情形都让多数命中必须由 SSD 供给，而 DRAM 暂存缓冲的需求按 O(context×concurrency) 增长会在高负载下被耗尽，按驱逐顺序落盘又把会话前缀打散，迫使 O(layers×blocks) 次碎片化小读。
article.method: FlatCake 把 DRAM 与 SSD 作为统一 64 位 GVA 地址空间中的同级介质，利用 KV 块 write-once、不可变、按会话作用域整体复用的性质，在创建时按会话连续、layer-major 顺序直接写入目标介质，之后不再迁移。三个组件分工：FC-GVA 在写时把块绑定到介质并把介质、节点、偏移编码进 64 位地址，实现 O(1) 路由与零回写的会话粒度回收；FC-MAS 用 DRAM-ready 与 SSD-preparing 双队列隔离快慢请求，SSD 预取按 size-aware HRRN 排序、完成后按原始到达时间重新入队；FC-CIO 把写时布局与读时 sort-merge 合并结合，经 GDS 把每层连续区间流入双缓冲的有界 GPU HBM 窗口，与逐层计算重叠。系统实现在 SGLang 中，约 8.8K 行 C++/CUDA 与 7.1K 行 Python，不改模型 runner 与 attention kernel。
article.results: 在 Claude Code 生产 trace 与 DeepSeek-V4-Flash（8×B200）上，FlatCake 在 0.1–1.0 QPS 全程维持 94.16%–94.57% 的交付命中率，距 trace 的 94.72% 前缀复用上限不到 0.6 个百分点，而 Mooncake 从低负载 87.9% 跌到 0.5 QPS 以上的 64.26%。1.0 QPS 时平均 TTFT 为 7.57 s（Mooncake 为 12.24 s，1.6×；仅 DRAM 层为 17.51 s，2.3×），P50 TTFT 为 6.26 s（1.8×），总吞吐为 98.3K token/s（1.6×）。SSD 读带宽 5.03 GB/s，为 Mooncake 2.69 GB/s 的 1.9×；平均预取延迟 1.64 s，Mooncake 则从 3.16 s 升到 9.50 s（峰值高 5.8×）；读写放大方面消除 Mooncake 6.51×–6.72× 的 SSD 读放大。Llama-3.1-70B（TP4，4×A100，8K–128K 上下文）上平均 TTFT 比 Mooncake 低 1.5×–2.4×、比 Mooncake-GDS 最多低 1.8×；64K 时 Mooncake-GDS 为 6.60 s、FlatCake 为 3.74 s（1.8×），吞吐 8.6K 对 14.0K token/s。消融显示去掉 FC-MAS 后平均 TTFT 增加 10%–11%、P99 增加 27%。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把 KV 缓存存储的核心问题从「在层级间搬数据」改写为「在写入时决定数据放在哪里」，说明 write-once 的不可变语义足以支撑扁平化设计，对长上下文 agent 类负载的 SSD 回读路径尤其关键。
article.limitations: 评估主要建立在单条 Claude Code 生产 trace 与两个模型／两代 GPU 上，跨工作负载的普适性仍需更多 trace 验证。写时放置依赖 radix 引用计数、轮次、回复长度阈值 τ 与 L_agent 等引擎信号来预测复用作用域，这些阈值的选取依据与误判率论文未给出具体数字；一旦判错，块只会以 SSD 带宽而非 DRAM 带宽被服务，虽然论文称误判代价不对称，但未量化最坏情况。
article.figure_caption_zh: FlatCake 架构：(a) 控制路径由 FC-GVA 把块键映射为 64 位 GVA 并在写时确定介质，FC-MAS 分离 DRAM-ready 与 SSD-preparing 两条队列；(b) 数据路径上 DRAM 命中走 cudaMemcpyAsync，FC-CIO 经 GDS 把合并后的 SSD 读流入有界 GPU 暂存窗口。

figure.caption: architecture. (a)~Control path: maps block keys to 64-bit GVAs with write-once placement~( {182}), and separates DRAM-ready and SSD-preparing queues~( {183}). (b)~Data path: DRAM hits use {cudaMemcpyAsync}, while streams coalesced SSD reads via GDS~( {184}) into a bounded GPU staging window.

page_papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
page_papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

Abstract.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
Keywords:
Retrieval-augmented generation, multi-hop question answering, question decomposition
1.
Introduction
Figure 1.
Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on a 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). Top: the gold chain, which passes through two bridge entities the question never names. (a) HippoRAG 2, a graph-based method, finds the first bridge entity (Kevin Drew) but no passage about his band or Toronto. (b) LogicRAG, which plans its sub-questions in advance, searches for the city of “the performer” before finding the performer (dependency error). (c) IRCoT, which keeps all retrieved passages in its long prompt, has the whole chain there and even states that the band is based in Toronto, but then loses track of this fact (tracking error).
Large language models (LLMs) now perform strongly across a wide range of language tasks
(
OpenAI, 2023
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Yet because their knowledge is stored in their parameters, they often answer incorrectly when that knowledge is outdated or missing, and they may hallucinate
(
Huang et al., 2025
)
. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
(
Lewis et al., 2020
;
Gao et al., 2023
)
mitigates this by retrieving passages from an external corpus and grounding the answer in them, which improves accuracy on knowledge-intensive tasks without retraining the model.
A single retrieve-then-generate step suffices when one passage holds the answer, but it falls short on multi-hop question answering
(
Yang et al., 2018
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Trivedi et al., 2022
)
, where answering one question requires chaining several facts spread across different documents: retrieving with the question alone returns passages that match its surface terms, and these rarely cover every link of the chain. Graph-based RAG methods
(
Edge et al., 2024
;
Gutiérrez et al., 2024
;
Gutiérrez et al., 2025
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026a
;
Wu et al., 2026
)
address this by building a graph over the corpus that links entities and passages, then retrieving passages by following links from the entities in the question. However, a multi-hop chain runs through
bridge entities
that the question never names and that only become known once an earlier step is answered. Because most graph-based methods retrieve once per question, starting from the entities the question names, they can reach the bridge entities only by following graph links from those entities, which rarely gets past the first one: for most of these methods, the full evidence chain is retrieved for only 6–10% of 3-hop MuSiQue questions (Figure
1
a, Table
3
).
Iterative RAG methods
(
Trivedi et al., 2023
;
Press et al., 2023
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
instead aim to find these bridge entities directly: they decompose the question into sub-questions and alternate between retrieval and LLM reasoning, so each answered sub-question supplies the bridge entity needed by the next retrieval. However, their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, often within one call, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding the dependencies among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known, each of which leads to its own type of error. Specifically, a plan written before any sub-question is answered must guess bridge entities, and a wrong guess or a missing step misleads every later step (
planning errors
). The dependencies decided among the sub-questions may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so a sub-question is searched before the fact it needs is found (
dependency errors
), as in Figure
1
b. When an answer arrives, the LLM may fail to rewrite the sub-question that depends on it, which keeps a placeholder instead of the entity’s name, or may rewrite it with the wrong entity (
rewriting errors
). In a long, growing input, the LLM may also lose track of what it has already found (
tracking errors
), as in Figure
1
c. Moreover, fixed top-
k
k
retrieval, used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse by lowering the answer accuracy at each step. Finally, iterative methods discard their intermediate results once a question is answered, although multi-hop questions over the same corpus often share intermediate facts that could be reused.
Based on these observations, we propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs), until these accumulated QA pairs are enough to answer the original question. Each sub-question names every entity it asks about and does not depend on the answer to any other sub-question. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, and there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite. This avoids planning, dependency and rewriting errors, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: writing a sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Second, DeFT-RAG converts the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM. A QA table keeps every QA pair and is updated by rules, without any model call, so the LLM no longer has to keep track of what is known, which avoids tracking errors. A fine-tuned lightweight decision model (DM), a language model trained to answer yes/no questions with a probability
(
StartLux Labs, 2026
)
, makes a few yes/no decisions: whether a question can be answered directly, whether the QA pairs found so far are enough, and whether retrieved passages are relevant, so that the LLM sees more of the needed passages and fewer distracting ones. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls. Together, these designs raise the accuracy of each step and of the final answer, while making the intermediate answers reusable across questions. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We propose an incremental question decomposition that generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the QA pairs found so far. It removes the need to plan sub-questions, decide their dependencies or rewrite them, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task: writing the sub-question for the next missing piece of information.
•
We convert the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table, and yes/no decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight DM, such as whether retrieved passages are relevant. This aims to raise the accuracy of each step, and to leave the LLM only a few focused, fine-grained tasks that require text generation.
•
We design a QA cache that reuses the answers to earlier sub-questions for later questions that ask a sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls.
•
We evaluate DeFT-RAG on three multi-hop QA benchmarks with two LLM backbones. It achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method, and reusing answers through the QA cache further reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy. To support reproducibility, we release our code and prompts at
https://github.com/
Dingyi-Kang/DeFT-RAG
.

This section introduces RAG and multi-hop question answering, and the limitations of existing methods on such questions; Section
5
discusses related work in more detail.

2.2.
Multi-Hop Question Answering
A multi-hop question usually cannot be answered from a single passage
(

;

;

)
. Answering it requires an
evidence chain
of two or more facts, each stated in a passage of

For example, to answer “Where do greyhound buses leave from in the city where the performer of Darlings formed?”, one must first find that Darlings is an album by Kevin Drew, then that he formed his band, Broken Social Scene, in Toronto, and only then where Greyhound buses leave from there (the Toronto Coach Terminal). Kevin Drew and Toronto are the bridge entities (top of Figure

Vanilla RAG (Eq. (

2.3

2.4

2.3.
Graph-Based RAG

However, graph-based RAG still falls short in covering the full evidence chain once a question needs more than two hops: on MuSiQue, most graph-based methods retrieve the full chain for only 6–10% of 3-hop questions, barely above vanilla RAG (Table

alone would miss. As shown in Table
3
, iterative methods retrieve the full evidence chain for 19–41% of 3-hop questions, well above most graph-based methods.
However, iterative methods often fail, because they ask the LLM to perform several tasks, often within one call: planning sub-questions before any of them is answered, deciding the dependency links among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. Each of these tasks leads to its own type of error. First,
planning errors
: methods that plan the sub-questions in advance, such as LogicRAG
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
and REAP
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
, must guess bridge entities before finding them, and a wrong guess or a missing step misleads every later step. For example, asked “Who is the owner of the record label of the guitarist who performed on the Top Gun theme?”, LogicRAG’s plan asks for the label of the theme’s composer instead of first finding the guitarist, so it answers with the owner of the wrong label. Second,
dependency errors
: methods that link the sub-questions by their dependencies, such as LogicRAG and REAP, may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so a sub-question is searched before the fact it depends on is found. In Figure
1
b, LogicRAG searches for the city where “the performer” formed before it has found the performer, retrieves passages about bands from other cities, and never searches for the performer at all.
Third,
rewriting errors
: when the answer to a sub-question arrives, methods such as Hi-Q
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
and REAP must rewrite the sub-question that depends on it. The LLM may fail to do so, and the sub-question keeps a placeholder instead of the entity’s name, so retrieval often cannot find the passages about this bridge entity; or it may rewrite the sub-question with the wrong entity. Fourth,
tracking errors
: methods that carry their whole reasoning history in the prompt, such as IRCoT
(
Trivedi et al., 2023
)
and Self-Ask
(
Press et al., 2023
)
, must find what is already known within a long and growing input, and may miss a fact they have already found or ask for it again. In Figure
1
c, IRCoT’s input holds all three gold passages, and its reasoning states that the band is based in Toronto, yet it then follows a passage about Greyhound in Philadelphia and answers with the Philadelphia terminal.
Moreover, fixed top-
k
k
retrieval (Eq. (
2
)), used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse, because it lowers the answer accuracy of every step. With a small
k
k
, part of the needed evidence is missed; with a large
k
k
, the evidence is buried among distracting passages. Table
1
illustrates this on MuSiQue questions that can be answered in one retrieval step: widening the list from the top 5 to the top 10 passages raises how often all needed passages are present from 62% to 88%, yet accuracy barely changes (0.620 to 0.630); keeping only the gold passages from the top 10 raises it to 0.793. 2Wiki shows the same pattern. Since iterative methods answer several sub-questions in sequence, and each step depends on the answers before it, these errors add up across steps and greatly increase the chance that the whole process fails.

DeFT-RAG is built on three components (Figure

3.1

For example, once the QA table shows that the Rhine ends in the North Sea, “Where does the North Sea meet the Atlantic?” is self-contained, while “Where does that sea meet the Atlantic?” is not, because “that sea” points to an earlier step. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, which avoids the planning errors of §
2.4
. Since no sub-question depends on another, there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite, which avoids dependency and rewriting errors. More importantly, the LLM can focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: writing a sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Together, these improve the quality of the question decomposition and help DeFT-RAG find every bridge entity of the evidence chain: it retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any other system in Table
3
.

3.4.

Because a self-contained sub-question names everything it asks about, it has the same meaning, and the same answer, whichever original question it was written for. For example, “In which city is the headquarters of Sazerac Company located?” has the answer “New Orleans” whether it arises from a question about Barton Premium Blend or about Blanton’s, two whiskey brands made by that company. Fine-Tuning the Decision Model
The DM starts from the StartLux-Decision-4B weights
(
StartLux Labs, 2026
)
(Qwen3.5 architecture, 4B parameters), which were trained to answer yes/no and multiple-choice questions with probabilities that reflect how often the answer is right. We fine-tune it on data built only from the
training

To make the training inputs look like the test inputs, we split the training questions into groups of 1,000, and each group retrieves from a corpus made of its own passages, just as each test set retrieves from its own corpus. The labels come from the benchmarks’ gold annotations: a passage is relevant if it is a gold supporting passage; a question can be answered directly if all its supporting passages are retrieved; and the QA pairs found so far are enough once they include the answer to every step of the question’s gold decomposition (MuSiQue) or gold evidence (2Wiki). No test question or test-corpus passage appears in the training data, which has 48,036 training and 7,806 development examples (the latter from 15% of the training questions, held out from training). Related Work
Graph-based RAG.
Graph-based methods build a graph over the corpus offline and retrieve along it at answering time. GraphRAG
(
Edge et al., 2024
)
and LightRAG
(
Guo et al., 2025
)
extract entities and relations with an LLM and retrieve community summaries or entities, PathRAG
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
retrieves relational paths, HippoRAG
(
Gutiérrez et al., 2024
)
and HippoRAG 2
(
Gutiérrez et al., 2025
)
rank passages with Personalized PageRank from the question’s entities, MemGraphRAG
(
Wu et al., 2026
)
builds a layered graph of schemas, facts and passages, and LinearRAG
(
Zhuang et al., 2026
)
and G3RAG
(
Li et al., 2026
)
build their graphs without LLM extraction. All of these methods retrieve once per question, starting from what the question names, which rarely recovers the full evidence chain beyond two hops (§
2.3
). DeFT-RAG instead finds the bridge entities at answering time, one self-contained sub-question at a time, and retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any of these methods (Table
3
).
Iterative RAG.
IRCoT
(
Trivedi et al., 2023
)
uses each new chain-of-thought sentence as the next query, and Self-Ask
(
Press et al., 2023
)
poses follow-up questions within a single growing prompt. LogicRAG
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
and REAP
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
plan the sub-questions with their dependencies in advance, and Hi-Q
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
and REAP rewrite dependent sub-questions as answers arrive. In these methods, the LLM itself takes on several tasks, often within the same call: planning or writing the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them, keeping track of what is known, and deciding when to stop. DeFT-RAG instead lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: generating one self-contained sub-question for the next missing piece of information, which removes planning, dependencies and rewriting, and avoids their associated errors; tracking is handled by the QA table, and the yes/no decisions by the fine-tuned DM. Its LLM input stays short, 1,569 tokens per question against 6,140 for Self-Ask (Appendix
E
), and it achieves the highest accuracy of these methods in every setting (Table
2
).
Models for retrieval decisions.
Rerankers
(
Nogueira et al., 2020
;
Sun et al., 2023
)
re-score retrieved passages but still keep a fixed number, and Adaptive-RAG
(
Jeong et al., 2024
)
uses a trained classifier to choose between no, single and iterative retrieval; Self-RAG
(
Asai et al., 2024
)
, Search-R1
(
Jin et al., 2025
)
, R1-Searcher
(
Song et al., 2025
)
and Search-o1
(
Li et al., 2025
)
instead train the backbone LLM, or use a reasoning model, to make such decisions. DeFT-RAG uses one fine-tuned DM for the yes/no decisions at every step while the backbone stays unchanged, so any LLM can serve as the backbone, and fine-tuning the DM is much cheaper than training the backbone LLM.
6.
Conclusion
We presented DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework for multi-hop question answering built on three components: incremental decomposition into self-contained sub-questions, which avoids planning, dependency and rewriting errors; fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM, namely rule-based updates to a QA table and yes/no decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight DM; and a QA cache that reuses answers across questions. Across three benchmarks and two backbones, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines, with its largest gains on MuSiQue, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method; reusing answers reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy.

A question is answered directly only when the DM judges its passages sufficient (

How the thresholds were chosen.
The thresholds of 0.5 are the natural cut-off for yes/no probabilities that reflect how often yes is right, and were not tuned. The direct-answer threshold of 0.7 was chosen during development on stored answers of part of the test questions (2Wiki and the first 300 MuSiQue questions), and then kept fixed for all benchmarks and both backbones. The result depends little on this choice: moving the threshold to 0.6 or 0.8 changes the path of at most 13 of the 1,000 questions per benchmark and accuracy by at most 0.1 points on every benchmark (gpt-4o-mini). The reuse threshold of 0.8 was set strict by hand, because a wrongly reused answer carries an error into another question.

Appendix C
Decision Model Fine-Tuning Details
Training questions and corpora.
For each benchmark, we sample 3,000 questions from its training split, following the mix of hop counts or question types of the test set, and split them into groups of 1,000. Each group’s corpus consists of the passages of its own questions (MuSiQue about 13,000, 2Wiki about 5,200, HotpotQA about 9,600 passages per group, close to the test corpora of 11,656, 6,119 and 9,811). Every training request retrieves its top 10 passages from its group’s corpus with the embedder and query instruction of DeFT-RAG.
Labels.
All labels come from the training splits’ gold annotations.
Relevance
: a passage is relevant if it is a gold supporting passage; each request labels all gold passages and three randomly chosen other passages, while all ten passages stay in the request.
Direct answer
: yes if all gold supporting passages are among the top 10.
Enough facts
: built from the gold decompositions (MuSiQue) and gold evidence (2Wiki): the answers to only the first steps give “no”, the answers to all steps give “yes”, a wrong answer to a step gives “no”, and the answers to all steps plus an unrelated QA pair give “yes”. We add enough-facts items taken from runs of DeFT-RAG on training questions, labelled by the same rule, and items whose QA pairs use self-contained sub-questions, as DeFT-RAG writes them. The same-meaning decision is not fine-tuned.
Leakage checks.
All 1,000 test questions of each benchmark come from its official validation split; none of them is in the training data, and no training question text is identical to a test question. Training questions whose gold passage appears in any test corpus are skipped, so that no test-corpus passage is ever shown in training.
Training and probability adjustment.
The final data has 48,036 training and 7,806 development examples. LoRA settings are given in §
4.2
; training used micro-batches of 8,192 tokens, gradient accumulation to an effective batch equal to the base model’s single-GPU default, gradient checkpointing and gradient clipping at 1.0. A single temperature for yes/no probabilities is fitted on the development examples (1.08).

All systems use the same backbone, the same embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-4B, last-token pooling, with the query instruction applied to queries only), temperature 0,

Index.
DeFT-RAG, vanilla RAG and the iterative methods only embed the passages, which takes about five minutes per corpus and no LLM calls. The graph-based methods that extract a graph with the LLM need from about 2,100 (LightRAG) to 147,000 (MemGraphRAG) LLM calls and 11 to 114 million tokens per corpus, and up to 18 hours of build time; this cost is paid again when the corpus changes.
Answering.
DeFT-RAG gives the LLM fewer input tokens per question than every other iterative method (1,569, against 1,926 to 13,928), and it produces the fewest output tokens of all methods (33), because each task asks for a short output; it also makes fewer LLM calls than Self-Ask and Hi-Q (4.8, against 6.3 and 6.6). Its latency is the highest (median 9.9 s).
Where the latency comes from.
Most of the answering time of DeFT-RAG goes to its frequent calls to the local DM, which selects the relevant passages at every step and makes the other decisions. Per question, DeFT-RAG makes 7.0, 6.3 and 3.2 DM calls on MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA, at 1.6 to 1.8 s each, as the DM runs on one GPU, one request at a time, over inputs of up to ten passages. These calls take 12.5 of the 20.4 s mean answering time on MuSiQue, 10.3 of 16.7 s on 2Wiki and 5.2 of 7.8 s on HotpotQA, about 60 to 70%. With Jev in place of the DM, at about 0.16 s per call, the median latency falls from 9.9 to 5.0 s, and the mean answering time to 8.2, 7.7 and 3.6 s on the three benchmarks, while accuracy stays within 1.2 points of the DM’s (0.618, 0.857 and 0.867, against 0.629, 0.852 and 0.874). Most of the added latency thus comes from how the DM is served, not from the method itself.

The third sub-question is not self-contained: it asks for the birth date of a director who has not been named yet, and retrieval finds no answer. DeFT-RAG recovers in the next two steps, but the DM does not judge the four QA pairs enough, the loop reaches its step limit, and the fallback answers “Airheads”. On 2Wiki bridge-comparison questions, 38% of such nested sub-questions get no answer, against 4% of sub-questions that ask for a single relation, and 75 of 235 of these questions reach the step limit or repeat themselves; this is the main reason DeFT-RAG only matches Self-Ask on 2Wiki with gpt-4o-mini (Table

Where it fails: the right entity, the wrong fact.

DeFT-RAG first finds the right person (“Diego Maradona”), so it does not shift back to Messi; but it then asks for Maradona’s date of birth instead of the date he was signed, the DM accepts these QA pairs as enough, and the final answer (“30 October 1984”) is wrong. On 2Wiki with gpt-4o-mini, an analysis of the 148 wrong answers attributed only about 19 to the DM’s decisions; most of the others come from the backbone, such as nested sub-questions or wrong readings of correct passages.

article.headline: 多跳问答拆成自包含子问题并复用答案
article.lede: DeFT-RAG 让大模型每次只生成一个自包含子问题，把是非判断交给微调小模型，在三个多跳基准上胜过 13 个基线。
article.problem: 多跳问题的证据链要经过问题从未提及的桥接实体，图式 RAG 只从问题点名的实体检索一次，在 MuSiQue 三跳题上多数方法只有 6–10% 能取全证据链。迭代式 RAG 逐步检索，却把规划子问题、判定依赖、改写子问题和记录已知事实都压给大模型，导致规划、依赖、改写和跟踪四类错误沿步骤累积。
article.method: 作者提出 DeFT-RAG：每一步只根据原问题和已得到的问答对生成一个自包含子问题，子问题必须点名它要问的每个实体，因此无需预先规划、无需处理依赖、也无需改写。记录工作改由规则更新的 QA 表承担，相关性、能否直接作答、事实是否足够这三类判断交给用 LoRA 微调的 4B 决策模型。系统还把问答对存入 QA 缓存，后续问题若问到同义子问题就直接复用答案，省去检索与大模型调用。
article.results: 在 MuSiQue、2WikiMultiHopQA、HotpotQA 各 1000 题、gpt-4o-mini 与 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 两个骨干下，DeFT-RAG 在三项指标上均列第一。MuSiQue 准确率 0.629（gpt-4o-mini，比次优 Hi-Q 的 0.577 高 5.2 点）、0.636（Qwen3.6，比 0.583 高 5.3 点）；2Wiki 上为 0.852（与 Self-Ask 的 0.849 持平）和 0.867（比 LogicRAG 的 0.838 高 2.9 点）；HotpotQA 上为 0.874 和 0.871。三基准平均准确率 0.785 与 0.791。证据覆盖上，MuSiQue 三跳题有 46%、四跳题有 18% 拿到完整证据链，同时每题只给大模型 390 词段落，少于 vanilla RAG 的 870 词；每题输入 1569 token，低于 Self-Ask 的 6140。在 1000 道 MuSiQue 题共享 QA 缓存时，23.1% 的子问题由缓存作答，LLM 调用减少 12.9%，准确率 0.642 对 0.629（p=0.18）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“让大模型少干杂活”落到具体设计：生成、判断、记录三者分离，缓存又让同一语料上的中间答案可跨题复用，为多跳 RAG 提供了一条不依赖图索引预构建、且能换任意骨干模型的路线。
article.limitations: 代价是延迟：由于每一步都要调用本地决策模型，中位时延达 9.9 秒，为所有方法中最高，决策模型调用占答题时间约 60–70%。方法在需要嵌套子问题的 2Wiki 桥接比较题上明显吃力（这类嵌套子问题 38% 得不到答案，235 题中有 75 题触到步数上限），因此在 2Wiki 上只与 Self-Ask 持平；缓存复用只在 MuSiQue 上做了评测，决策模型的训练也依赖各基准训练集的黄金标注。
article.figure_caption_zh: DeFT-RAG 在示例三跳题上的流程：大模型只做三项细粒度文本任务（蓝色），所有是非判断由微调决策模型完成（橙色），QA 表由规则更新，第一个子问题因命中 QA 缓存而直接复用答案。

figure.caption: Overview of {} on the question of Figure~ {fig:motivation}. The LLM performs only three fine-grained tasks (blue), and a fine-tuned DM makes every yes/no decision (orange). The QA table, updated by rules, holds the QA pairs found for the question; the QA cache holds those found for other questions. The first sub-question was answered for an earlier question, so its answer is reused from the QA cache (marked ``cached'') without retrieval or an LLM call. Abstract
Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control.

Introduction
Table 1:
Comparison with representative human and humanoid motion datasets.

“Scenes” counts coarse environments.
“Constraints” and “Policies” count physical-constraint and control-policy families used in curation and execution verification, with real-world collection counted as one constraint setting.
“Agg.” denotes aggregation.
“–” marks unavailable and inapplicable entries.

The resulting dataset contains more than
10,000 hours
and
5 million physically executable humanoid motion sequences
, paired with corresponding human motions and aligned text, RGB video, speech, and music.

Humanoid Motion Generation and Control
A prevalent approach to semantic humanoid control follows a generator–tracker paradigm: a high-level model generates reference motions, which are executed by a low-level tracking policy.
OMG supports language, audio, and human-motion conditions; TextOp generates short-horizon motions from streaming text; and UniAct converts multimodal commands into motion tokens for whole-body tracking
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Xie et al., 2026
;
Jiang et al., 2025
)
.
Other methods directly couple semantic commands with robot actions or control-oriented motion representations
(
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Li et al., 2025b
)
.
Movens-Zero
retains the interpretable generator–tracker structure while learning its shared motion prior from diverse, execution-verified data; the latest robot state conditions online generation before low-level tracking.
2.2

Method

Experiments
We organize the experiments around three questions:
(1)

Experimental Setup
Benchmarks.
We evaluate on the public OMG benchmark, the EMDB and RICH datasets, and the source-disjoint
Movens-Intent
benchmark.
For OMG, we use the text- and audio-conditioned tracks from the released benchmark manifests
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
, containing 1,024 text-conditioned and 512 audio-conditioned test samples.
Each sample contains 60 future frames at 30 FPS, corresponding to a two-second prediction horizon.
For direct comparison, we retain OMG’s metric definitions and published baseline results, and evaluate
Movens-Zero
with the same manifest, evaluator, and HoloMotion execution path.
To prevent contamination, all source identities and near-duplicate motions associated with the OMG test manifests are excluded from
Movens-Zero
training data.
For video-conditioned evaluation, we follow the camera- and world-space protocols of GVHMR
(
Shen et al., 2024
)
on EMDB
(
Kaufmann et al., 2023
)
and RICH
(
Huang et al., 2022
)
.
Camera-space evaluation uses RICH and EMDB-1, while world-space evaluation uses RICH and EMDB-2.
For
Movens-Zero
, we retarget the predicted G1 motions back to SMPL and compare them with the native SMPL ground truth. We exclude all benchmark videos and near duplicates from training data.

Method

As shown in Table
3
,
Movens-Zero
achieves the best result on 12 of the 14 metrics of the OMG benchmark, demonstrating that unified intent understanding and motion generation can jointly preserve semantic alignment, motion quality, and physical executability. Relative to the strongest baseline for each metric, FID decreases from 24.68 to 10.13, a 59.0% reduction, while R@3 increases from 57.71% to 85.06%, a gain of 27.35 percentage points. MPJPE and g-MPJPE decrease by 2.5% and 11.8%, the fall rate reaches 0.29%, and J-Limit decreases from the best baseline value of 19.14% to 10.45%. These results show that the advantage of
Movens-Zero
extends beyond text–motion matching to tracking accuracy and execution stability after embodiment mapping.
On the source-disjoint
Movens-Intent
benchmark,
Movens-Zero
achieves the best or tied-best result on 10 of the 14 metrics. Its FID decreases from the strongest baseline value of 30.19 to 17.65, a 41.5% reduction. R@1, R@2, and R@3 reach 34.83%, 51.88%, and 62.57%, with R@3 exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.70 percentage points. C-Slide reaches 0.69, the second-best result. MPJPE decreases from the best baseline value of 35.26 to 33.40, a 5.3% reduction, while g-MPJPE decreases from 89.94 to 89.15, a 0.9% reduction. The fall rate is 0.00%, tied for the best result. Overall, these results characterize cross-source generalization in text alignment, motion fidelity, and robot execution stability.

, and values for the remaining smaller-data results. Expanding the training set from 10% to 100% increases Text R@3 from 6.34% to 10.30% for S (62.5% relative improvement). For XL, Text R@3 increases from 24.92% to 62.57% (151.1%). The corresponding reductions in validation FM loss are 23.3% and 55.2% for S and XL, respectively. For XL, the same data expansion reduces Video MPJPE from 110.55 to 40.90 mm (63.0%) and increases Audio BeatAlign from 0.38 to 0.61 (60.5%) and Tracking Score from 0.36 to 0.72 (100.0%). Speech R@3 for XL increases from 21.76% to 74.30%, a gain of 52.54 percentage points (241.5% relative improvement). At a fixed data fraction, scaling from S to XL increases Text R@3 by 18.58 percentage points with 10% data, compared with 52.27 percentage points with the full dataset. Across all six metrics in Figure
9
(g), the relative improvements from 10% to 100% training data increase with action-expert capacity. For example, Speech R@3 improves by 96.5% for S versus 241.5% for XL, while Tracking Score improves by 46.3% and 100.0%, respectively. These comparisons suggest that larger action experts can benefit more from additional training data, highlighting the complementary gains from scaling data and model capacity.
Figure 9:
Joint data–model scaling. (a–f) Six metrics versus action-expert size for five training-data fractions. (g) Relative improvements from 10% to 100% training data at each fixed model size, normalized by the corresponding 10% value. Reductions in FM loss and MPJPE, and increases in the other scores, are positive.
Data curation and verification.
To separate the effects of quality and quantity, we construct size-matched training subsets from successive stages of the
Movens-5M
pipeline. All variants contain the same number of motion sequences and use the same optimization-token budget. The upper block of Table
9
follows a cumulative setup. Visual and human-motion filtering first removes clips with missing subjects, temporal anomalies, near-static content, or unreliable motion recovery. Closed-loop physical refinement then repairs local artifacts such as contact errors, jitter, self-intersection, and foot sliding, while converting human motion into reference trajectories that satisfy robot embodiment and joint constraints. Tracking verification subsequently rejects candidate motions that cannot be executed stably under a common closed-loop simulation criterion. Finally, distribution balancing prevents frequent motions and scenes from dominating training, allowing a fixed sample budget to cover more long-tail behaviors. Because each row includes all preceding stages, this experiment measures the marginal change produced by adding each stage rather than independent single-factor effects. Specific gating rules are listed in Appendix Table
10
. Human-motion inspection and repair, as well as motion retargeting and execution verification, are detailed in Appendices
A.2
and
A.3
, respectively.
Modality-aligned training.
We further use leave-one-modality-out ablations that remove text–motion, video–motion, or audio–motion alignment training. Audio alignment includes both music-conditioned and speech-conditioned generation. Each variant masks only the corresponding condition, while the original motion samples continue to participate in training through the remaining tasks. The action-expert size, optimization steps, and token budget are held fixed. The lower block of Table
9
reports generation metrics for the modalities retained during alignment training, together with Tracking Score. Condition-specific metrics for the excluded modality are not reported in this ablation. The complete seven-task mixture and input forms are provided in Appendix Table
13
, while aligned motion chunks and condition processing are detailed in Appendix
D
. These controlled comparisons examine how joint alignment affects generation under the remaining conditioning modalities, although a single leave-one-out experiment is insufficient to attribute cross-metric changes to one independent mechanism.

Ablations of data curation and modality-aligned training on the
Movens-Intent
benchmark.

Conclusion
In this work, we introduce
Movens-5M
, a large-scale omni-modal humanoid motion dataset constructed from Internet videos.
Movens-5M
employs an automatic data pipeline to convert diverse human videos into multimodally annotated, physically refined, and executable humanoid motions.

Experiments on public benchmarks and
Movens-Intent
demonstrate that
Movens-Zero
jointly maintains intent alignment, motion fidelity, and stable robot execution under text, video, speech, and music conditions. Data- and model-scaling experiments further show consistent performance improvements as non-duplicated training-data coverage and action-expert capacity increase.
Further analyses highlight the importance of data diversity and physical executability for effective scaling.
In future work, we plan to extend the Movens data and model family to richer human–object interactions, additional humanoid embodiments, and broader real-world applications.

article.headline: Movens-5M：万小时可执行人形动作数据
article.lede: 作者发布超1万小时、500万条可执行人形动作序列的Movens-5M数据集，并训练Movens-Zero。
article.problem: 人形动作基础模型的扩展受限于多样且机器人可执行的数据稀缺，同时难以从异构多模态输入中联合学习并支持实时闭环控制。现有生成器–跟踪器方案常把语义生成与底层执行分开验证，缺少统一的数据与模型尺度实验。
article.method: 作者用自动流水线从互联网视频构建Movens-5M：超1万小时、500万条物理可执行的人形动作序列，配有对应人体动作及对齐文本、RGB视频、语音和音乐。数据经视觉/人体动作过滤、闭环物理精修、跟踪验证和分布平衡。Movens-Zero保留生成器–跟踪器结构，从执行验证数据中学习共享动作先验，并以最新机器人状态条件化在线生成，再交给底层跟踪。
article.results: 在OMG基准上，Movens-Zero在14项指标中12项最优：FID从24.68降至10.13（降59.0%），R@3从57.71%升至85.06%（增27.35个百分点），MPJPE和g-MPJPE分别降2.5%和11.8%，跌倒率0.29%，J-Limit从19.14%降至10.45%。在源分离的Movens-Intent文本条件下，14项指标中10项最优或并列最优：FID从30.19降至17.65（降41.5%），R@3为62.57%，比最强基线高0.70个百分点，MPJPE从35.26降至33.40（降5.3%），g-MPJPE从89.94降至89.15（降0.9%），跌倒率0.00%。音乐条件下，Movens-Zero在12项中9项最优或并列最优：BeatAlign 0.60（基线0.59），FID-k和FID-g为53.44和2.31，分别改善33.6%和13.2%，跌倒率0.00%，但J-Limit为15.32%，最佳基线为2.05%。语音条件下，14项中10项最优：FID从30.66降至23.15（降24.5%），R@3为74.30%，比最强基线62.40%高11.90个百分点，MPJPE和g-MPJPE从34.83和89.82降至32.63和76.38（降6.3%和15.0%），跌倒率0.00%，但C-Slide 0.75、J-Limit 4.93%，最佳基线分别为0.40和2.00%。数据–模型扩展实验显示，XL规模下训练数据从10%增至100%，Text R@3从24.92%升至62.57%（相对提升151.1%），Speech R@3从21.76%升至74.30%（相对提升241.5%），Video MPJPE从110.55降至40.90 mm（降63.0%）。
article.why_it_matters: 如果互联网视频能稳定转化为可执行人形动作，数据瓶颈有望从真实机器人采集转向自动流水线与物理验证。该工作还显示数据规模与动作专家容量存在互补增益，为后续多模态人形基础模型提供可复现的扩展路径。
article.limitations: 音频条件下J-Limit为15.32%，远高于最佳基线2.05%；语音条件下C-Slide为0.75、J-Limit为4.93%，仍逊于最佳基线0.40和2.00%，说明关节限位与接触一致性仍是短板。作者也指出，留一模态消融不足以把跨指标变化归因于单一机制，数据流水线为累积实验，难以分离各阶段独立贡献。

journals.title: Chinese PhD students in clinical medicine can graduate without a thesis — more degrees to follow
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03480-7

This expands the country's ‘practical PhD’ programme beyond engineering students.
journals.blurb: 《自然》报道，中国临床医学博士生可在不提交学位论文的情况下毕业，并将“实践型博士”项目从工程类学生扩展到更多学位。该报道称更多学位将跟进。对机器学习研究生而言，这反映出博士培养评价可能更强调实践成果，但报道未给出机器学习领域的具体数字。

journals.title: Author Correction: mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11350-5

Author Correction: mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis
journals.blurb: 《Nature》于2026年11月2日在线发布了一则作者更正，涉及论文“mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis”。该更正针对mTORC1在结节性硬化症中驱动细胞自主性星形胶质细胞反应性的原始研究，提醒读者在引用或复现相关结论时核对更新版本。对机器学习研究生而言，这类更正提示在构建文献数据集或复现流程前应检查论文的勘误状态。
